result.question: 兩級(local-small → cloud-large)自主 agent 架構的可行性與反駁證據,約束在一台已在跑其他負載的 NVIDIA T4 16GB(g4dn.xlarge, 4 vCPU, Turing SM75, 無 bf16 / 無 FP8)上,服務一個語音對話 + ROS 2 機器人迴路。需對抗式驗證:(1) 路由/升級決策是否本身即未解問題(router 準確率、誤升/漏升率、小模型信心校準、cascade 端到端品質是否低於直接用大模型);(2) Qwen3 在 T4 僅 9–11 GB 餘量上的第三方實測 TTFT / tokens-per-second 能否低於現有 Bedrock Sonnet-5 首 token p50 = 900 ms,含 SM75 對 FlashAttention-2 / Marlin / AWQ / GPTQ 的支援與與既有 TensorRT 進程共存;(3) ≤14B 開放權重小模型的 function-calling 與多步 agent 可靠性(BFCL v3/v4、τ-bench)及中文/粵語是否隨尺寸崩塌得比英文快;(4) 具身機器人上「自主」的風險、agent loop 外部確定性檢查器的必要性(驗證 0.4% vs 28.3%、37.6%→56.9% 這組數字)、兩級架構新增的攻擊面、EU AI Act Art 50 合成音訊標記責任歸屬;(5) 至少兩個替代設計(單一雲端模型 + reasoning-effort 旋鈕、小模型降級為分類器/檢索器、推測解碼)在同一 T4 約束下的延遲/顯存/成本比較。
result.summary: Map each of the five stated axes to the single most falsifiable, number-bearing literature it depends on, and phrase every query to surface adversarial evidence (reproduction failures, regressions, unsupported-kernel errors) rather than vendor claims. The load-bearing comparisons are: router/calibration error rates against the cascade premise, third-party Turing measurements against the measured 900 ms baseline, and alternative-design cost/latency curves against the two-tier design itself.

angles.label: routing / cascade / deferral + small-model calibration (primary contradiction)
angles.query: LLM cascade router accuracy 2025 2026 deferral abstention small model confidence calibration overconfidence logprob vs self-consistency vs verbalized confidence RouteLLM FrugalGPT critique reproduction failure cascade end-to-end quality worse than large model
angles.rationale: Directly attacks the hidden premise that a cheap, reliable "I don't know" detector exists: router accuracy, false-escalate vs false-keep rates, quantified small-model overconfidence, and explicit negative/critical follow-ups to RouteLLM/FrugalGPT.

angles.label: T4 / Turing inference reality check (third-party measured TTFT and tok/s)
angles.query: Qwen3 4B 8B 14B 30B-A3B NVIDIA T4 Turing sm75 benchmark tokens per second time to first token vLLM SGLang llama.cpp FlashAttention requires Ampere bf16 unsupported AWQ GPTQ Marlin kernel Turing compatibility 16GB VRAM
angles.rationale: Produces the hard SM75 kernel-support matrix (no FA2/bf16/FP8; whether Marlin/AWQ/GPTQ actually accelerate rather than only save VRAM) plus independent measured TTFT to falsify or confirm the sub-900 ms local-tier claim under a 9-11 GB residual budget and 4 vCPU.

angles.label: small-model agentic / tool-calling reliability + Chinese-Cantonese degradation
angles.query: BFCL v3 v4 tau-bench AgentBench open-weight models under 14B function calling accuracy gap versus frontier multi-turn error compounding failure modes hallucinated arguments infinite loop forgetting tool results Chinese Cantonese multilingual degradation with model size
angles.rationale: Quantifies the real cost of autonomy at <=14B: single-step vs multi-step accuracy gap, characteristic failure-mode rates, and whether Chinese/Cantonese collapses faster than English as parameters shrink - the same trap that already vetoed the local guard model.

angles.label: embodied-agent safety, new attack surface, and 2026 compliance
angles.query: embodied LLM robot unsafe plan rate SafeAgentBench hazardous plans 28.3% scaling 3B to 671B safety 37.6% 56.9% deterministic external safety checker outperforms stronger model runtime shield prompt injection propagation through cascade denial-of-wallet escalation EU AI Act Article 50 synthetic audio machine-readable marking obligation
angles.rationale: Verifies provenance and scope of the cited 0.4%/28.3% and 37.6%->56.9% figures, seeks evidence that an out-of-loop deterministic verifier beats a smarter in-loop model, and covers cascade-specific attack surface plus who owns Art 50 audio marking when TTS and reasoning sit in different tiers.

angles.label: alternative designs and their measured cost / latency curves
angles.query: reasoning effort parameter low medium high measured latency cost accuracy tradeoff curve 2026 single model versus model cascade; fine-tuned sub-1B intent classifier or embedding router beats general small LLM routing benchmark; speculative decoding draft model single GPU batch size 1 speedup memory contention
angles.rationale: Supplies the head-to-head data for candidates A/B/C: effort-knob curves on one cloud model, sub-1B fine-tuned classifiers/embedding routers vs a general small LLM as router, and whether draft-verify speculative decoding is viable when the draft must share one already-loaded T4.

results.title: Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models (arXiv 2608.05064, 2026-08-05)
results.snippet: The single most on-target paper for the primary contradiction: 11 models spanning 0.5B-14B (i.e. exactly the Qwen3-4B/8B/14B band that fits in 9-11 GB on a T4) on ARC-Challenge + TruthfulQA, 25,168 local predictions. Verdict is negative for the user's premise: 'Certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to only three model-task pairs and to none at 10%' — i.e. 19 of 22 model-task pairs could NOT be certified to self-defer even at a permissive 20% error budget, and zero at 10%. Also quantifies the fix and its ceiling: Platt scaling gets ECE down to ~0.02, but temperature scaling is infeasible for 8 of 22 pairs (hit the floor within 1pp). Directly falsifiable claim to carry into the report: a <=14B local model asked 'do I know this?' cannot meet a robot-safety-grade risk budget without an external calibrator, and even with one it only reaches 20% risk on 14% of configurations.

results.title: Opportunity Is Not Realizability: Selection-Valid Diagnostics for Multi-LLM Routing (arXiv 2608.08265, 2026-08-08)
results.snippet: Separates the routing opportunity that EXISTS from the share a real router can CAPTURE, with selection-valid (post-selection-corrected) intervals — which is precisely the inferential error most RouteLLM-lineage papers make. Numbers: certified population oracle gap of 9.7-30.7 points on every task, but 'the strongest deployable prompt router recovers only 7.5-14.4% of it'; abstract states 'most of the gap remains'. This is the strongest single refutation of 'small first, escalate the hard ones': the oracle two-tier system is worth 10-30 points, and the best known prompt-only router (the only kind cheap enough to run before the small model answers) banks roughly one tenth of that. Note it measures prompt routers (pre-generation), which is the exact regime the project needs to beat a 900 ms Bedrock TTFT.

results.title: The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers (arXiv 2606.07587, 2026-05-27)
results.snippet: Systematic adversarial replication across 21 routing methods and five benchmarks — the 'reproduction failure' evidence the query asked for, in aggregate form rather than one-off. Finding: 'Many methods, including kNN, achieve very similar accuracy and converge to a narrow performance range that remains far below the oracle router.' The plateau result means published router gains are not method-dependent: a trivial kNN baseline matches the elaborate learned routers, which implies the reported wins come from the benchmark's easy-query mass, not from actual difficulty detection. Use this to argue that engineering effort spent on a better router in this project has a measured ceiling and that any custom router should be benchmarked against kNN-on-embeddings before it is believed.

results.title: Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts (arXiv 2605.07395, 2026-05-08)
results.snippet: 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks, and it reports the two failure modes the query asked to quantify. (a) Degenerate router behavior: standard routers 'collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal)', i.e. the router learns to always keep the query local and still scores well — the false-keep failure mode, invisible under aggregate accuracy. (b) The cost of that collapse: 13-17 percentage points of opportunity cost versus the oracle. (c) It also attacks the measurement itself: 'a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts including systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness', meaning LLM-judge-scored routing benchmarks overstate how separable hard queries are. Critical for a robot loop: always-keep-local is the failure the aggregate metric rewards.

results.title: R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help (arXiv 2605.16604, 2026-05-15)
results.snippet: The strongest counter-evidence — include it to avoid a one-sided report, but note the domain dependence, which is itself the decisive number. Reported: '94.3% HumanEval+ success with 0.60% LLM escalation', versus TextWorld where it 'recovers from 64.6% SLM-only to 98.2% at 41.7% escalation'. Read together, escalation rate swings 0.6% -> 41.7% (70x) between a single-turn code task and an interactive multi-step embodied-style task. The project's target workload (voice dialogue + ROS 2, multi-step, stateful) is far closer to TextWorld than to HumanEval, so the honest projection is a ~40% escalation rate, which destroys most of the claimed cost saving while adding the local model's latency to 40% of turns. This is the paper to cite for 'deferral works' AND for 'it works least where this project needs it'.

results.title: Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation (arXiv 2607.24440, 2026-07-27)
results.snippet: Answers the 'which confidence signal actually works on a small model' sub-question AND couples it to the T4's mandatory quantization. Qwen2-VL 2B-7B, 5,700 predictions: internal error-detection AUROC 0.80-0.98 versus verbalized-confidence AUROC 0.61-0.69 ('weak, often at chance'); abstract: 'Scale sharply improves the model's internal uncertainty signal while its verbalized confidence stays weak and often at chance.' The T4-specific kill shot: 4-bit quantization drops internal AUROC 0.95 -> 0.80 and the verbalized-confidence PARSE rate 99% -> 64%. Since 9-11 GB of headroom forces 4-bit for anything above ~8B, the project would be running the model in exactly the regime where both the usable signal (logprobs) degrades and the asked-for signal (verbalized) fails to even parse a third of the time. Corroborated by arXiv 2607.22034 (small VLMs: verbalized confidence near-constant 0.87-0.90, AUROC ~0.50, while token probability reaches AUROC 0.92-0.99) and arXiv 2606.29490 (verbal confidence tracks commitment, not correctness; logprobs track evidence).

results.title: The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers (2026-05-27)
results.snippet: Strongest single piece of evidence bearing on candidate B and on the router premise generally. Verified abstract: 21 routing methods across 5 benchmarks converge to "a narrow performance range that remains far below the oracle router" — and plain kNN over embeddings is inside that band, i.e. a cheap embedding router is not measurably worse than learned classifiers, pairwise rankers, or confidence-based routers. Diagnosed cause is a "predictability bottleneck": routers learn global averaged per-model performance trends, not query-specific signal, so they "solve overlapping easy queries but collectively fail on hard queries that require instance-specific routing decisions" — precisely the escalate-when-I-don't-know case the two-tier design depends on. Implication for this project: paying VRAM for a general small LLM as router buys nothing over a sub-1B embedding/kNN router; and neither reaches oracle. Levers that did help: larger training sets, stronger encoders, end-to-end fine-tuning (all supervised-data costs, not zero-shot prompting). Opposing datapoint surfaced in the same sweep and worth adversarial checking: PyroDash (arXiv 2607.20327, token-level small→large deferral) claims 64.04% accuracy, +6.36pp over an LLM-only baseline at 20.4% lower cost.

results.title: The Price of Thinking: Reasoning Effort as a Model-Specific API Contract (2026-08-16)
results.snippet: Direct measured cost/quality curve for candidate A (effort knob on one cloud model) on the exact model family in play. Pre-registered comparison of Sonnet 5 with explicit high effort vs effort omitted, 30 AIME 2026 items × 5 calls = 150 observations: mean cost +$0.01031 per call for high effort, cost per correct answer $0.08665 (high) vs $0.07662 (omitted), accuracy delta +0.0133 with CI [-0.0267, +0.0467] — no statistically detectable accuracy gain. Cuts two ways for the user's design: it supports candidate A's mechanism existing and being cheap to leave at default, but it refutes any claim that dialing effort up is a reliable quality dial you can trade against a local tier; on this task the knob was pure cost. Caveats to state explicitly: single model, single benchmark (competition math, not voice dialogue or tool-calling), single collection date, and the paper does not report latency — so the effort→TTFT curve the project actually needs (vs the measured 900 ms p50 first token) is still evidence-insufficient.

results.title: Discourse-Aware Dual-Track Streaming Response for Low-Latency Spoken Dialogue Systems (DDTSR) (2026-02-26)
results.snippet: The best-matched alternative design in the whole sweep for a voice + robot loop, and it is a strictly weaker-authority role for the small model than the user's plan: the small model never decides anything, it emits "minimal-committal discourse connectives" while the large model reasons in parallel, with ASR/LLM/TTS overlapped (listen-while-thinking, speak-while-thinking). Measured 19–51% response-latency reduction versus conventional cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS pipelines, described as plug-and-play across LLM backbones and robust across utterance lengths, with curriculum learning used to keep the early filler coherent with the later reasoning output. This attacks the project's real latency target (perceived time-to-first-audio) without spending the 9–11 GB of T4 headroom on a decision-making local LLM. Gaps to verify from the PDF before adopting: the abstract does not state the small model's parameter count, the hardware, or a naturalness/coherence score, and Kokoro-82M/CosyVoice TTS barge-in behaviour is untested here.

results.title: UCCI: Calibrated Uncertainty for Cost-Optimal LLM Cascade Routing (2026-05-11)
results.snippet: The most rigorous small→large cascade measurement found, and it quantifies the calibration problem the user asked about. 4B → 12B cascade on H100s, production NER workload of 75,000 queries: 31% inference-cost reduction (95% CI [27%, 35%]) at fixed micro-F1 = 0.91, beating entropy thresholding, split-conformal routing, and FrugalGPT-style learned thresholds, using real outputs and measured latency rather than simulated routing. Critical qualifier: the raw small-model confidence was badly calibrated — expected calibration error 0.12, only reaching 0.03 after isotonic regression on token-level margins. So a working cascade required a labelled calibration set and a post-hoc calibrator, not the model's own self-assessment. Boundaries that conflict with this project: the task is closed-set NER (a scorable single-label output), not open-ended Cantonese dialogue or multi-step tool use where no per-query error label exists; hardware is H100 (bf16/FP8 available), so none of its latency numbers transfer to Turing SM75.

results.title: Speculative Decoding: Performance or Illusion? (2025-12-31)
results.snippet: Head-on empirical challenge to candidate C. Measures multiple speculative-decoding variants on production vLLM and reports "substantial gaps between observed and theoretical upper bounds." Two mechanisms named that are fatal on a single shared T4: verification by the target model dominates execution time, and acceptance length varies markedly across output-token positions, requests, and datasets — so the speedup is neither stable nor predictable per turn, which is what a voice turn-taking budget needs. Note the framing mismatch the project must state plainly: speculative decoding presumes the large model runs locally, so it cannot accelerate a Bedrock GPT-5.6 Sol call at all; it is only relevant if the target model is itself on the T4, where a draft model plus a target model plus the resident ~3.2 GB (YOLO26s TRT engine, Kokoro-82M, MediaPipe, FunASR) must share 9–11 GB. Related benchmark worth citing alongside: SPEED-Bench (arXiv 2604.09557) finds synthetic inputs overestimate real-world speculative throughput.

results.title: An Interpretable Latency Model for Speculative Decoding in LLM Serving (2026-05-14)
results.snippet: Supplies the load-contention curve that decides candidate C under this project's specific constraint of a GPU already running other workloads. Builds an interpretable latency model validated against extensive vLLM measurements while sweeping verifier and drafter sizes, prefill/decode lengths, request rates, draft lengths, and acceptance probabilities; it uses Little's Law to infer effective batch size and decomposes latency into load-independent and load-dependent parts across prefill, drafting, and verification — explicitly to explain "why speedups often diminish as server load increases." That is the same failure geometry as a T4 time-slicing between a TensorRT detector, a TTS model, MediaPipe, and streaming ASR: drafting is extra load-dependent work, so the batch-size-1 idle-GPU speedup numbers quoted in most speculative-decoding papers are the wrong operating point for this machine. Limitation for our use: the measurements are on datacenter serving hardware, not Turing, and the paper models throughput/latency rather than VRAM fragmentation or CUDA-context overhead from co-resident processes, so those T4 co-tenancy costs remain evidence-insufficient.

results.title: Using large language models for embodied planning introduces systematic safety risks (DESPITE benchmark)
results.snippet: PROVENANCE CONFIRMED for the user's cited figures — this is the source. DESPITE: 12,279 tasks spanning physical and normative dangers, fully deterministic validation, 23 models. Best model fails to produce a plan on only 0.4% of tasks yet produces dangerous plans on 28.3%. Across 18 open-weight models from 3B to 671B, planning ability spans 0.4-99.3% while safety awareness stays roughly flat at 38-57% (i.e. the user's 37.6%->56.9% is the endpoint pair of that band); proprietary reasoning models reach 71-81%, so the ceiling is NOT absolute — it is open-weight-bound. Paper's own framing (planning x safety is multiplicative, scale buys planning not danger-avoidance) directly supports decoupling safety from the planner. SCOPE CAVEAT: it is a text/simulated planning benchmark, not physical robot trials, and it does NOT itself test an external deterministic checker — so the user's implied 'therefore add an out-of-loop verifier' is an extrapolation, not this paper's measured result.

results.title: NEXUS: Continual Learning of Symbolic Constraints for Safe and Robust Embodied Planning
results.snippet: Closest direct evidence for 'deterministic checker outside the loop beats a smarter in-loop model'. Explicitly decouples physical feasibility from safety specifications and converts probabilistic LLM risk assessments into DETERMINISTIC constraints, evaluated on SafeAgentBench with claims of higher task success while refusing unsafe instructions and resisting adversarial attacks. Companion evidence for the tool-calling layer: arXiv 2607.19356 (NEXUS: Structured Runtime Safety for Tool-Using LLM Agents) reports F1 0.949, 0% attack success rate at 99% control-allow on indirect prompt injection, and +27.3 percentage points over rule-only intervention selection — note that last number cuts BOTH ways: pure deterministic rules were 27.3pp worse than rules+calibrated risk scoring, so 'deterministic only' is refuted; the supported claim is 'deterministic envelope + a scorer', not 'deterministic instead of a model'.

results.title: Kill-Chain Canaries: Stage-Level Tracking of Prompt Injection Across Attack Surfaces and Model Safety Tiers
results.snippet: Directly attacks the two-tier premise: 950 runs, 5 frontier LLMs, 6 surfaces, 5 defense conditions, tracked through EXPOSED -> PERSISTED -> RELAYED -> EXECUTED. Every model was fully EXPOSED; outcomes diverged only downstream — Claude blocked injections at memory-write (0/164 ASR) while GPT-4o-mini RELAYED at 53% and DeepSeek showed 0%/100% variance by surface. Implication for local-small -> cloud-large: the cheap front tier is the relay, so the weaker model's 53%-class relay rate becomes the system's injection entry rate regardless of how well the cloud tier is aligned. Reinforcing: arXiv 2410.07283 (Prompt Infection) shows self-replicating LLM-to-LLM payloads across connected agents, and arXiv 2608.00747 (When Prompts Control Robots, Aug 2026) is the first systematic study of prompt injection in multi-agent LLM ROBOTIC systems, finding attacks propagate between agents via shared prompt structures, including indirect injection through perception modules (relevant given YOLO/vision text in the loop).

results.title: EU AI Act Article 50 — Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
results.snippet: Answers the 'who marks the audio in a two-tier stack' question. Art 50(2) puts the machine-readable marking duty on PROVIDERS of AI systems generating synthetic audio/image/video/text, including general-purpose AI systems, and requires markings that are 'effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible'; Art 50(1) puts the human-interaction disclosure duty on providers; Art 50(4) puts deepfake/AI-content DISCLOSURE on DEPLOYERS. Application date 2 August 2026 (already in force as of today). Mapping to this project: the marking obligation attaches to whoever provides the audio-GENERATING component (Kokoro-82M / CosyVoice TTS tier), not the text-reasoning tier (Sonnet/GPT-5.6) — so splitting reasoning to cloud does NOT move the Art 50(2) watermark duty off the local machine, while shipping the robot to users makes you both provider and deployer and thus liable under 50(1), 50(2) and 50(4) simultaneously. Exemptions listed are narrow (assistive editing that does not substantially alter input; law-enforcement authorisation).

results.title: SafeAgentBench: A Benchmark for Safe Task Planning of Embodied LLM Agents
results.snippet: The canonical prior benchmark and an independent corroboration that in-loop model quality does not buy safety: 750 curated tasks, 10 hazard categories, 3 task types, in SafeAgentEnv with 17 high-level actions — the most safety-conscious baseline agent still reached only a 10% rejection rate on hazardous tasks. Also gives the false-positive side that any external checker proposal must budget for: arXiv 2607.15218 reports LLM-judge baselines wrongly rejecting SAFE tasks at 24.7-39.0% FPR on SafeAgentBench, with its own hidden-state detector at 86.2-87.7% accuracy and still 11.7-13.7% FPR. For a voice+ROS 2 loop that means a naive out-of-loop LLM verifier would refuse roughly a quarter to a third of legitimate commands — the deterministic-envelope design must be a typed action/parameter whitelist, not an LLM judge.

results.title: Overthinking Loops in Agents: A Structural Risk via MCP Tools
results.snippet: Quantifies the denial-of-wallet exposure a router/escalation path adds: a malicious tool server induces cyclic agent behaviour with resource amplification up to 142.4x tokens while no individual step looks suspicious, and decoding-time concision controls are shown insufficient. Adjacent measurements for the same threat class: arXiv 2607.01518 (Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based ROBOTIC Systems) reports 6.96x latency amplification, and 4.74x via merely PRINTED TEXT in the camera's view — a physical-world trigger that applies directly to a robot with a vision tier feeding the LLM; arXiv 2602.07652 (Agent-Fence) ranks Denial-of-Wallet as the highest operational risk class across deep research agents; arXiv 2606.07968 (RecurGuard) detects 99% of OverThink and 92% of ExtendAttack instances via runtime reasoning-token monitoring, i.e. the mitigation is again an out-of-loop deterministic budget counter rather than a better model. Consequence for this design: any 'small model escalates when unsure' rule is an attacker-controllable spend lever unless a hard per-session escalation quota exists.

results.title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Measuring Cross-Lingual Policy Retention in Tool-Using Agents (2026-08-13)
results.snippet: The single most decisive source for this angle. 8 models x 41 languages x 6 parallel tool-use benchmarks, 2.38M rollouts, third-party academic measurement (not vendor). Findings: frontier models retain only 71-73% of their ACTION policy when the same task is posed in a non-English language under greedy decoding (i.e. ~27-29% of tool-call sequences change), and explicitly that cross-lingual policy consistency 'below roughly 10B parameters it breaks down'. That directly contradicts putting a <=14B (realistically 4B-8B at 9-11GB VRAM) Qwen3 in front of a Chinese/Cantonese voice loop as a decision-maker: the degradation the guard-model round already hit is confirmed to reappear in tool-calling, not just safety classification. It also finds agents route non-English tasks through English as a causally load-bearing pivot and refuse to stop even when instructed - which adds hidden latency and a translation failure point ahead of ROS 2 actions. Caveat to verify in the PDF: the 41-language list was not confirmed from the abstract page to include Cantonese specifically (Chinese/zh likely; yue unconfirmed). Also reports a measurement artifact that inflated one model's reported accuracy 26x and >50% chance agreement between unrelated traces without correction - a warning that any local BFCL/tau-bench reproduction on the T4 needs trace-level scoring, not answer matching.

results.title: When the API Speaks the Wrong Language: Revisiting Post-Training for Multilingual Tool Use (2026-08-12)
results.snippet: Names and isolates the exact failure mode a Cantonese/Mandarin voice front-end would produce: 'Argument Language Mismatch' (ALM) - the model picks the CORRECT tool but emits argument VALUES in an inconsistent language, so the call is semantically right and 'operationally invalid'. For a ROS 2 loop this is the worst class of error because it passes schema validation and reaches the actuator/topic layer before failing (or worse, matches a wrong enum). Paper reports LLM API-calling reliability 'degrades in multilingual settings' generally and compares SFT vs RL post-training as mitigations, i.e. the fix is training data you do not have, not prompting. Note: exact per-model/per-language ALM rates were not extractable from the abstract page and must be read from the PDF before quoting a number - treat the mechanism as evidence-supported and the magnitude as evidence-insufficient.

results.title: The Constraint Tax: Measuring Validity-Correctness Tradeoffs in Structured Outputs for Small Language Models (2026-05-20)
results.snippet: Quantifies the trap in 'just use constrained decoding so the small model always emits valid tool JSON'. On Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B and SmolLM2-1.7B, hard answer-only schema decoding raises schema validity from 61.5% to 100.0% while LOWERING answer accuracy from 19.7% to 11.0%, and raises the wrong-but-schema-valid share from 49.5% to 88.9%. Directly falsifiable-claim material: grammar constraints convert loud parse failures into silent wrong actions, so a downstream deterministic checker (angle 4) cannot rely on 'it parsed' as a signal. Sizes tested are below the project's 4B-8B candidates so the magnitude is an upper bound, but the direction (validity up, correctness down, wrong-valid up) is the mechanism that matters for a robot that executes whatever validates.

results.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Calling Agents with Iterative Reward Calibration (2026-04-03)
results.snippet: The strongest CONFLICTING evidence against a blanket 'small models cannot do agentic tool calling' claim, and worth flagging to the user as such. On tau-bench, MT-GRPO takes Qwen3.5-4B from 63.8% to 66.7% (+2.9pp) and Qwen3-30B-A3B from 58.0% to 69.5% (+11.5pp), reported against GPT-4.1 at 49.4% and comparisons to GPT-4o / Claude Sonnet 4.5. Two things cut both ways: (a) a 4B model at 66.7% on a two-domain customer-service benchmark still fails ~1 in 3 tasks, which is not an autonomy budget for a physical robot; (b) the headline requires multi-turn RL training on the target domain - the untrained baselines (58.0-63.8%) are what an off-the-shelf Qwen3 checkpoint on the T4 would actually deliver, and tau-bench is English text-only with no speech, no Cantonese, no ROS 2 action space.

results.title: R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help (2026-05-15)
results.snippet: Gives the deferral-rate numbers that decide whether the local tier actually saves anything, and they vary by ~70x across task types: 94.3% HumanEval+ success at only 0.60% LLM escalation, but TerminalBench 93.3% at 33.9% escalation and TextWorld 98.2% at 41.7% escalation. TextWorld/TerminalBench are the interactive, stateful, multi-step regimes closest to a ROS 2 dialogue loop - there the small model hands off on ~34-42% of turns, which means the user pays local TTFT PLUS the 900ms Bedrock TTFT on a third to a half of turns. Under the project's constraint that local TTFT must beat 900ms to have any point, that escalation rate is the number to test first. Third-party academic, not vendor; SLM backbones are unnamed in the abstract so map-to-Qwen3-4B is unverified.

results.title: Measuring Hong Kong Massive Multi-Task Language Understanding (HKMMLU) (2025-05-04)
results.snippet: Absolute grounding for the Cantonese/HK degradation claim, independent of tool-calling: on 26,698 HK-context multiple-choice questions, even DeepSeek-V3 'struggles to achieve an accuracy of 75%, significantly lower than that of MMLU and CMMLU'. If a ~671B-class frontier model loses that much on Hong Kong / Cantonese material relative to English MMLU and Mandarin CMMLU, a 4B-8B local model is being asked to operate in the project's worst-covered language at the smallest size - the same coverage argument that already vetoed Llama Guard 4/3, ShieldGemma and Granite Guardian here. Companion sources found in the same sweep: arXiv 2408.16756 'How Well Do LLMs Handle Cantonese?' (Cantonese, 85M speakers, scant NLP representation) and arXiv 2511.10664 which reports smaller open models (LLaMA-2 13B, Mistral 7B) 'lag substantially in fluency and accuracy' on Cantonese colloquialisms.

claims.claim: The "unsolvability ceiling" that justifies routing headroom is substantially an evaluation artifact, not a real capability gap — meaning published cost-savings estimates for small-model-first cascades are inflated. Directly undercuts the premise that a cheap first tier has a large, measurable set of queries it can safely own.
claims.quote: we show that a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts: (i) systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness, (ii) truncation under fixed generation budgets, and (iii) output format mismatches ... Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated

claims.claim: Trained routers do not learn a genuine "can the small model handle this?" signal: standard routers degenerate to always predicting the cheapest tier (~79% of queries labelled smallest-tier-optimal), and this collapse is confirmed by random-feature and shuffled-label controls (i.e. the router performs no better than a feature-free majority baseline).
claims.quote: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls

claims.claim: The router collapse carries a quantified 13-17 percentage-point opportunity cost versus an oracle/cost-sensitive router — a concrete falsifiable number for how much end-to-end quality a naive learned escalation policy leaves on the table.
claims.quote: incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost

claims.claim: Reliable measurement of a two-tier setup requires dual-judge validation and exact-match anchoring plus cost-sensitive objectives; LLM-as-a-judge alone (rewarding verbosity) and fixed generation budgets (truncation) will mis-measure which tier is adequate.
claims.quote: We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives.

claims.claim: Evidence scope is 206,000 query-model pairs over six English text benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) with Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families — no Qwen3, no Chinese/Cantonese, no tool-calling or latency measurement, so it constrains the routing-decision question but says nothing about T4 throughput or Chinese-language degradation.
claims.quote: a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families

claims.claim: Verbalized (self-reported, in-words) confidence from small open-weight models is a near-useless error detector and barely improves with scale: error-detection AUROC only 0.61 -> 0.69 going 2B -> 7B, versus 0.80 -> 0.98 for internal (logit/logprob-derived) signals. This directly refutes the design of asking a local small model 'do you know this / should I escalate?' in natural language; if a local deferral signal is used at all it must be read from logits, not from the model's words.
claims.quote: mean error-detection AUROC 0.80 to 0.98 from 2B to 7B ... Verbalized confidence remained weak: "mean 0.61 to 0.69" ... "gap between what the model knows and what it says widens rather than closes with size"

claims.claim: 4-bit quantization is nearly free in accuracy but expensive in uncertainty quality: accuracy falls only -1.6 points while internal error-detection AUROC falls 0.95 -> 0.80 and the verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses 99% -> 64%. Because the T4 budget (9-11 GB free, no bf16/FP8) forces 4-bit weights, the quantized local model's ability to know it is wrong degrades far more than benchmark accuracy suggests - benchmark-accuracy-based sizing will overestimate router reliability.
claims.quote: Accuracy cost: "-1.6 points" ... Internal signal degradation: "internal AUROC 0.95 to 0.80" ... Parse rate collapse: "verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses from 99% to 64%"

claims.claim: A 36% failure rate in merely PARSING a small model's stated confidence under 4-bit quantization means a verbalized-confidence router needs a defined fallback for roughly one in three requests; a cascade that treats unparseable confidence as 'confident' silently suppresses escalation, and one that treats it as 'unsure' escalates ~36% of traffic unconditionally, destroying the claimed cost saving.
claims.quote: verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses from 99% to 64%

claims.claim: At a fixed memory budget, a larger 4-bit model beats a smaller full-precision one on BOTH task accuracy and uncertainty signal quality (7B-4bit: internal AUROC 0.98). For the T4's ~9-11 GB, this argues for Qwen3-8B-class at 4-bit over Qwen3-4B at FP16, contradicting the intuition of picking the smallest model that fits.
claims.quote: 7B-4bit gives both the best accuracy and the best uncertainty signal (internal AUROC 0.98)

claims.claim: Evidence scope is limited: the study is a single-author arXiv preprint (12 pages, 4 figures) on Qwen2-VL 2B/7B over 5,700 vision predictions under six photographic degradations at three severities - i.e. a vision-language perception task, not text tool-calling or Chinese/Cantonese dialogue - so the calibration numbers are indicative for a Qwen-family small model on a degraded-input task but are NOT direct evidence about routing accuracy in a speech-plus-ROS-2 agent loop.
claims.quote: 5,700 predictions spanning six realistic photographic degradations at three severities ... 12 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: this https URL

claims.claim: On AIME 2026 (30 items x 5 calls = 150 calls) with Sonnet 5, specifying explicit high reasoning effort produced NO detectable accuracy gain over omitting the effort parameter: contrast +0.0133 with a 95% CI spanning zero (-0.0267 to +0.0467). This directly undercuts Candidate A's premise that an effort knob buys a usable quality gain at the top of the dial.
claims.quote: The corresponding accuracy contrast was +0.0133 [-0.0267, +0.0467]; we did not detect an accuracy difference.

claims.claim: The explicit-high-effort contract cost measurably more per call than omitting the parameter: +$0.01031 per call (95% CI +$0.00204 to +$0.01974), i.e. the cost side of the effort dial is real and statistically detectable while the quality side is not.
claims.quote: Mean delivered cost was $0.01031 per call higher under the explicit-high contract

claims.claim: Cost per correct answer was WORSE under explicit high effort than under the omitted contract ($0.08665 vs $0.07662, ~13% more expensive per correct answer), so on this task the effort knob was a net-negative efficiency trade.
claims.quote: Cost per correct answer was $0.08665 under the high-effort contract and $0.07662 under the omitted contract.

claims.claim: Omitting the reasoning-effort parameter is not a neutral default but carries model-specific semantics that differ across providers (Anthropic effort vs OpenAI reasoning_effort vs Gemini thinking_budget); the paper offers no empirical data on the non-Anthropic parameters, so cross-provider effort curves remain unmeasured here.
claims.quote: model-specific omission semantics

claims.claim: The paper reports NO latency or wall-clock measurements and no output/thinking token counts, and explicitly bounds its conclusions to one model, one task, and one collection date - so it cannot be used to claim an effort knob meets or misses the project's 900 ms first-token latency bar.
claims.quote: the resulting claims are bounded to the model, task, and collection date studied.

claims.claim: Small-model confidence used for cascade escalation is badly miscalibrated out of the box: raw token-level margin uncertainty has ECE = 0.12, and only post-hoc isotonic regression brings it to 0.03. This directly supports the thesis that a cheap, reliable "I don't know" signal does not exist by default — it must be manufactured with labeled data.
claims.quote: UCCI cuts inference cost by 31% (95% CI: [27%, 35%]) at micro-F1 = 0.91 while reducing ECE from 0.12 to 0.03.

claims.claim: The router is not free and not zero-shot: it requires fitting isotonic regression on a per-workload labeled set, with only O(n^{-1/3}) convergence of calibration error — i.e. an order-of-magnitude reduction in ECE needs ~1000x more labeled samples. The reported result used a 75,000-query labeled production workload. A project with no labeled Cantonese voice/ROS2 corpus cannot obtain this router.
claims.quote: isotonic calibration achieves O(n^{-1/3}) sample complexity for expected calibration error (ECE)

claims.claim: Even in a best-case, narrowly-scoped setting (single-turn named entity recognition, 4B vs 12B, H100), the measured cascade win is only 31% cost reduction — no quality gain, and the operating point is pinned at micro-F1 = 0.91 rather than at the large model's ceiling. There is no evidence here for cascades on multi-turn agentic or tool-calling workloads.
claims.quote: On a production named entity recognition workload of 75,000 queries served by 4B and 12B instruction-tuned LLMs on H100 GPUs, UCCI cuts inference cost by 31% (95% CI: [27%, 35%]) at micro-F1 = 0.91

claims.claim: The paper itself indicts the prior cascade/routing literature (explicitly including FrugalGPT-style methods) for reporting routing gains that were simulated from global accuracies and nominal API list prices rather than measured end-to-end — i.e. published cascade savings are, by this author's account, systematically unverified.
claims.quote: All cascade results use end-to-end routing on actual model outputs and measured H100 latency, not simulated routing from global accuracies or nominal API prices.

claims.claim: The paper's stated motivation is that deployed routers today are uncalibrated and need per-workload hand-tuning — an admission that as of 2026 the escalation-decision mechanism is an open engineering problem, not a solved component one can drop into an architecture.
claims.quote: most deployed routers use uncalibrated confidence scores and require per-workload threshold tuning

claims.claim: Under selection-valid (multiplicity-corrected) confidence intervals, no deployable router in the study is certifiably better than the single best fixed model: the certified oracle opportunity is 9.7–30.7 accuracy points per task, the strongest deployable prompt router recovers only 7.5–14.4% of it (ARC-C 14.4%, HellaSwag 9.3%, GSM8K 7.5%, MMLU 7.6%), and the simultaneous interval over the best of eleven tested routing policies has lower limit zero on every task. This directly contradicts the premise that a cheap front-stage router can capture the gain implied by 'route hard queries elsewhere'.
claims.quote: selection-valid intervals certify a population oracle gap of 9.7–30.7 points on every task, yet the strongest deployable prompt router recovers only 7.5–14.4% of it, and the simultaneous interval for the best of eleven tested policies has lower limit zero throughout

claims.claim: Model confidence signals carry information mainly on items the strongest fixed model already answers correctly, so confidence fails precisely on the queries a deferral mechanism must catch — the 'I don't know this one, escalate' signal is where calibration is least useful. This falsifies the assumption that small-model confidence can serve as a reliable escalation trigger.
claims.quote: confidence being informative mostly on items the strongest fixed model already solves

claims.claim: The only confidence-based selector reaching usable accuracy (temperature-scaled confidence: .877 on ARC-Challenge, .673 on HellaSwag) is a POST-inference selector that requires querying every candidate model, which eliminates the cost/latency saving that motivates a two-tier cascade; no pre-answer signal achieves comparable selection quality.
claims.quote: For post-inference selectors (Table 7), temperature-scaled confidence reaches .877 accuracy on ARC-C and .673 on HellaSwag, but these require querying all candidates—not pre-answer signals.

claims.claim: Published routing/cascade wins may be statistical artifacts: comparing a router against the best fixed model selected on the same evaluation examples invalidates paired inference, and full-information oracle gaps describe outcomes no deployable router can observe. Any prior claim of routing superiority that lacks selection-valid intervals is therefore not evidence that routing works.
claims.quote: testing against a best fixed model selected on the same examples invalidates paired inference, and a full-information oracle sees outcomes no deployable router observes

claims.claim: External-validity limit for the two-tier (local-small to cloud-large) question: the confirmatory pool contains only small open-weight checkpoints from 0.5B to 7B (TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B) on ARC-Challenge/HellaSwag/GSM8K/MMLU at 200-300 items each — no frontier or proprietary model is included, so the result bounds small-to-small routing, not small-to-frontier deferral.
claims.quote: The confirmatory pool contains exclusively small open-weight models: TinyLlama (1.1B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B–3B), Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini (3.8B), and Mistral-7B. No frontier or proprietary models are included.

claims.claim: Verbalized self-confidence from open-weight models 0.5B-14B has near-useless error-discrimination power: AUROC for detecting its own errors is ~0.5 (chance) below 2B and reaches only 0.63-0.66 at 14B. This directly attacks the premise of a local small-model router: the signal it would use to say "this one is too hard, escalate" barely separates its own correct from incorrect answers.
claims.quote: AUROC for error detection is modest everywhere: models below 2B sit near 0.5...the largest models reach only 0.63 to 0.66

claims.claim: There is a distribution-free impossibility result: if a model's stated confidence always exceeds 1/2, no temperature T>0 can calibrate it, and its ECE is lower-bounded by (1/2 - accuracy). This bound is not theoretical-only: 8 of 22 model-task pairs measured sat on that infeasibility floor within one percentage point. So the standard cheap fix (temperature scaling on a held-out set) provably cannot rescue a small model's confidence for deferral.
claims.quote: For every T>0 the calibrated confidences satisfy ĉᵢ>1/2, and ECE ≥ ½−acc

claims.claim: Under a formal risk-controlled deferral procedure (200-question calibration set), only 3 of 22 model-task pairs earned 'certified autonomy' at a 20% risk budget, and ZERO pairs qualified at a 10% risk budget. Concretely the certified cases were Qwen2.5-14B on ARC (99.8% coverage, 8.1% realized risk), Qwen2.5-7B on ARC (93.3%, 10.8%), and Qwen2.5-14B on TruthfulQA (43.6% coverage, 14.2% risk) -- i.e. the hard task forced the 14B model to defer 56% of traffic and still exceeded 10% risk. For a robot loop demanding better than 10% error, no model in this size class is certifiable.
claims.quote: certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to only three model-task pairs

claims.claim: Post-hoc calibration fixes the number but not the ordering: Platt scaling drives ECE as low as 0.02, yet because any strictly monotone calibration map preserves the risk-coverage frontier, calibration cannot improve which items get deferred -- only where the threshold sits. Reporting a low ECE for a local router is therefore not evidence that the router will escalate the right queries.
claims.quote: strictly monotone calibration preserves the risk-coverage frontier

claims.claim: Overconfidence does not shrink with scale in the verbalized channel: median stated confidence stays between 0.80 and 1.00 in every one of the 22 model-task pairs regardless of size, so larger models improve raw ECE only by getting more answers right (Qwen2.5-0.5B: 33.7% accuracy, uncalibrated ECE 0.497; Qwen2.5-14B: 91.8% accuracy, ECE 0.023), not by becoming more honest. Caveat limiting transfer to this project: the evaluation is English-only (ARC-Challenge, TruthfulQA), so Chinese/Cantonese calibration is untested and likely worse.
claims.quote: Median verbalized confidence is nearly constant across sizes, between 0.80 and 1.00 in every model–task pair.

claims.claim: Speculative decoding's speedup is load-dependent and erodes as serving load rises, so SD gains measured in isolated/fixed-batch benchmarks do not transfer to a loaded server — directly undercutting candidate C (small model as draft accelerator) on a T4 that is already running other GPU workloads.
claims.quote: While prior work demonstrates substantial speedups in isolated or fixed-batch settings, the behavior of SD in production serving systems remains poorly understood: request load varies over time, and effective batch size emerges from the serving system rather than being directly controlled or observed. ... The model accurately describes observed latency, explains why speedups often diminish as server load increases

claims.claim: Even under the most favorable configuration the authors tested, the load-dependent cost coefficient of speculative decoding exceeds 1 (i.e. drafting adds per-request demand that competes for GPU service), meaning SD speedup shrinks with load in most practical settings rather than only in edge cases.
claims.quote: speedup generally decreases with load ... "C2,R typically exceeds 1 even in its most favorable configuration"

claims.claim: All measurements in this paper are on NVIDIA A100 SXM GPUs (1x for ≤20B models, 4x for Llama-3.1-70B, 8x for Qwen3-235B-A22B); no Turing/SM75/T4 data is reported, so the paper provides no evidence that speculative decoding is viable on a T4 with ~9-11 GB free VRAM.
claims.quote: All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 SXM GPU, except for Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, which uses 4 NVIDIA A100 SXM GPUs, and Qwen3-235B-A22B, which uses 8 NVIDIA A100 SXM GPUs.

claims.claim: The measurement sweep covers draft lengths of 1-10 tokens and artificially enforced acceptance probabilities of 50%-100% with prefill/decode lengths in {256,512,768,1024} on vLLM 0.13.0, i.e. acceptance rate was controlled rather than observed from real draft-target pairs, so reported behaviour is a parametric model, not an end-to-end quality-preserving benchmark.
claims.quote: vLLM version 0.13.0 ... Draft lengths: "1 to 10 tokens" ... acceptance rates "50% to 100%" enforced by "overriding vLLM's rejection sampling strategy" ... "prefill and decode lengths over {256,512,768,1024} tokens, yielding 16 prefill–decode combinations"

claims.claim: Speculative decoding requires the drafter and the verifier to be co-located in the same serving system (drafting and verification are components of the same per-request demand decomposition), so a two-tier design whose large model lives behind a remote Bedrock API cannot use SD at all — SD is an alternative to, not a variant of, local-small-to-cloud-large routing.
claims.quote: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a smaller draft model to propose multiple tokens that are verified by a larger target model in parallel. ... we ... decompose per-request demand into load-independent and load-dependent components for prefill, drafting, and verification.

claims.claim: In a multi-agent LLM pipeline, which model sits at the memory-write node is the single highest-impact safety decision: with a strong model at the write node injections were blocked 0/164 (0% ASR), while a small/cheap model (GPT-4o-mini) at the same position relayed injections onward ~53% of the time. Directly falsifiable prediction for the proposed two-tier design: putting Qwen3-4B/8B upstream of GPT-5.6 Sol as the first responder / memory writer creates a ~50%-order relay channel that the cloud model's own alignment cannot recover, i.e. the front small model is a new attack surface, not a filter.
claims.quote: Claude blocks all injections at memory-write (0/164 ASR), GPT-4o-mini propagates at 53%, and DeepSeek exhibits 0%/100% across surfaces from the same model.

claims.claim: Prompt-injection outcome is determined by pipeline architecture rather than by per-model safety: exposure was universal across all five frontier models, and only the downstream stages (PERSISTED / RELAYED / EXECUTED) diverged. This supports treating the local-small -> cloud-large hop as an architectural attack path that must be measured stage-by-stage (did the small model persist the payload into memory? did it relay it into the cloud prompt?), and refutes the assumption that a safety-aligned large backend makes the front stage's exposure harmless.
claims.quote: every model is fully exposed, yet outcomes diverge downstream

claims.claim: All four defense mechanisms evaluated failed on at least one of six attack surfaces purely because of channel mismatch, with no adversarial adaptation required. Falsifiable implication: a deterministic external checker for this robot must be instantiated per channel (ASR transcript, vision/OCR text, tool output, retrieved memory, DDS/ROS 2 topic payload); a checker validated on one channel should be assumed to fail on another until re-tested.
claims.quote: all four defenses fail on at least one surface due to channel mismatch alone, no adversarial adaptation required

claims.claim: A single model's injection success rate is not a stable model property: DeepSeek ranged from 0% to 100% ASR across surfaces within the same model, over a 950-run / 5-model / 6-surface / 5-defense-condition grid. This falsifies using one published safety number (or one internal spot check) to justify a routing/guard decision for the small front model.
claims.quote: 950 runs, five frontier LLMs, six attack surfaces, and five defense conditions

claims.claim: Injection payloads hidden as invisible white-font text in PDFs matched or exceeded the success rate of visible-text attacks, showing that non-human-perceptible channels are at least as dangerous as visible ones — relevant because the robot ingests machine-only channels (ASR hypotheses, OCR of scene text, tool results) that no human reviews before they reach the LLM.
claims.quote: Invisible whitefont PDF payloads matched or exceeded visible-text attack success rates

claims.claim: The user's cited pair of numbers (0.4% planning failure vs 28.3% dangerous plans) is CONFIRMED as originating from this paper — DESPITE, a 12,279-task benchmark with deterministic validation across 23 models. The claim is supported by evidence, and its scope is: the SAME single best-planning model, evaluated on embodied household-style planning tasks.
claims.quote: To evaluate safe planning systematically, we introduce DESPITE, a benchmark of 12,279 tasks spanning physical and normative dangers with fully deterministic validation. Across 23 models, even near-perfect planning ability does not ensure safety: the best-planning model fails to produce a valid plan on only 0.4% of tasks but produces dangerous plans on 28.3%.

claims.claim: The user's second cited pair ('3B→671B safety only climbs 37.6%→56.9%') is CONFIRMED in substance but the abstract states the range as 38-57% over 18 open-source models — i.e. scaling the model buys planning ability (0.4%→99.3%, a ~248x relative gain) while safety awareness moves by under 20 percentage points. Falsifiable corollary for this project: 'use a bigger/stronger cloud model and it will be careful enough' is refuted by evidence.
claims.quote: Among 18 open-source models from 3B to 671B parameters, planning ability improves substantially with scale (0.4-99.3%) while safety awareness remains relatively flat (38-57%). We identify a multiplicative relationship between these two capacities, showing that larger models complete more tasks safely primarily through improved planning, not through better danger avoidance.

claims.claim: Even the best category of model measured — proprietary reasoning models — tops out at 71-81% safety awareness, so a cloud System-2 planner (e.g. GPT-5.6 Sol class) still leaves roughly 1 in 5 dangerous situations unrecognised; no model in 23 reached a safety level that would justify letting the LLM be the last line of defence before a robot actuator.
claims.quote: Three proprietary reasoning models reach notably higher safety awareness (71-81%), while non-reasoning proprietary models and open-source reasoning models remain below 57%.

claims.claim: This paper does NOT provide direct evidence that an external deterministic checker outside the agent loop outperforms 'a stronger model being careful' — the word 'deterministic' here refers to the benchmark's offline validation of plans, not to a runtime guard in the robot's control path. The support for external checkers is therefore INDIRECT (scaling is shown not to fix safety); the head-to-head comparison is EVIDENCE-INSUFFICIENT from this source.
claims.quote: a benchmark of 12,279 tasks spanning physical and normative dangers with fully deterministic validation

claims.claim: Applicability limit for this project: the benchmark measures text-level plan safety in simulated embodied settings and (per the paper's task construction) English-language tasks — it does not measure Chinese/Cantonese safety awareness, nor a voice-driven ROS 2 loop, so the 28.3% figure should be treated as a lower bound rather than a transferable rate for this project's Chinese-language robot.
claims.quote: Large language models are increasingly used as planners for robotic systems, yet how safely they plan remains an open question.

claims.claim: Router design choice is essentially irrelevant: across 21 routing methods × 5 benchmarks, the top-5 methods differ by only 0.22 pp on average, and on 4 of 5 benchmarks 69–75% of ALL swept configurations (method × encoder × architecture × seed) land within 0.02 pp of the empirical ceiling. Simple frozen-encoder kNN ranks top-2 on all five benchmarks. Falsifiable implication for this project: no amount of engineering effort on the escalation policy will move end-to-end quality, because the ceiling is a property of the routing problem, not the router.
claims.quote: The resulting distribution shows a broad plateau: on four of five benchmarks, 69–75% of configurations fall within 0.02 pp of the empirical ceiling. ... It shows that the leading methods form a tight cluster: the top-5 methods differ by only 0.22 pp on average. Notably, simple frozen-encoder retrieval methods such as kNN [22] and KMeans [25] appear in [the top ranks]

claims.claim: The best achievable router sits 10–30 pp below the per-query oracle router, and the strongest known interventions barely dent it: scaling training data 10× (30k→300k queries), upgrading the encoder from ModernBERT-base (~110M) to ModernBERT-large (~340M), AND end-to-end fine-tuning together yield only up to +2.13 pp, closing just 14.6% of the oracle gap. Verified per-benchmark: RouterBench best 80.39% vs oracle 91.69%; EmbedLLM 67.51% vs 97.97% (30.5 pp).
claims.quote: even the plateaued configurations remain 10 to 30 pp below the oracle router, showing that current methods have [not closed the gap] ... we obtain a combined accuracy gain of up to 2.13 pp, closing 14.6% of the oracle gap. Nevertheless, a substantial gap remains

claims.claim: Routers fail specifically on the queries that require escalation. Hard queries (few models answer correctly, global-best model wrong) are only 11.1%–35.4% of test traffic but account for 69.9%–90.8% of the total oracle gap; the hard-query gap is 0.621–0.869 versus 0.020–0.064 on easy queries, a 10.7×–38.5× ratio. Spread among the 12 routers on hard queries is only 3.0–21.9 pp, i.e. they share the same failures, and they select from only 2–3 models regardless of difficulty. This directly refutes the premise 'a cheap mechanism can reliably detect I-do-not-know-this-one'.
claims.quote: hard queries make up only 11.1%–35.4% of each benchmark, yet account for 69.9%–90.8% of the overall gap. This is because the hard-query gap is large (0.621–0.869), exceeding the easy-query gap (0.020–0.064) by 10.7–38.5×. Meanwhile, the spread among the 12 routers on hard queries is only 3.0–21.9 pp, indicating that routers share the failure of routing hard queries.

claims.claim: The routing method most structurally similar to the user's proposed two-tier small→large deferral — HybridLLM, a confidence-based binary small-vs-large deferral router — is the WORST of all 21 methods evaluated: 66.12% average routing accuracy versus 77.01% for the best (Zooter) and ~76.9% for trivial kNN, i.e. roughly 11 pp below the plateau. Per-benchmark: RouterBench 71.67, Nine-by-30k 60.46, EmbedLLM 46.87, R2-Bench 73.99, CARROT 77.62. Confidence-based deferral is not merely at the plateau; it is measurably below it.

Scope caveat that limits how far this paper refutes a two-tier cascade: the study covers only single-shot routing over fixed model pools, and explicitly excludes cascades, ensembles, and post-hoc rejection. However, the authors separately predict that routers learning population-level priors will underserve non-English queries — the same failure mode this project already hit with guard models — making Chinese/Cantonese traffic a predicted hard region for any learned router.
claims.quote: Our study is restricted to single-shot routing over fixed model pools; cascades, ensembles, post-hoc rejection, and dynamically changing pools fall outside our scope and may scale differently. ... may underserve subpopulations infrequent in the training distribution—non-English queries, niche domains, atypical formatting—exactly the hard regions where current routers already fail.

results.title: Bear the Tokens: FP16 and Suffix Decoding to 9,000+ Tokens a Second (Tesla T4, vLLM 0.15.1)
results.snippet: Single most useful third-party measurement found. Tesla T4 (sm_75, 16GB, 320 GB/s, 65 TFLOPS FP16), vLLM 0.15.1, Qwen2.5-0.5B, 512-in/512-out, batch=50: FP16 + suffix decoding = 9,052 tok/s self-test / 7,800 tok/s independently re-verified by H2Loop, P99 TTFT 353.73 ms, P99 TPOT 6.54 ms; AWQ-INT4 best variant = 5,955 tok/s, P99 TTFT 354 ms, TPOT 11.24 ms. Two load-bearing points for the T4 angle: (a) explicit sm_75 kernel matrix — FlashAttention-2 needs sm_80+, FP8 needs sm_89+, BF16 tensor cores absent, Marlin INT4 needs sm_80+, so only AWQ GEMM INT4 (slower than Marlin) + FlashInfer + CUDA graphs are usable; (b) FP16 BEAT AWQ-INT4 on this T4 — i.e. on Turing INT4 quantization saved VRAM (1 GB -> 200 MB) but LOST throughput because the fast Marlin path is unavailable. Caveat that must be stated: the model is 0.5B, ~8-16x smaller than the Qwen3-4B/8B tier the project contemplates, and the TTFT figure is at batch 50, so it is an upper bound on load, not a single-request p50.

results.title: vLLM docs — Supported Hardware for Quantization Kernels (Volta/Turing/Ampere/Ada/Hopper matrix)
results.snippet: Official vLLM matrix giving the SM75 answer directly: AWQ ✓ Turing, GPTQ ✓ Turing, INT8 W8A8 ✓ Turing, GGUF ✓, bitsandbytes ✓ — but Marlin ✗ Turing (Ampere 8.0+ only) and FP8 W8A8 ✗ Turing (Ada 8.9+ only). Architecture-to-SM mapping stated (Turing = 7.5, Ampere = 8.0/8.6, Ada = 8.9). Corroborating detail from the same doc family: FP8 weight-only W8A16 via 'FP8 Marlin' claims capability >= 7.5, so 'FP8 model loads on T4' means dequant-to-FP16 weight-only, NOT FP8 compute. Net: on T4 quantization is a VRAM tactic, not a speed tactic — the accelerated INT4 kernel path (Marlin) is architecturally closed. Note this is a v0.6.1-pinned doc page (the /latest/ and /features/quantization/supported_hardware/ paths 404 today), so the 2026 matrix should be re-verified against the current release before being quoted as-is.

results.title: vLLM issue #29743 — [Feature]: Turing support in Qwen3-VL backends (T4/T4G, SM75) — closed 'not planned'
results.snippet: Direct evidence that the local tier's software stack is unsupported, not merely slow, and that upstream declined to fix it (opened 2025-11-30, closed 2026-03-31 as not planned/stale). Reporter on a T4G (cc 7.5, 4 vCPU Neoverse-N1, vLLM 0.11.3.dev, torch 2.9.1) serving Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct: vLLM logs 'Your device NVIDIA T4G (with compute capability 7.5) doesn't support torch.bfloat16. Falling back to torch.float16'; FLASH_ATTN is gated to sm80+, XFORMERS does not give FA2, FlashInfer/Triton crash in the ViT path (TypeError: linear(): argument 'input' must be Tensor, not NoneType), and TORCH_SDPA 'is no longer registered' in the current backend registry. The only workaround the reporter found is --enforce-eager, measured at 'less than 10 tokens/s ... ~20% throughput'. Also notes the same class of failure for GPT-OSS-20B on T4 (discuss.vllm.ai). Model loading alone took 8.59 GiB and ~80 s for a 4B-class VL model — relevant to the 9-11 GB residual budget.

results.title: vLLM issue #36589 — [Bug]: SM 7.5 extreme slowness, hangs indefinitely on T4 (vLLM 0.17.0, Qwen3.5-27B, 4xT4) — still open
results.snippet: Open bug (filed 2026-03-10, last activity 2026-07-19) showing the SM<8.0 path is still broken in current vLLM. Server logs give measured single-stream decode of ~22-23 tok/s and ~2 concurrent requests at ~42-43 tok/s aggregate on 4xT4, with 'Avg prompt throughput: 1.7 tokens/s' spikes, GPU KV-cache usage climbing after requests finish, and the engine emitting 'No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds' — i.e. multi-second-to-minute stalls, exactly the latency-jitter failure mode that matters for a voice/ROS 2 loop. Also documents that the fix suggested in the linked V100 issue #36357 (fall back to TORCH_SDPA for the multimodal encoder on compute capability < 8.0, 'where FlashAttention 2 is unavailable') does not resolve it. Useful as evidence for tail-latency risk and for the claim that Turing is an untested/regressing configuration upstream.

results.title: Dao-AILab/flash-attention — official README requirements (FA2 = Ampere/Ada/Hopper; Turing punted to a separate repo)
results.snippet: Upstream primary source for the hard architectural constraint: FlashAttention-2 with CUDA requires 'Ampere, Ada, or Hopper GPUs (e.g., A100, RTX 3090, RTX 4090, H100). For Turing GPUs (T4, RTX 2080), see the separate flash-attention-turing repo', and FlashAttention-3 requires H100/H800 with CUDA >= 12.3. This is the root cause behind the vLLM Turing failures above and should be cited as the authoritative (vendor-of-the-kernel, not marketing) statement that the T4 has no first-party fused-attention path — the prefill-side lever that would be needed to get TTFT under the measured 900 ms Bedrock baseline.

results.title: ssiu/flash-attention-turing — third-party FlashAttention-2 for Turing GPUs (125 stars)
results.snippet: The one partial escape hatch, and its limits are decisive. Community CUDA implementation for Turing: head dims 64 and 128, forward and backward, causal masking, GQA, varlen; measured up to 2.19x (non-causal) and 1.95x (causal) faster than PyTorch attention on forward, up to 1.35x/1.51x on backward, reaching ~66% of compute throughput on long sequences. Critically it explicitly does NOT support KV caching (nor dropout or local masking), and the README shows no vLLM/SGLang integration — so it can accelerate a prefill-style forward pass but cannot serve the autoregressive decode loop an agent needs. Falsifies any plan that assumes 'someone backported FA2 to T4, so the kernel gap is solved'.

claims.claim: A small-large split in which the small model makes NO routing or content decision — it only emits non-knowledge-bearing discourse connectives to start speaking early while the large model always performs all reasoning in parallel — cut user-perceived waiting latency on SD-Eval/8B from 1003 ms (single-stream cascade) to 548 ms (-45.4%) with essentially no quality loss (G-Eval consistency 4.77 vs 4.76 baseline; UTMOSv2 3.12 vs 3.16). This is direct measured support for the project's 'candidate B/C' family (small model as accelerator/masker, not agent) and it sidesteps the routing-accuracy problem entirely because there is no deferral decision to get wrong.
claims.quote: On SD-Eval with the 8B model, DDTSR reduces average waiting latency from 1003 ms (SSC) and 861 ms (SDC) to 548 ms, corresponding to a 45.4% reduction. ... DDTSR achieves a consistency score of 4.77 and a coherence score of 4.49, nearly identical to SSC (4.76 / 4.54) and SDC (4.77 / 4.46). In terms of speech quality, UTMOSv2 scores of DDTSR are also on par with baselines (e.g., 3.12 vs. 3.16 on SD-Eval with 8B), indicating that concatenating TTS outputs from two tracks does not degrade perceptual naturalness.

claims.claim: The deployment topology is exactly local-small + remote-large: a fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B connective model plus streaming ASR (sherpa-onnx) plus streaming TTS (CosyVoice2) all co-resident on ONE consumer GPU (RTX 4090D), with the Qwen3-8B/32B reasoning backbone reached over a remote API. But the small model is not drop-in: it required supervised fine-tuning on extracted connectives, curriculum-learning optimization, and an entropy-based confidence gate (emit only when Conf(k) > tau), so the 'plug-and-play' claim applies to swapping the LARGE backbone, not to the small model.
claims.quote: The connective model is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B and fine-tuned to generate fast, non-knowledge-bearing connective utterances, enabling early speech emission with minimal latency. For main content reasoning, we employ two larger backbones, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, which are accessed via remote APIs to decouple heavy inference from the real-time pipeline. ... The connective model, streaming ASR, and streaming TTS are all deployed locally on a single RTX 4090D GPU.

claims.claim: Perceived latency became almost independent of the cloud model's size: waiting latency was 548 ms with an 8B backbone and 549 ms with a 32B backbone on SD-Eval (vs 1003 ms and 1124 ms for the sequential cascade), because first-speech emission depends only on the local lightweight model. This supports choosing the strongest available cloud model (e.g. GPT-5.6 Sol) rather than a weaker/faster one, since backbone latency is hidden rather than paid.
claims.quote: Owing to the proposed small–large model synergy, the system is able to maintain consistently low latency (500 ms in SD-Eval and 800 ms in SpokenNativQA) regardless of the capacity of the underlying large model. This is because early response emission primarily relies on the lightweight model, whose inference time is largely insensitive to the scale of the main reasoning model.

claims.claim: Counter-evidence to any cascaded (ASR-LLM-TTS) architecture: commercial end-to-end speech models measured in the same harness were faster than the best cascaded design — Doubao-realtime 352 ms (SD-Eval) / 366 ms (SpokenNativQA) and Qwen3-Omni-Flash-Realtime 626 ms / 634 ms average waiting latency, versus DDTSR's 548 ms / 741 ms. So the paper's own table shows a monolithic speech model beating the optimized two-track cascade by ~1.5-2.1x on perceived latency; the paper defends the cascade on modularity and controllability grounds, not latency.
claims.quote: These results demonstrate that DDTSR effectively brings cascaded systems into the sub-second response regime, approaching the responsiveness of end-to-end real-time speech models.

claims.claim: The gain is strongly scenario-dependent and does not generalize uniformly: the 45.4% waiting-latency reduction on SD-Eval fell to 17.5% (931 ms -> 741 ms, 8B) on SpokenNativQA, tracking the frequency of turn-initial connectives (94% of turns in SD-Eval vs 38% in SpokenNativQA). Both benchmarks are English (SD-Eval accent/age/environment subsets; SpokenNativQA English subset only), so there is NO evidence in this paper for Mandarin or Cantonese, the decisive language axis for this project.
claims.quote: latency variations across datasets are mainly attributed to differences in the frequency and distribution of connective connectives. Datasets with more frequent (94% in SD-Eval and 38% in SpokenNativQA) turn-initial connectives naturally allow earlier commitments and thus achieve lower effective latency, whereas datasets with fewer such opportunities exhibit relatively higher waiting times.

claims.claim: The machine-readable marking obligation for synthetic audio attaches to the PROVIDER of the AI system that generates the audio, not to the upstream model that produced the text. In a two-tier (local TTS + cloud LLM) architecture this means the marking duty lands on the local tier (Kokoro-82M / CosyVoice TTS) and on the integrator who ships it as a system — it cannot be delegated to Bedrock/GPT-5.6 Sol, because the cloud model emits text, not audio.
claims.quote: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

claims.claim: Article 50 obligations become applicable on 2 August 2026 (per Article 113), confirming the date stated in the research premise. Since today is 2026-08-22, the obligation is already live, not forthcoming.
claims.quote: Date of entry into force: 2 August 2026

claims.claim: A voice-conversation robot triggers a second, independent obligation from Art 50(1): the system must be DESIGNED so the human is informed they are talking to an AI, with the duty on the provider (i.e. whoever builds the two-tier system), unless AI-ness is obvious to a reasonably well-informed observer. This is a design-time requirement on the integrator, not a runtime prompt-level behaviour that can be assigned to either model tier.
claims.quote: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious...

claims.claim: Disclosure must occur no later than the first interaction/exposure and in a clear, distinguishable, accessibility-conformant manner — which forecloses a design where the disclosure is emitted only after the cloud tier is consulted or only when the escalation path fires; the local tier must be able to satisfy it on its own on turn one.
claims.quote: The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. The information shall conform to the applicable accessibility requirements.

claims.claim: The marking obligation is qualified by technical feasibility, cost of implementation, and state of the art — so an argument that watermarking a small local TTS model is infeasible is legally available in principle, but it is a bounded, evidence-requiring defence (state of the art in audio watermarking), not a blanket exemption. The narrow written exceptions (assistive standard editing / no substantial alteration of deployer input, law enforcement) do not cover a conversational robot generating fresh speech.
claims.quote: effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art

result.publishDate: Living document (no article publish date shown); the provision it reproduces has a stated date of entry into force of 2 August 2026. Fetched 2026-08-22.

claims.claim: Speculative decoding's ceiling is a ~1.7-2x decode-throughput gain even in the most favorable regime (batch size 1) on an H100 with a production engine (vLLM v0.10.1.1) — i.e. it is a sub-2x accelerator, not an order-of-magnitude one, and it changes only decode speed, since the target model still performs all verification. Bears directly on candidate C: treating Qwen3 as a draft/accelerator buys at most ~2x on decode and cannot substitute for the 900 ms Bedrock TTFT baseline.
claims.quote: All experiments are conducted using vLLM v0.10.1.1...on NVIDIA H100 with 80 GB of memory. ... speedup of EAGLE over the non-SD baseline decreases from 1.73× to 1.21× as the batch size increases from 1 to 128.

claims.claim: A separate small draft model (the exact shape of a 'Qwen3-small drafts for a large model' design) is the WORST-performing speculative decoding variant measured: it consistently loses to EAGLE-3 and in some cases even to training-free n-gram, because proposal overhead reaches ~37.5% of target-model execution time on Qwen3-8B. This is evidence against the user's implicit hope that a local small Qwen3 can pay for itself as a drafter.
claims.quote: draft-model–based speculative decoding consistently underperforms EAGLE-3 and, in some cases, even the training-free nn-gram method

claims.claim: Speculative decoding requires the TARGET model to execute the verification pass, and verification dominates total execution time — so the technique is intrinsically co-located (draft and target on the same accelerator/engine) and cannot be split across a local T4 drafter and a remote Bedrock-hosted target. Acceptance length is also highly unstable across token positions, requests and datasets, so per-turn latency is not predictable.
claims.quote: Our results show that verification by the target model dominates the execution, while acceptance length varies markedly across output token positions, requests, and datasets.

claims.claim: Speculative decoding speedup degrades monotonically with batch size and can become an outright slowdown: tree-based EAGLE/EAGLE-3 with k=21 falls below 1x speedup on all tested workloads and both models by batch size 64, because the system becomes compute-bound and verifying rejected tokens is pure waste. On a GPU already shared with other resident workloads (YOLO/TTS/ASR contending for SMs), the compute-bound failure mode is reached earlier than the batch-size axis alone suggests.
claims.quote: by batch size 64, the k=21 tree falls below 1× speedup on all workloads for both models ... As the batch size grows, the system becomes increasingly compute-bound, making the overhead...of verifying rejected tokens more costly, thus leading to smaller speedups.

claims.claim: Published speculative decoding speedup numbers are systematically optimistic: prior evaluations used research prototypes and unrealistically small batch sizes, and even at batch size 1 the measured performance falls short of the theoretical/oracle bound (oracle ~2.75x vs ~2.1x achieved on InstructCoder at batch 1). Any vendor or paper-claimed SD speedup should be discounted rather than taken as a planning number.
claims.quote: yet its real-world effectiveness remains unclear as prior evaluations rely on research prototypes and unrealistically small batch sizes ... Comparing measured performance with theoretical bounds reveals substantial gaps between observed and theoretical upper bounds

claims.claim: SUPPORTED (with same-backbone control): an external deterministic symbolic checker beats prompt-based "tell the model to be careful" safety on the same GPT-4 backbone. On 299 safe + 299 unsafe SafeAgentBench tasks, NEXUS (Evolved) reaches Unsafe Reject Rate 89.30% / Unsafe Success (i.e. violation) Rate 1.67% and Safe SR 75.25%, while the best prompt-augmented baseline (ProgPrompt + Safety LLM) gets Unsafe RJ 74.91% / violation 6.35% and its Safe SR *falls* 63.21%→60.20%; every "+Safety LLM" baseline loses safe-task SR and gains false refusals (ReAct 48.16→45.48 SR, RJ 2.34→5.01). Caveat: the checker is not absolute — 10.7% of unsafe tasks are still not refused.
claims.quote: This confirms that LTL-based hard constraints provide a strictly defined safety boundary, superior to the probabilistic guardrails of prompt-based methods.

claims.claim: REFUTES the "stronger/more capable planner is safer" assumption inside the same system: growing only the capability model raises task success but *lowers* safety. Ablation: PDDL-only evolution lifts Safe SR 55.18%→69.57% but drops Unsafe RJ 78.93%→64.55% and raises jailbreak violation rate 1.67%→2.34%; LTL-only (safety) evolution lifts Unsafe RJ to 87.29% while adding only +3.35 points of Safe SR. Capability and safety are separate axes that must be improved by separate mechanisms.
claims.quote: The ablation reveals a critical insight: PDDL-only evolution improves task capability but degrades safety. Unsafe RJ drops from 78.93% to 64.55% because expanded action schemas create more pathways to unsafe states. Conversely, LTL-only evolution improves safety (Unsafe RJ 87.29%) but barely affects task success (+3.35%).

claims.claim: CONFLICTS with a low-latency voice loop: this style of external symbolic verification costs 16.19–34.32 s wall clock per task even after evolution, and 54.86–57.19 s at cold start, versus 18.32–31.92 s for unguarded baselines. That is 18×–63× the project's 900 ms Bedrock first-token p50, so a plan-level formal checker can only sit on a deliberative/pre-action path, never in the conversational turn.
