claims.quote: Although this comes with a computational cost of averaging nearly one minute per task—with the majority of this time allocated to risk learning as detailed in Section 5.5—the Evolved version maintains this rigorous safety profile while significantly improving latency.

claims.claim: SUPPORTED: LLM-based semantic safety layers are defeated by heuristic jailbreak templates, while checking the *generated plan* instead of the *user instruction* is far more robust. Under jailbreak, prompt-augmented baselines' Unsafe RJ collapses (ProgPrompt+Safety 74.91%→44.82%, MLDT+Safety 71.90%→42.81%, ReAct+Safety 69.90%→49.16%, Lota-Bench+Safety 64.88%→51.17%) and violations rise (e.g. Lota-Bench+Safety 5.35%→25.08%), whereas NEXUS degrades 89.30%→72.24% RJ with 0.67% violations.
claims.quote: Under jailbreak attacks, baselines augmented with safety modules exhibit a marked increase in violation rates and a decrease in effective refusals, suggesting that heuristic attacks successfully bypass semantic alignment layers. ... by grounding safety checks in the generated action plan rather than the adversarial user instruction, NEXUS effectively decouples risk assessment from linguistic manipulation.

claims.claim: CAVEAT on "deterministic checker": the hard constraints are still authored by an LLM, and single-pass generation is unreliable. Greedy NL→LTL decoding yields 19.65% syntax-error rate, 61.42% semantic accuracy and only 42.14% downstream Unsafe RJ; reaching 0% syntax error / 88.27% semantic accuracy / 89.30% RJ requires multi-sample generation plus formal verification at 17.59 s per formula (38.02 s for the N=5,K=7 variant, 90.11% SA). Determinism is only at enforcement time, not at specification time.
claims.quote: As shown in Table 3, greedy decoding suffers from a high syntax error rate and limited semantic accuracy, indicating that one-shot NL-to-LTL translation is brittle.

claims.claim: Cross-lingual action-policy retention collapses below roughly 10B parameters: the paper reports that after normalising for each model's own reproducibility, four frontier models converge at 71-73% policy retention under greedy decoding, but "below roughly 10B parameters it breaks down." This is direct evidence against putting a <=14B (and especially <=8B) open-weight model in charge of tool-calling decisions for non-English (Chinese/Cantonese) input, and it is measured on the ACTIONS (tool calls), not final answers.
claims.quote: Normalised by their own reproducibility, four very different frontier models converge under greedy decoding, each keeping 71-73% of its action policy across languages, with model identity explaining only 5.7% of the variance. Below roughly 10B parameters it breaks down, and the ordering among smaller models is largely an artifact of a chance floor we measure by permutation rather than assume.

claims.claim: Published rankings among small multilingual tool-using models are not trustworthy for model selection: the paper finds the ordering among sub-10B models is "largely an artifact of a chance floor" measured by permutation. Falsifiable implication for this project: choosing Qwen3-4B vs Qwen3-8B on published multilingual agentic leaderboard deltas is selecting on noise, so the local tier's tool-calling reliability must be measured in-project, not inherited from benchmarks.
claims.quote: the ordering among smaller models is largely an artifact of a chance floor we measure by permutation rather than assume

claims.claim: The cross-lingual divergence in tool-use policy is structural, not a sampling/temperature artifact: it survives greedy decoding in every model x benchmark cell and stays flat as temperature rises. Falsifiable prediction for this project: setting temperature=0 on the local Qwen3 tier will NOT recover the non-English action-policy gap, so decoding-config tuning is not a mitigation.
claims.quote: Divergence proves structural, not sampling noise: it survives greedy decoding in every cell and stays flat as temperature rises, even as models grow less self-consistent.

claims.claim: Tool-using agents internally pivot non-English tasks through English, the pivot is causally load-bearing (confirmed by a pre-registered prediction across four models), and models refuse to abandon it when instructed. This means a Chinese/Cantonese voice loop inherits an uninstructable English translation stage inside the agent's reasoning, adding a failure surface that prompt engineering cannot remove.
claims.quote: Agents route non-English tasks through English; this pivot is causally load-bearing, confirmed by a pre-registered prediction across four models, and models will not abandon it when told to.

claims.claim: Measured multilingual agent failure can be manufactured entirely by the harness rather than the model: a single trace-extraction regex suppressed one model's measured accuracy by ~26x, while its accuracy on readable outputs barely moved. Any in-project Chinese/Cantonese tool-calling eval must therefore validate its own parser before attributing a gap to the small model.
claims.quote: a single trace-extraction regex, not the model, manufactured a multilingual failure: two worked examples raise one model's measured accuracy twenty-sixfold while its accuracy on readable outputs barely moves

claims.claim: Even a purpose-built, learned, calibrated step-level router does NOT close the quality gap to the frontier model: R2V reaches 94.3% / 98.2% / 93.3% success on HumanEval+ / TextWorld / TerminalBench versus LLM-only at 98.8% / 98.7% / 98.1%. The cascade is cheaper but strictly worse end-to-end on all three benchmarks, and the residual gap is explicitly attributed to failures that are only identifiable in hindsight, not from online risk features. This directly contradicts the assumption that a two-tier local-small→cloud-large design is quality-neutral.
claims.quote: Method HumanEval+ TextWorld TerminalBench / SR (%) LLM% SR (%) LLM% SR (%) LLM% / SLM-only 91.9 0.0% 64.6 0.0% 81.1 0.0% ... R2V (ours) 94.3 0.6% 98.2 41.7% 93.3 33.9% / Oracle Router 98.6 8.1% 98.6 35.4% 97.8 18.4% / LLM-only 98.8 100% 98.7 100% 98.1 100% ... The remaining gap to the oracle, which reaches 97.8% SR with 18.4% LLM calls, indicates that some shell-task failures are identifiable in hindsight but not yet fully captured by the current online risk features.

claims.claim: Token-level logprob/entropy confidence from a small model is an unusable escalation signal in an interactive, partially observable task: the entropy router on TextWorld stayed at exactly the SLM-only success rate (64.6%) while escalating 0.0% of steps — i.e. it never detected any of the 35.4% of steps belonging to failed episodes. On TerminalBench the entropy router escalated only 4.1% and reached 87.4% vs LLM-only 98.1%. This is direct evidence against 'let the small model judge its own uncertainty via logprobs' for a robot/voice loop with noisy observations.
claims.quote: The SLM-only policy reaches only 64.6% SR, and the entropy router remains at 64.6% with 0.0% escalation, showing that token uncertainty alone misses many observation-induced failures.

claims.claim: Cheap non-learned escalation rules degenerate to 'always call the big model': the hand-written heuristic (verifier-rule) router escalated 99.9% of steps on TextWorld and 66.0% on TerminalBench, effectively collapsing into LLM-only execution and destroying the cost saving. Conversely, the learned router requires BOTH verifier scores AND token-entropy features — removing either drops TextWorld from 98.2% to 62.6% SR (below SLM-only), and entropy-only routing yields no gain (64.6% SR). So there is no simple, feature-poor detector that both works and is cheap.
claims.quote: The heuristic router reaches 98.4% SR, but at 99.9% escalation, effectively collapsing to LLM-only execution. ... TextWorld collapses to 62.6% SR when either verifier or entropy features are removed, and entropy-only routing stays near SLM-only performance at 64.6% SR.

claims.claim: The 'do I know this?' evidence source is near-chance on the hardest benchmark and the router stays badly calibrated there: the TerminalBench process verifier scores 0.406 (success steps) vs 0.398 (failure steps), episode-level AUROC 0.508 and Brier 0.276; the full router's ECE on TerminalBench is 0.162, degrading to 0.238 when token log-probabilities are unavailable (closed-API case). Verifier AUROC is only 0.856 on HumanEval+ and ~0.78 on TextWorld. Calibrated difficulty estimation is therefore benchmark-dependent and unreliable in the most heterogeneous, tool-noisy setting — the setting closest to a ROS 2 robot.
claims.quote: On the held-out test split, the verifier achieves episode-level AUROC 0.508 and Brier score 0.276, reflecting near-chance separation when local step scores are mean-aggregated. ... TerminalBench is more sensitive: no-entropy drops from 93.3% to 90.9% SR and worsens ECE from 0.162 to 0.238

claims.claim: The routing mechanism's own cost is heavily front-loaded and its inference-time cost is 5x local decode, and the paper never measures wall-clock latency at all — cost is a token-count proxy (cLLM/cSLM = 50). Building the router required behavioral cloning + verifier-guided DPO + candidate generation on 4x H100 80GB, roughly 300-480 H100 GPU-hours for the main grid (360-576 with ablations), with frontier-model teacher trajectories (Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro). At inference the SLM must sample K=5 candidate actions per step for the verifier/entropy features. Only the router MLP itself is cheap: ~10,000 parameters on CPU. Under a shared T4 with ~9-11 GB free, 5x sampling per step plus verifier scoring makes the local tier's latency advantage unproven by this paper.
claims.quote: At each step t, the distilled SLM samples K = 5 candidate actions ... with vLLM ... All GPU-bound stages were executed on a single server with four NVIDIA H100 80 GB SXM GPUs. ... Summing over three benchmarks and four backbones yields roughly 300-480 GPU-hours for the main experiments reported in the paper. ... The router has approximately 10,000 parameters and runs entirely on CPU. ... we use alpha = 0.20, epsilon = 0.10, Brier calibration weight 1.0, and cost ratio cLLM /cSLM = 50.

claims.claim: Hard schema-constrained decoding on sub-2B models buys structural validity at a large cost in real accuracy: schema validity rises 61.5% -> 100.0% while answer accuracy FALLS 19.7% -> 11.0% (a 44% relative drop) and wrong-but-schema-valid outputs rise 49.5% -> 88.9%. Measured over 15,000 commodity-GPU generations on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B. This contradicts the common engineering assumption (implicitly relied on by any 'small local model emits a constrained JSON tool call / routing decision' design) that constrained decoding is free.
claims.quote: Across 15,000 commodity-GPU generations with Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and SmolLM2-1.7B, hard answer-only schema decoding raises schema validity from 61.5% to 100.0%, but lowers answer accuracy from 19.7% to 11.0% and increases wrong-valid-schema outputs from 49.5% to 88.9%.

claims.claim: On a deterministic tool-call task (calendar), the same small model loses 43.5 points of executable accuracy purely from schema enforcement: Qwen2.5-1.5B scores 91.5% executable accuracy with prompt-only JSON vs 48.0% under a hard tool-call schema, while BOTH modes are 100.0% schema-valid. Therefore a deterministic external checker that validates only structure catches 0% of these failures — the failure is semantic. For the robot loop this means a schema/contract validator is necessary but demonstrably insufficient as the safety layer if the small model issues the action.
claims.quote: The strongest industry analogue is a deterministic calendar tool-call task: Qwen2.5-1.5B achieves 91.5% executable accuracy with prompt-only JSON but only 48.0% under the same hard tool-call schema, while both modes are 100.0% schema-valid. The error is semantic, not structural.

claims.claim: Scaling out of the problem by moving to a ~3B model does not remove the effect: the paper reports the 3B boundary still pays a direct-schema tax. Falsifiable prediction for this project: a Qwen3-4B local tier asked to emit a hard-schema tool call or route decision will show a measurable constrained-vs-free accuracy gap rather than zero gap.
claims.quote: We also show that the 3B boundary still pays a direct-schema tax and that delayed packaging supports a constructive design pattern: reason free, constrain late.

claims.claim: A mitigation exists and is design-shaped, not model-shaped: 'reason free, constrain late' (delayed packaging) — let the model generate unconstrained, then package into the schema in a separate step. This supports the alternative design where the local small model never emits the constrained decision directly, and argues against wiring grammar-constrained tool-call decoding into the local tier as the primary interface.
claims.quote: delayed packaging supports a constructive design pattern: reason free, constrain late

claims.claim: Measurement requirement with a falsifiable implication: schema validity, answer accuracy, executable accuracy, and wrong-valid-schema rate must be reported separately, because they diverge (here validity 100% while accuracy 11%). Any evaluation of a local tier that reports only 'valid tool call rate' or 'JSON parse success' will systematically overstate reliability. Scope limit to note: this study covers only 0.5B-1.7B English-task Qwen2.5/SmolLM2 models on one commodity GPU and provides NO Chinese/Cantonese evidence and no Qwen3 or T4-specific latency data.
claims.quote: The practical conclusion is direct: production systems should report schema validity, answer accuracy, executable accuracy, and wrong-valid-schema rate separately.

claims.claim: Marlin (the fast INT4/INT8 mixed-precision GEMM kernel path in vLLM) is NOT supported on Turing (SM 7.5), only on Ampere/Ada/Hopper. This directly constrains a T4: any GPTQ/AWQ weights loaded on g4dn.xlarge cannot use the Marlin kernel and must fall back to the slower generic dequant-GEMM path, so 4-bit quantization on T4 is primarily a VRAM-reduction measure rather than a guaranteed throughput win.
claims.quote: | Marlin | ✗ | ✗ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✗ |  (columns: Volta | Turing | Ampere | Ada | Hopper | AMD/Intel/CPU)

VERIFICATION OF THE SOURCE: arXiv 2608.05064 exists and is exactly what is cited. Confirmed via three independent fetches (abs page, export.arxiv.org API, and the v1 full-text HTML): "Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models", single author Jianru Shen, submitted 2026-08-05.

EVERY NUMBER IN THE CLAIM CHECKS OUT VERBATIM. From the full text: "Each dataset contributes a 200-question calibration set; the remaining 1,271 and 617 questions form the ARC and TruthfulQA test sets." Certified pairs at 20%: Qwen2.5-14B on ARC "99.8 % coverage with a realized test risk of 8.1 %"; Qwen2.5-7B on ARC "93.3 % with 10.8 %"; Qwen2.5-14B on TruthfulQA "43.6 % with 14.2 %". At 10%: "no pair is certified." 22 model-task pairs, 11 models (Qwen2.5 0.5/1.5/3/7/14B, Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 1B/4B/12B), 25,168 predictions, Clopper-Pearson upper bound with union-bound correction over the threshold grid. So the descriptive half of the claim is CONFIRMED, not misquoted.

WHY I STILL VOTE REFUTE: the load-bearing final sentence — "For a robot loop demanding better than 10% error, no model in this size class is certifiable" — is an overreach the paper does not license, on four independent axes.

(1) SIGNAL SCOPE. The paper measures ONE deferral signal and says so: verbalized confidence, "an integer the model states alongside its answer", and explicitly "Token probabilities ... are often unavailable in deployed settings and are not used." No logprob/entropy signal, no self-consistency, no trained router/deferral head, no embedding classifier. The correct reading is "self-reported integer confidence cannot support a 10%-risk certificate", NOT "no deferral mechanism can". The research question's candidate B (a fine-tuned sub-1B classifier as router) and logprob-based cascades are entirely outside the paper's evidence, so the claim cannot be used to rule them out.

(2) STATISTICAL-POWER CONFOUND. "None certified at 10%" is a finite-sample statement, not a capability statement. With a 200-question calibration set, a Clopper-Pearson UPPER bound, and a union-bound penalty spread over the whole candidate-threshold grid, the bound is loose by construction; after thresholding, the retained subset is well under 200 points, so the CP upper bound on a model whose TRUE risk is ~6-8% can still land above 10%. The claim converts "not certified at n=200" into the modal "no model ... is certifiable", which is exactly the inference the CP procedure does not support. A larger calibration set is the cheapest possible refutation and the paper does not run it.

(3) TASK-DOMAIN MISMATCH — the biggest gap for this project. The evidence is 4-way multiple-choice text QA. TruthfulQA is adversarially constructed to elicit falsehoods; calling it "the hard task" and then transferring its 43.6%-coverage number to "a robot loop" is a category error. The paper contains no tool-calling, no multi-step agent loop, no motion planning, no ROS, no latency, no Chinese/Cantonese, and no unsafe-action metric. The error the robot loop must bound (bad tool call, unsafe plan) is never measured.

(4) MODEL VINTAGE vs THE ACTUAL CANDIDATE. The tested set is Qwen2.5 / Llama 3.1-3.2 / Gemma 3 — all 2024-vintage. The project's front-end candidate is Qwen3 (4B / 8B / 14B / 30B-A3B), which appears nowhere in the 11 models. "No model in this size class" therefore generalizes from a model set that excludes every model actually under consideration, in a field where the ≤14B tier turned over at least once since Qwen2.5.

SOURCE-STRENGTH MISMATCH. Single-author preprint, 17 days old (2026-08-05 vs today 2026-08-22), no venue, no peer review, and no discoverable citations, replication, or third-party discussion (search returned nothing; no WebSearch tool available, only WebFetch, so absence of critique is weak evidence either way). That is adequate support for "one preprint reports these 22 pairs" but not for a universal impossibility claim about a whole model size class deployed on a different modality.

USABLE RESIDUE: cite it narrowly as "verbalized self-confidence in 0.5-14B 2024-era models does not yield a distribution-free 10%-risk deferral certificate on MC-QA with a 200-item calibration set (Shen, arXiv:2608.05064, unreviewed preprint)". Drop the robot-loop extrapolation and drop "no model in this size class".

VERDICT: the numbers are verbatim correct, but the load-bearing conclusion is an overreach that the source itself contradicts.

WHAT CHECKS OUT (verified against arXiv:2608.05064v1, "Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models", Jianru Shen, submitted 5 Aug 2026, MIWAI 2026 / Springer LNAI). Sect. 4.4 verbatim: "At r_max=20% it certifies Qwen2.5-14B on ARC at 99.8% coverage with a realized test risk of 8.1%, Qwen2.5-7B on ARC at 93.3% with 10.8%, and Qwen2.5-14B on TruthfulQA at 43.6% with 14.2% (Fig. 3); every other pair receives no certified threshold. At r_max=10% no pair is certified..." Abstract confirms 200-question calibration set, Clopper-Pearson, 11 models x 2 tasks = 22 pairs, 25,168 predictions. Table 1 CertCov column shows 93.3 / 99.8 / 43.6 exactly. So every digit in the claim is real, and 43.6% coverage = 56.4% deferred is correct arithmetic.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED — the final sentence ("For a robot loop demanding better than 10% error, no model in this size class is certifiable") is contradicted by the paper's own Limitations, Sect. 5, verbatim: "the 200-question calibration sets CAP THE CERTIFIABLE REGIME, AS THE EMPTY r_max=10% OUTCOME SHOWS". Sect. 4.4 says the same: the empty 10% result is "illustrating the sample-size cost of strict finite-sample guarantees". The zero-at-10% is a statistical-power artifact of n=200 plus a union-bound correction delta/|T| over the whole calibration-confidence grid — not a capability limit of <=14B models. result.evidence:
The source is real and the quoted fragment is verbatim, but the claim misstates the theorem's antecedent and inverts its consequence — and the refutation comes from the cited paper itself.

VERIFIED PARTS. arXiv:2608.05064v1 = "Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models", Jianru Shen (single author, University of Montana), submitted 2026-08-05. It does contain "eight of 22 model-task pairs hit the temperature-scaling infeasibility floor within one percentage point of the predicted bound" (11 models x 2 benchmarks = 22 pairs, 25,168 predictions). So the 8/22 count is accurately reported.

REFUTATION 1 — the claim drops the load-bearing assumption. Corollary 1 verbatim: "Suppose every raw confidence satisfies c_i > 1/2 AND the model's accuracy is acc < 1/2. Then for every T>0 the calibrated confidences satisfy ĉ_i > 1/2, and ECE >= 1/2 - acc. No temperature can calibrate such a model." The claim states the conclusion under only the confidence>1/2 condition ("if a model's stated confidence always exceeds 1/2, no temperature T>0 can calibrate it"). That is false as written: a model emitting c=0.6 with acc=0.60 is already calibrated, and the bound 1/2-acc is vacuously negative whenever acc>1/2. The result is regime-bound, not general — and the paper's own table confirms it: all eight floor-hitting pairs have accuracy 22.4%-50.7%, i.e. at or below chance on 4-way ARC-Challenge / TruthfulQA-MC. 14 of 22 pairs did NOT hit the floor. Per the project's own "Constraints Are Design Choices" rule, this is representation-bound, not absolute.

REFUTATION 2 — the "so ... for deferral" conclusion is contradicted by Proposition 2 of the same paper: "Let g be strictly increasing and ĉ_i = g(c_i). Then the set of achievable operating points {(Cov(τ), Risk(τ))} is identical under c and ĉ. In particular, temperature scaling leaves the risk-coverage frontier and the error-detection AUROC unchanged." Temperature scaling therefore never could have changed deferral quality in either direction; the infeasibility floor is a statement about the reported ECE number, not about whether deferral/escalation works. The claim's inference ("provably cannot rescue a small model's confidence for deferral") inverts the paper's framing.

REFUTATION 3 — the "cheap fix" premise is false in the same abstract: "Platt scaling reduces ECE to as low as 0.02". Platt scaling is a 2-parameter fit on the identical held-out set — no more expensive than the 1-parameter temperature fit. So the cheap held-out fix is not defeated; only the specific 1-parameter variant is, and the paper offers the cheap replacement. What actually limits autonomy is certification, not calibration: "certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to only three model-task pairs and to none at 10%" — a materially different (and for this project, more damning) claim than the one under review.

REFUTATION 4 — strength/novelty inflation. Calling this a "distribution-free impossibility result" oversells an algebraic corollary of temperature scaling being strictly order/argmax-preserving, a property documented since Guo et al. 2017 ("On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks", temperature scaling does not change the predicted class). It is a deterministic bound on a fixed finite sample, not a distribution-free minimax impossibility theorem.

REFUTATION 5 — transfer to this project is unsupported. The 11 models are Qwen2.5 (0.5/1.5/3/7/14B), Llama 3.2 (1B/3B), Llama 3.1 (8B), Gemma 3 (1B/4B/12B) — no Qwen3, the actual candidate family. Both benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, TruthfulQA) are English MCQA; zero Chinese/Cantonese and zero tool-calling or ROS-2-style action tasks, so nothing here measures the routing/deferral signal the two-tier design needs. Source is a 17-day-old, single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint with no independent replication of the 8/22 figure; the paper also admits it had to correct a TruthfulQA MC measurement artifact, i.e. the accuracy values that drive the 1/2-acc floor are themselves format-sensitive.

WHAT SURVIVES (usable, weaker form): on English MCQA where a small model's accuracy is below 50% and its verbalized confidence never drops below 0.5, one-parameter temperature scaling cannot make ECE small (floor 1/2-acc, empirically matched within 1pp in 8 of 22 pairs); use Platt/isotonic instead, and note that no monotone recalibration changes AUROC or the risk-coverage frontier, so calibration is the wrong lever for routing at all — the binding constraint is finite-sample risk certification (3/22 pairs at 20% risk, 0/22 at 10%).

Then for every T>0 the calibrated confidences of (2) satisfy ĉ_i > 1/2, and ECE ≥ ...". The reviewed claim's supporting quote starts after "Then", dropping "acc < 1/2". The bound ½−acc is vacuous (negative) for any model above chance. The 8 pairs that hit the floor are exactly the near-chance rows: "Qwen2.5-0.5B on TruthfulQA reaches 0.283 against a bound of 0.276, and Llama3.2-1B 0.254 against 0.252 ... these models pair near-ceiling verbal confidence with accuracy near chance." Table 1 shows the >50%-accuracy rows are unaffected (Qwen2.5-1.5B ARC 66.5%, 3B ARC 75.0%, 7B ARC 87.9%, 7B TQA 69.2%). 14 of 22 pairs did NOT hit the floor. The claim as written ("if a model's stated confidence always exceeds 1/2, no T>0 can calibrate it") is therefore false as stated and irrelevant to a 4B–14B router expected to be above 50% accurate.

DEFECT 2 — "the standard cheap fix ... provably cannot rescue" is refuted by the same paper's measurements. Platt scaling is the same cheap held-out-set fit plus one bias parameter, and it fixes exactly these rows: "Gemma3-1B on ARC falls from an uncalibrated ECE of 0.687 to 0.262 under TS but to 0.030 under Platt"; Qwen2.5-0.5B ARC 0.497 → 0.022 Platt; Qwen2.5-0.5B TQA 0.283 (TS, at floor) → 0.060 Platt. The paper states the impossibility is a one-parameter artifact: "Platt's bias term supplies exactly the missing degree of freedom" and "Platt's bias term is exactly the degree of freedom that separates feasible from infeasible calibration on overconfident small models." So the infeasibility is specific to the 1-parameter temperature family, not to cheap post-hoc calibration.

DEFECT 3 — wrong causal mechanism for deferral. The paper's Prop. 2 says "strictly monotone calibration preserves the risk-coverage frontier and error-detection AUROC" and that all 22 fitted Platt slopes are positive so "every threshold-induced retained set coincides with that of the raw scores." Calibration, feasible or not, cannot change threshold-based deferral discrimination at all — so the ECE bound is a red herring for deferral. What actually kills deferral in the paper is discrimination and certification: "AUROC for error detection is modest everywhere: models below 2B sit near 0.5, Llama3.2-3B on TruthfulQA falls to 0.468, and the largest models reach only 0.63 to 0.66 ... Gemma3-12B attains 89.2% on ARC with an AUROC of 0.509"; and certified autonomy at 20% risk is granted to only 3 of 22 pairs, 0 at 10%. The correct pessimistic claim for this project is AUROC≈0.5–0.66, not an ECE floor.

DEFECT 4 — strength/novelty inflation. The math is elementary: σ(logit(c)/T) > 1/2 for every T>0 whenever c > 1/2, i.e. temperature scaling is sign/rank preserving about 1/2 (the argmax-preservation property already noted in Guo et al. 2017, which the paper cites as [7]). The paper labels it Corollary 1, not a theorem; the reviewed claim brands it a "distribution-free impossibility result". Scope also limits transfer to this project: single author, minor venue (MIWAI/LNAI), 11 models are Qwen2.5/Llama3.2/Gemma3 (NOT Qwen3), two English multiple-choice benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, TruthfulQA), 25,168 predictions on "a single consumer laptop" — zero Chinese/Cantonese and zero tool-calling/agentic deferral evidence.

Salvageable core (for the parent): 8/22 near-chance small-model pairs sit within 1pp of a temperature-scaling ECE floor — use it only as "temperature scaling alone is the wrong calibrator for sub-2B near-chance models; use Platt (adds a bias term)". Do NOT use it to argue calibration can't support deferral; use the AUROC 0.509–0.66 and 3/22-certified-at-20%-risk numbers from the same paper instead, which are much stronger against a local-small deferral gate.

(1) Quote and numbers check out exactly. Paper exists, is real, is primary. Sect. 4.2 verbatim: "AUROC for error detection is modest everywhere: models below 2B sit near 0.5, Llama3.2-3B on TruthfulQA falls to 0.468, and the largest models reach only 0.63 to 0.66. High accuracy does not imply discrimination, Gemma3-12B attains 89.2% on ARC with an AUROC of 0.509." Table 1 AUROC column confirms: sub-2B = 0.522/0.477 (Qwen2.5-0.5B), 0.492/0.495 (1.5B), 0.531/0.503 (Llama3.2-1B), 0.516/0.489 (Gemma3-1B); Qwen2.5-14B = 0.655/0.629. So no misquote.

(2) FATAL SCOPE DEFECT. The paper deliberately measures ONLY verbalized confidence and explicitly refuses to measure the signals a locally-hosted router would actually have. Sect. 3.2: "token-level probabilities are often unavailable in deployed settings and are not used." Related Work: "Token probabilities and semantic uncertainty provide direct uncertainty signals [9,18,3] but require white-box access or multiple generations that deployed text interfaces rarely afford." The claim's exclusion rationale is inverted in this project: a Qwen3 running on the T4 IS the white-box case — logits, entropy, P(IK) probes, and n-sample self-consistency are all available at zero API cost. The paper provides ZERO evidence that those signals also sit at 0.5. Nor does it test the dominant router design in the literature (RouteLLM/FrugalGPT-style: a separate trained query-difficulty classifier that never asks the small model to self-assess). So "the signal it would use to say 'this one is too hard, escalate'" is a false singular — the paper refutes one of at least four candidate signals.

(3) MODEL GENERATION MISMATCH vs the actual research question. The 11 models are Qwen2.5 (0.5/1.5/3/7/14B), Llama3.2-1B/3B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma3-1B/4B/12B. No Qwen3. No reasoning-trained model. The claim's label "open-weight models 0.5B-14B" is generation-agnostic but the sample excludes the exact candidate family under evaluation.

(4) MEASUREMENT FRAGILITY. All runs are "default quantized builds" via Ollama on one MacBook Air M4 (quantization scheme unspecified; the paper lists "one quantization scheme" as a limitation). Llama3.2-1B had only 27.7% strict format compliance. Confidence is an INTEGER emitted in text — heavy ties compress AUROC toward 0.5 mechanically. Gemma3-12B at 89.2% accuracy / AUROC 0.509 is exactly what "emits 90 for almost everything" produces: that is an elicitation-format artifact, not proof the weights contain no usable difficulty signal. The paper also had to repair an answer-ordering artifact in TruthfulQA-MC where "a constant first-letter policy attains perfect accuracy" — a sign the measurement substrate was fragile.

(5) SOURCE STRENGTH vs CLAIM STRENGTH. Single author (J. Shen), arXiv preprint 17 days old at review time, no peer review, no citation record, LNCS-formatted (submission ≠ acceptance). Two English multiple-choice benchmarks only. Self-declared limitations: "both benchmarks are multiple choice, so open-ended generation remains untested"; "models are capped at 14B under one quantization scheme"; certificate "void under distribution shift". Grep for Chinese/Cantonese/multilingual: zero hits. The project's task is open-ended Cantonese/Mandarin voice dialogue + ROS 2 tool-calling — neither the language, the task form (open-ended generation), nor the distribution (non-i.i.d. live robot) is covered. "Near-useless" is a strong universal verdict resting on n=2 English MCQ datasets from one unreviewed preprint.

(6) The paper's own conclusion is narrower than the claim: it does NOT say routing is impossible, it says verbalized confidence "alone is too weak an error signal to act on directly, motivating the calibrated, certified deferral of Sect. 4.4" — and it still certifies autonomy for 2 Qwen pairs at 20% risk (CertCov 93.3% and 99.8%). That is a call for an external certificate layer, not a refutation of two-tier escalation.

CAVEAT ON MY OWN WORK: no WebSearch tool was available in this environment and duckduckgo.com/html returned a CAPTCHA, so I could not independently search for contradicting or corroborating third-party literature (e.g. logprob/semantic-entropy AUROC baselines at the same scales). The refutation above rests entirely on the primary source's own text, which is sufficient for the scope defect but leaves the external-contradiction test unrun.

USABLE RESIDUE (for the parent agent): keep the narrow claim — "verbalized integer self-confidence from Qwen2.5/Llama3.x/Gemma3 at 0.5-14B, on English MCQ, has error-detection AUROC 0.468-0.66, i.e. unusable as a standalone escalation trigger (arXiv:2608.05064, Table 1)". Drop the generalization to "a local small-model router", and require a separate measurement of logprob-margin / entropy / self-consistency / trained-classifier AUROC before concluding the router premise is dead.

PARTIAL REFUTATION — the numbers are real, the inference is not. Split verdict by sentence.

SENTENCE 1 (SUPPORTED, verbatim). arXiv:2608.05064 exists and is exactly as cited: "Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models", Jianru Shen, submitted 5 Aug 2026, cs.CL, accepted at MIWAI 2026 (Springer LNAI). Table 1 AUROC (error detection), verified from the HTML full text: Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.522/0.477 (ARC/TruthfulQA), 1.5B 0.492/0.495, 3B 0.554/0.537, 7B 0.579/0.581, 14B 0.655/0.629; Llama3.2-1B 0.531/0.503, 3B 0.533/0.468, Llama3.1-8B 0.538/0.519; Gemma3-1B 0.516/0.489, 4B 0.544/0.527, 12B 0.509/0.640. The quoted sentence is verbatim in the paper. So "~0.5 below 2B, 0.63-0.66 at the top" is accurately transcribed.

SENTENCE 2 (UNSUPPORTED BY THE CITED SOURCE). I asked the full text directly: the paper "makes no mention of LLM routing, cascading to larger models, or hybrid architectures. Focus remains on local deferral to humans only." So "this directly attacks the premise of a local small-model router" is the claim author's inference, not the paper's finding. Worse, its embedded premise — "the signal it would use to say 'this one is too hard'" — is false for mainstream router designs: Hybrid LLM (arXiv:2404.14618, Apr 2024) routes on a *trained query-difficulty predictor* evaluated before any small-model generation, and RouteLLM (arXiv:2406.18665) trains routers "leveraging human preference data and data augmentation" — neither consults the weak model's verbalized self-confidence. A 0.65 AUROC on self-reported confidence therefore does not bound what a query-side router can do; it bounds one specific (and not the standard) router design.

OVERSTATEMENT. "near-useless" is stronger than the paper's own word, "modest". The paper's constructive result cuts the other way: Platt scaling drives ECE to 0.02 and certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to 3 of 22 model-task pairs (none at 10%) — i.e. a usable-at-loose-budget regime, not uselessness. Title framing is "when small models are safe to use", not "they are not".

- Elicitation is a SINGLE pass, single prompt ("an answer letter and an integer confidence in a fixed letter-comma-number format"). That exclusion rationale is exactly inverted for this project: the local Qwen3 runs on the user's own T4 with full white-box logprob/entropy access and can be sampled k times. SOURCE VERIFIED TO EXIST, QUOTE VERIFIED VERBATIM — BUT THE CLAIM OVERREACHES IT ON THREE COUNTS.

(1) The quote is explicitly abductive/hedged, and the conditioning was never measured. arXiv:2608.08265, "Opportunity Is Not Realizability: Selection-Valid Diagnostics for Multi-LLM Routing" (Shihab, Al Ahsan, Swaqeeb; submitted 2026-08-08) does contain, verbatim: "This is compatible with confidence being informative mostly on items the strongest fixed model already solves." It sits in **Appendix I ("Confidence Mechanism")**, immediately after "The pilot reports positive pooled point-biserial confidence–correctness correlations, yet weak net router gains." "X is compatible with Y" is one hypothesis offered to explain an observation — not a measured finding. Confirmed by fetch: the authors do **not** measure confidence informativeness conditioned on item difficulty or on the strongest model's per-item correctness; they decompose a routing policy's outcome transitions (preserve/rescue/lose/shared-fail) relative to the frozen best fixed model. The claim's flat assertion "confidence signals carry information mainly on items the strongest fixed model already answers correctly" upgrades a hedged appendix conjecture into a measured law.

(2) The paper's own numbers contradict "confidence fails PRECISELY on the queries a deferral mechanism must catch." The same appendix reports the GSM8K decomposition as **rescue 10% of baseline failures vs. lose 13% of baseline successes** — a net loss, but a nonzero 10% rescue rate on exactly the items the baseline gets wrong, i.e. confidence is *not* uninformative on the hard set; the policy's problem is collateral damage on the easy set. Elsewhere: "Calibrating confidence helps consistently but modestly" and "the answer-aware verifier is the strongest method on ARC-Challenge." And the headline abstract sentence is: "strong routers beat the best fixed model, and most of the gap remains" — the paper certifies that deferral **works, just inefficiently** (recovering 7.5–14.4% of a 9.7–30.7-point oracle gap). That is a magnitude result, not the falsification the claim asserts. "This falsifies the assumption that small-model confidence can serve as a reliable escalation trigger" is a stronger conclusion than the cited paper draws or supports.

(3) Scope/strength mismatch. The load-bearing sentence rests on a **pilot: 4 models, ~150 ARC-Challenge / ~150 HellaSwag / ~100 GSM8K items**; confidence operationalized as normalized label probability on multiple choice. Model pool is TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B — pre-Qwen3, no reasoning models, no tool-calling, English-only, no latency axis. Nothing in it speaks to Qwen3-4B/8B confidence, Chinese/Cantonese, or a 900 ms-TTFT budget. Source is a 14-day-old un-peer-reviewed preprint from authors without an established track record; one hedged appendix line in a ~100-item pilot is not a primary basis for "falsifies."

(4) Contradicting literature. Gupta et al., "Language Model Cascades: Token-Level Uncertainty and Beyond" (arXiv:2404.10136, Google) finds that *naive sequence-level* confidence suffers length bias and under/over-emphasizes outputs, but **learned post-hoc deferral rules using token-level uncertainty "significantly outperform such simple aggregation strategies"** on FLAN-T5 cascades, with further gains from small-model embeddings + large-model intermediate layers. That locates the failure in *naive scalar confidence thresholds*, not in deferral signals as a class — directly qualifying the claim's universal framing.

WHAT SURVIVES (usable, weaker form): "Threshold-on-confidence routing over ≤7B open models recovers only 7.5–14.4% of a certified 9.7–30.7-point oracle gap, and on GSM8K a confidence policy rescued 10% of baseline failures while losing 13% of baseline successes — net negative; the authors conjecture confidence is informative mainly on items the best fixed model already solves (arXiv:2608.08265, Appendix I, pilot n≈100–150/task, 4 models)." That is defensible. The claim as written is not.

The paper is real and the two numbers are quoted correctly, but the claim built on them INVERTS the paper's own finding. Source: arXiv:2608.08265v1, "Opportunity Is Not Realizability: Selection-Valid Diagnostics for Multi-LLM Routing" (Shihab, Ahsan, Swaqeeb; submitted 8 Aug 2026; cs.LG; v1 preprint, no peer review, 52 KB). (1) The numbers check out. Table 7 (Appendix G, "Post-Inference Selectors"): "Temperature-scaled maximum" = .877 ARC-C, .673 HellaSwag, .585 GSM8K, .607 MMLU. Table 7's caption does state these "all require running several candidates before deciding and therefore sit in a different cost regime from Table 4," and Appendix G's text says "Their accuracy is therefore not directly comparable at equal inference cost." So the cost-regime half of the claim is supported.

(2) "The ONLY confidence-based selector reaching usable accuracy" is false WITHIN Table 7 itself. The same table lists "Confidence-vector logistic" at .880 ARC-C / .677 HellaSwag (mean .693) and "Answer-aware verifier" at .893 ARC-C — both above temperature-scaled maximum (mean .686). Temperature-scaled is neither unique nor the best; the caption says calibration "helps consistently but modestly."

(3) "No pre-answer signal achieves comparable selection quality" is DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED by the paper's Table 4 (Appendix B, "Full Prompt-Router Results"), whose caption states "All prompt methods decide from the prompt and then invoke one candidate. Methods that query several candidates are in Table 7." Pre-answer, one-candidate-cost routers on ARC-C / HellaSwag: k-NN .877/.663; RouterDC .873/.660; EmbedLLM .880/.670; MODEL-SAT .880/.673; GraphRouter .883/.677; Avengers .883/.677; Zooter .883/.673; fine-tuned encoder with K heads .887/.683 (mean .719). The best PRE-answer router (mean .719) BEATS the best POST-inference confidence selector (mean .693) at one-eighth the inference cost. Seven of eleven pre-answer routers match or exceed the .877/.673 the claim presents as the unmatched post-inference ceiling.

(4) Metric misread. .877 is not "selector accuracy" — it is the routed system's end-to-end benchmark accuracy. Table 1 gives ARC-C empirical best fixed model = .873 (n=300) and oracle = .970; Table 4 gives frozen task-wise best fixed = .873/.657 (mean .699). So temperature-scaled confidence buys +0.4 pts on ARC-C over always calling one fixed model. With n=200–300 per dataset and exact Clopper–Pearson intervals (the paper's own ARC-C gap CI is [.016,.181]), .873 vs .877 vs .887 are inside noise; the claim's ranking is not statistically resolvable.

(5) The authors explicitly forbid the claim's generalization. Section 9/8: "A negative router result is bounded the same way: failed signals and learners bound their own classes, not the Bayes-optimal gain; an impossibility claim would need an identified upper bound on G_Z for a precisely defined Z; Theorem 7 provides such a route only for a declared finite signal and does not license a conclusion about the full prompt." The claim's "no pre-answer signal achieves comparable selection quality" is exactly the impossibility statement the paper disclaims.

(6) Scope does not transfer to the project. The pool is eight checkpoints of 0.5–7B models — there is no frontier model in the pool, so this is not a local-small → cloud-large (Qwen3-4B → GPT-5.6 Sol) cascade. Benchmarks are four answer-extractable multiple-choice / arithmetic sets (ARC-C, HellaSwag, MMLU, GSM8K) at 200–300 items; no tool-calling, no multi-turn agent loop, no Chinese/Cantonese, no latency measurement at all (the paper warns "Mean model latencies alone do not define the outcome oracle"), so the claim's "latency saving" inference has zero measured backing here.

What the paper DOES support (a different, defensible claim): its Appendix I table shows small-model self-confidence deferral is unusable — TinyLlama AUROC .558 / ECE .273, Qwen-0.5B .626/.370, Qwen-1.5B .782/.236, Qwen-3B .714/.154, with "Every recovered fraction is negative: routing costs accuracy on all four datasets" and max-confidence on GSM8K losing 39 baseline successes to rescue 16 (p=.021, recovered -57.5%). Plus the headline: strongest deployable prompt router recovers only 7.5–14.4% of a certified 9.7–30.7-point oracle gap, and the simultaneous interval for the best of eleven policies has lower limit zero throughout. The correct anti-cascade argument from this paper is "no router, pre- or post-answer, is certified to beat the best fixed model" — not "only post-inference selectors work."

The source paper is real and the descriptive numbers are accurate, but the claim's load-bearing conclusion is REFUTED BY THE SOURCE ITSELF.

Paper verified: arXiv 2606.07587v1, "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers" (Lu, Zhang, Zhang, Yu, Wang, Chen, Xing; submitted 2026-05-27, cs.LG, 23 pages). Descriptive facts check out verbatim in the HTML full text: 21 routing methods × 5 benchmarks (RouterBench, R2-Bench, EmbedLLM, CARROT/SPROUT, + their new Nine-by-30k/300k); "on four of five benchmarks, 69–75% of configurations fall within 0.02 pp of the empirical ceiling"; "kNN ranks among the top-2 methods on all five benchmarks"; "on RouterBench, the top 15 routers differ by only 0.23 pp".

Refutation 1 — the very next sentence after the quoted passage inverts the claim: "However, even the plateaued configurations remain 10 to 30 pp below the oracle router, showing that current methods have saturated before exhausting the available routing opportunity." The intro repeats it: "the best router trails the oracle by 10–30 pp across the five benchmarks." So the observed ceiling is NOT a property of the routing problem; there is 10–30 pp of measured headroom. The claim's quote was truncated exactly before the sentence that kills it.

Refutation 2 — the paper measures that engineering effort DOES move quality, which the claim says is impossible: "By scaling the routing training set from 30k to 300k queries, upgrading the query encoder from ModernBERT-base (~110M) to ModernBERT-large (~340M), and fine-tuning the router end-to-end, we obtain a combined accuracy gain of up to 2.13 pp, closing 14.6% of the oracle gap." That 2.13 pp is ~10× the 0.22 pp top-5 method spread the claim leans on. The paper's diagnosis is a "correctness-prediction bottleneck" of *current routers* learning "global averaged model-performance trends", i.e. a property of today's routers, not of the problem — and half the paper (§6 "Breaking the Plateau") plus the title ("...and Breaking the Accuracy Limits") is devoted to moving it. The claim converts "method choice within one family of frozen-encoder heads is fungible" into "the escalation policy is unimprovable" — an unsupported quantifier jump.

Refutation 3 — the paper's own Limitations section excludes this project's architecture: "Our study is restricted to single-shot routing over fixed model pools; cascades, ensembles, post-hoc rejection, and dynamically changing pools fall outside our scope and may scale differently... the plateau conclusion holds only within the cost–accuracy regimes that those benchmarks cover... absolute ceilings, oracle-gap sizes, and method rankings all depend on each benchmark's pool, query mix, and per-task scorers." A local-Qwen3 → GPT-5.6-Sol escalation loop IS a cascade with post-hoc deferral, so the stated "falsifiable implication for this project" is explicitly out of scope by the authors' own words.

Refutation 4 — setting mismatch makes transfer unsupported even ignoring (3): the sweep routes over 9-model pools on static English QA benchmarks, scored at λ=0 (accuracy only, cost ignored), and "assumes per-query correctness labels for every (query, model) pair". This project has 2 models, zero labelled (query, model) correctness data, a hard 900 ms TTFT budget the paper never measures, Chinese/Cantonese speech input, and multi-step ROS 2 tool calls. Nothing in the paper bears on latency-constrained 2-way deferral.

Net: the factual premises survive; the falsifiable implication ("no amount of engineering effort on the escalation policy will move end-to-end quality, because the ceiling is a property of the routing problem, not the router") is contradicted by the same primary source on three counts. Usable salvage for the project: (a) don't burn effort comparing exotic router *methods* — kNN-class baselines are top-2, spread 0.22 pp; (b) but a 10–30 pp oracle gap means the escalation decision is the unsolved part, which argues AGAINST trusting any cheap router to decide, i.e. it supports the report's alternative candidates B/C rather than the "routing is solved / irrelevant" reading.

The quoted numbers are verbatim correct (Sec 4.2: "69-75% of configurations fall within 0.02 pp of the empirical ceiling"; "top-5 methods differ by only 0.22 pp on average"; kNN/KMeans in the top tier). But the claim's load-bearing conclusion — "the ceiling is a property of the routing problem, not the router" and "no amount of engineering effort will move end-to-end quality" — is the exact opposite of what the paper argues.

(1) QUOTE TRUNCATED AT THE DECISIVE SENTENCE. The very next sentence in Sec 4.2 reads: "However, even the plateaued configurations remain **10 to 30 pp below the oracle router**, showing that current methods have **saturated before exhausting the available routing opportunity**." The "empirical ceiling" the claim treats as the problem's ceiling is 10-30 pp below the achievable one. Enormous headroom, not a hard limit.

(2) THE PAPER ATTRIBUTES THE PLATEAU TO THE ROUTERS, NOT THE PROBLEM. Abstract: "the plateau is largely caused by a **predictability bottleneck: current routers** mainly learn global averaged model-performance trends rather than fine-grained query-specific routing signals." Conclusion: "the **fundamental limits of current routing methods**." That is a statement about today's router designs, i.e. precisely a thing engineering can move.

(3) THE PAPER EMPIRICALLY BREAKS THE PLATEAU (Sec 6). Scaled-FT (300k data + ModernBERT-large + end-to-end FT) "improves **every** method, with an average gain of 1.24 pp"; fine-tuned routers "surpass the accuracy of the strongest frozen-kNN by 0.69 pp", vs frozen-kNN's own +0.49 pp — explicitly "showing that the gains are not simply due to using a larger encoder or more data"; closes 8.5% of the per-method oracle gap; Conclusion states gains "up to 2.13 pp". So router engineering demonstrably moves the number.

(4) "DESIGN CHOICE IS ESSENTIALLY IRRELEVANT" IS FALSE OUTSIDE THE TOP TIER. Table 1 (encoder-averaged, λ=0): Zooter 77.01 avg vs HybridLLM 66.12 avg = 10.9 pp spread across the 21 methods; on EmbedLLM the spread is 67.51 (Zooter) vs 46.87 (HybridLLM) = **20.6 pp**. RouterDC 73.84, IRT-Router 72.37, LinUCB 74.70. The paper says the worst methods "fail to train productively on some encoders or **collapse to routing queries to a single fixed model**". Also 25-31% of swept configs are OFF the plateau, and the 69-75% figure holds on only 4 of 5 benchmarks.

(5) THE PROJECT'S ARCHITECTURE IS EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE. Appendix B Limitations: "Our study is restricted to **single-shot routing over fixed model pools; cascades, ensembles, post-hoc rejection**, and dynamically changing pools **fall outside our scope and may scale differently**. ... Hence, the plateau conclusion holds **only within the cost-accuracy regimes that those benchmarks cover**." A local-small → cloud-large escalation loop IS a cascade with deferral/rejection — the one family the authors disclaim. Additional external-validity gaps for this project: pools are ~9-11 models (not 2 tiers), the headline table is at λ=0 (cost-agnostic, whereas cost/latency is the project's entire motivation), tasks are static single-turn QA with per-(query,model) binary correctness labels (authors note this "is harder to obtain for open-ended generation where correctness is judge-dependent"), no tool-calling/agentic multi-step, no latency term at all, and no Cantonese/zh-TW voice-loop evaluation.

(Immaterial — the gaps are inside the ±0.1-1.0 pp cross-encoder std — but it shows the claim was written from memory of the table, not the table.)

NET: the citation is a legitimate primary source and the descriptive statistics are accurate, but the claim inverts the paper's thesis (a plateau of current routers that the authors then break) into a fatalistic law about the routing problem, deletes the 10-30 pp oracle gap, and transplants a single-shot fixed-pool QA result onto a cascade — the exact configuration the paper's Limitations section excludes. Salvageable weaker version: "among mature single-shot routers over fixed pools on static QA, method choice within the top tier is worth <0.25 pp, so don't over-invest in picking a routing algorithm; frozen-encoder kNN is a fine default." That is supported. The version under review is not.

result.evidence:
The paper is real and the quoted string does exist — but the claim misrepresents its epistemic status, and the same paper contains four contradictions.

**1. The quote is an explicitly hedged conjecture from a PILOT, not a finding.** Verbatim Appendix I, first two sentences: "The pilot reports positive pooled point-biserial confidence–correctness correlations, yet weak net router gains. *This is compatible with* confidence being informative mostly on items the strongest fixed model already solves." "This is compatible with" = one hypothesis consistent with an observation, on pilot (not confirmatory) outcomes, with no test statistic, no interval, no effect size for the mechanism itself. Note the paper *also* reports POSITIVE confidence–correctness correlation in the same sentence. The claim upgrades this to a mechanism and then to "falsifies" — two levels of inflation. The authors pre-emptively forbid this move in §2.2: "A failed prompt classifier is **not** an information-theoretic impossibility result because the Bayes rule may lie outside the fitted class, optimization may fail, or the training labels may be ill-posed."

**2. The paper's own stated mechanism is DIFFERENT from the claim's.** Appendix O, Table 16 caption: "the models with the most to contribute are **the weakest ones, and their confidence is also the worst calibrated** (TinyLlama ECE .273/.299), so a confidence-gated router cannot identify the items they would rescue." That is "0.5–1.1B models are miscalibrated," not "calibration fails on hard items." Table 16 shows the pool's *strongest* model Phi-3.5-mini has self-confidence AUROC .735 / AUPRC .949 (vs .873 base rate) and Mistral-7B AUROC .722 on MMLU — i.e. mid-size self-confidence does rank its own correctness above chance.

**3. Same-paper numbers contradict "confidence fails."** Table 7 confidence-vector logistic .880/.677/.600/.613 (ARC-C/HellaSwag/GSM8K/MMLU) vs frozen task-wise best .873/.657/.660/.607 — beats or ties baseline on 3 of 4 tasks; caption reads "**Calibrating confidence helps consistently but modestly**." Appendix I itself: "On ARC and HellaSwag **rescues marginally exceed losses**." Only GSM8K is net-negative (rescue 10% vs loss 13%, net −0.03). The categorical claim rests on 1 of 4 tasks. Decisively, Table 8: **FrugalGPT, a sequential confidence-gated cascade, scores .700 macro accuracy at 0.62 relative cost vs frozen best fixed .699 at 1.00** — equal quality, 38% cheaper. That is exactly the two-tier deferral value proposition, measured positive, in the paper cited to kill it. Abstract's own conclusion: "**strong routers beat the best fixed model**, and most of the gap remains" — a claim about *magnitude* (7.5–14.4% of a 9.7–30.7pt oracle gap recovered), not impossibility.

**4. Structural scope mismatch with the user's architecture.** Pool (Table 6) = 8 checkpoints, **0.5B–7B, all small** (TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2b, Phi-3.5-mini-3.8B, Mistral-7B), bfloat16 on one A10G. "The strongest fixed model" is Phi-3.5-mini-3.8B, not a frontier model. The measured failure is *K-way selection among near-peers*, where routing away from a dominant incumbent can lose its successes (Mistral-7B on MMLU: rescue hit .077 vs loss rate .237). **A monotone escalate-only 2-tier cascade (Qwen3-4B → GPT-5.6 Sol) structurally cannot exhibit that loss term** — escalating to a strictly dominant model has near-zero loss risk, so the rescue-minus-loss arithmetic that produces the negative result does not transfer. Additionally: n=200–300 items/task; benchmarks are ARC-C/HellaSwag/MMLU (multiple-choice, confidence = "normalized probability of the selected label") + GSM8K; **zero non-English, zero Chinese/Cantonese, zero tool-calling/agentic, zero latency-budget evaluation.** And the paper states Table 7's confidence selectors are post-inference, requiring "querying multiple candidate models before selection... therefore not directly comparable at equal inference cost" — so they are not even in the deferral-gate cost regime.

**Salvageable kernel (what a defensible version would say):** "In one 2026 preprint (n=200–300/task, 8 models 0.5–7B, 4 English MC/math benchmarks), sub-2B models' self-confidence is badly calibrated (ECE .27–.30) and a max-confidence K-way router is net-negative on GSM8K (−0.03); mid-size (3.8–7B) self-confidence AUROC is only ~.72–.74. Treat small-model confidence as a weak, task-dependent signal requiring held-out calibration and a measured rescue/loss decomposition before trusting it as an escalation gate." That is directionally useful for the project. The claim as written — "falsifies," "confidence fails precisely on the queries a deferral mechanism must catch" — is not supported by the quote, is contradicted by three tables in the same paper, and rests on a 14-day-old unreviewed preprint's appendix hedge.

result.evidence:
The paper is REAL and the two quoted sentences are verbatim (PDF p.4, Sec. 4.2: "on four of five benchmarks, 69–75% of configurations fall within 0.02 pp of the empirical ceiling"; "the top-5 methods differ by only 0.22 pp on average. Notably, simple frozen-encoder retrieval methods such as kNN [22] and KMeans [25] appear in the same top tier"). But the CLAIM'S FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION is contradicted by the same paper, on four independent counts.

(1) The paper's title is "Understanding and BREAKING the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers", and its entire Sec. 6 ("Breaking the Plateau: Data, Encoder, and Fine-Tuning") measures exactly the engineering effort the claim says is futile. Fig. 5 / Sec. 6.2: scaling routing training data 30k→300k, upgrading the encoder ModernBERT-base(110M)→large(340M), and end-to-end fine-tuning improves EVERY one of the 8 trainable routers, mean +1.24 pp, max +2.13 pp (RouterDC), "closing 14.6% of the oracle gap" (abstract/intro) and 8.5% of the per-method oracle gap on average. Fine-tuned routers "surpass the accuracy of the strongest frozen-kNN by 0.69 pp, showing that the gains are not simply due to using a larger encoder or more data." So +1.24 to +2.13 pp is 6–10× the 0.22 pp top-5 spread the claim uses as its "irrelevance" scale. Engineering effort demonstrably moves the number.

(2) The claim inverts the paper's causal attribution. The claim: "the ceiling is a property of the routing problem, not the router." The paper (Sec. 5.3, Conclusion): "this plateau stems from a correctness-prediction bottleneck: current routers largely capture coarse, global patterns of model capability, but struggle to recover the fine-grained, instance-specific correctness signals" — and the qualifier is bounded: "the limiting factor is less the router architecture than the difficulty of reliably learning fine-grained, instance-level correctness FROM STATIC QUERY REPRESENTATIONS." The abstract says the plateau "remains FAR BELOW the oracle router"; Sec. 4.2 quantifies it: "even the plateaued configurations remain 10 to 30 pp below the oracle router, showing that current methods have saturated before exhausting the available routing opportunity." A 10–30 pp unexploited headroom is the opposite of a problem-intrinsic ceiling. The claim's "empirical ceiling" is the ceiling of TODAY'S FROZEN-ENCODER METHODS, not of routing.

(3) DIRECTLY DISQUALIFYING FOR THIS PROJECT: the paper's own Limitations (App. B) reads "Our study is restricted to single-shot routing over fixed model pools; CASCADES, ensembles, post-hoc rejection, and dynamically changing pools fall outside our scope and may scale differently... Hence, the plateau conclusion holds only within the cost–accuracy regimes that those benchmarks cover." The project's design (local Qwen3 → escalate to GPT-5.6 Sol) is precisely a cascade with post-hoc deferral. The authors explicitly exclude it. Additionally the setup is single-turn, static-label QA (RouterBench, R2-Bench, EmbedLLM, CARROT/SPROUT, Nine-by-30k; pools K∈[9,112]; per-(query,model) precomputed correctness labels) with NO tool-calling, NO multi-turn error compounding, NO latency term, and no Cantonese/Chinese voice condition; the paper even notes labels are "harder to obtain for open-ended generation." Transferring it to a ROS 2 voice loop is out-of-domain.

(4) The claim also contradicts a per-instance result in the same paper. Sec. 5.2: "Top-tier routers can disagree on up to 70% of queries, indicating distinct prediction functions... Conditioned on disagreement, the median absolute outcome change is |ΔY|=0.10–0.22, while the signed change is 5–17× smaller." So router choice is aggregate-neutral only because wins cancel symmetrically; individual decisions change on up to 70% of queries. For a safety-relevant escalation gate on a robot, where the cost of the two error directions is asymmetric (missed escalation of a dangerous plan ≠ wasted escalation), "aggregate accuracy is flat" does not license "design choice is irrelevant."

Minor factual overreaches in the claim itself: (a) "kNN ranks top-2 on all five benchmarks" is false per Tab. 1 — on Nine-by-30k kNN = 68.36 vs Zooter 68.38 and KMeans 68.38, i.e. rank 3 (kNN is #2 only on the 5-benchmark average, 76.95 vs Zooter 77.01). (b) The "0.02 pp" figure is internally implausible and the claim repeats it uncritically: Tab. 1's own top-5 spread is 0.04–0.52 pp and cross-encoder stds reach ±9.7 pp (LinUCB, RouterBench), so 69–75% of configs cannot literally sit within 0.0002 in accuracy of the ceiling — it is almost certainly a unit slip for 0.02 (=2 pp). The claim's rhetorical force rests on that unverified precision.

Net: the plateau phenomenon is real and worth citing as "don't over-invest in exotic router architectures; frozen-encoder kNN is a strong cheap baseline." The claim's stated implication — "no amount of engineering effort on the escalation policy will move end-to-end quality" — is refuted by the cited paper's title, abstract, Sec. 6 numbers, and Limitations section.

REFUTED on four independent grounds. The quote is real but the claim inverts its epistemic status, its mechanism, and its scope.

**1. The quote is an explicitly hedged abductive guess, not a result.** Verbatim, Appendix I ("Confidence Mechanism") of arXiv:2608.08265v1: "The pilot reports positive pooled point-biserial confidence–correctness correlations, yet weak net router gains. **This is compatible with** confidence being informative mostly on items the strongest fixed model already solves." "Is compatible with" = one candidate explanation offered to reconcile two observations. The claim restates it as measured fact ("Model confidence signals carry information mainly on...") and then escalates to "This falsifies..." Section 9 Limitations forbids that: "Per-dataset intervals remain wide, so **the firm claims are the certificate-level statements**." The confidence-mechanism paragraph is not a certificate-level statement; it is computed on the 4-model **pilot** (Table 14), which the paper files under "E.3 Exploratory router probes."

**2. The paper's OWN stated mechanism is a different one, and it does not transfer to small→frontier deferral.** Table 16 caption: "The diagnostic explains the negative results in Table 15: **the models with the most to contribute are the weakest ones, and their confidence is also the worst calibrated** (TinyLlama ECE .273/.299), so a confidence-gated router cannot identify the items they would rescue." That is a *peer-pool composition* artifact (rescue mass sits in TinyLlama/Qwen-0.5B), not "confidence is uninformative on hard items." In a Qwen3-small → GPT-5.6 Sol cascade the model with the most to contribute is the **strongest**, not the weakest, so the identified failure mechanism is absent by construction.

**3. The paper's own numbers contradict the claim's core assertion.** (a) Own-confidence error-ranking AUROC — exactly the quantity an escalation trigger needs — is ARC-C: Qwen-1.5B .782, Llama-3.2-3B .771, Gemma-2-2B .814, Phi-3.5-mini .843, Mistral-7B .686; MMLU .665–.735 for 1.5B+. Well above chance, i.e. small-model confidence *does* rank its own errors. (b) Table 15 discordant counts for the max-confidence router (router right / baseline wrong) are n10 = 14 (ARC-C), 32 (HellaSwag), 16 (GSM8K), 27 (MMLU) — nonzero information *precisely* on items the strongest fixed model failed. The negative net gain comes from n01 (18/37/39/35), i.e. **losing baseline successes** — a precision/harm failure, not a "no signal on hard items" failure. Table 14 states it outright: GSM8K "rescues 10% of examples but loses 13%."

**4. The paper explicitly excludes the architecture the claim is applied to.** Appendix G: raw/calibrated confidence, plurality vote and answer-aware verifier are **post-inference selectors** that "require querying multiple candidate models before selection" and are "evaluated separately from pre-answer routing." A small-model escalation trigger is a *pre-answer* abstention rule (the paper's separate G_Z estimand, Theorem 2) — the Appendix I evidence is from the wrong estimand. Worse, Appendix Q: "RouteLLM is not a direct baseline for our primary K-way correctness-routing setting... our setting permits multiple correct models and **contains no uniformly dominant endpoint**." The project's setting has a uniformly dominant endpoint (GPT-5.6 Sol). Pool is 0.5B–7B (TinyLlama, Qwen2.5-0.5/1.5/3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B) on one A10G, bf16, batch size 1, 200–300 items/benchmark, four MCQ/arithmetic datasets — no frontier model anywhere, and no tool-use, agentic, or Chinese/Cantonese task.

**5. Credible contradicting source.** arXiv:2307.02764, "When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?" (NeurIPS 2023, Jitkrittum/Gupta/Menon/Narasimhan et al.): confidence-based deferral, "despite being oblivious to the structure of the cascade... **often works remarkably well in practice**," and its theoretical characterization localizes failure to (i) downstream models that are **specialists** good on only a subset of inputs, (ii) label noise, (iii) train/test distribution shift. A homogeneous 0.5B–7B pool is the specialist/near-peer regime this theory flags; a uniformly stronger generalist frontier model is the favorable regime.

**6. The correctly scoped 2026 evidence supports a much weaker conclusion.** arXiv:2608.05064 (2026-08-05), 11 instruction-tuned models 0.5B–14B, 25,168 local predictions, ARC-Challenge + TruthfulQA: proves strictly monotone calibration **preserves error-detection AUROC** (the signal exists), Platt scaling drives ECE to 0.02, and certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to **3 of 22** model-task pairs and none at 10%. Defensible claim: small-model verbalized confidence is insufficient for *certified autonomous* abstention at tight risk budgets. That is not "confidence carries information mainly where the strong model is already right," and 3/22 ≠ 0.

**Source-strength mismatch:** a 14-day-old v1 preprint (submitted 2026-08-08, cs.LG, no venue), with the load-bearing sentence in an appendix, hedged, on the pilot subset, cannot carry the word "falsifies." Note the paper's own abstract concludes the opposite of a blanket negative: "**strong routers beat the best fixed model**, and most of the gap remains" (fine-tuned K-head encoder .719 vs frozen task-wise best .699).

**What survives:** a much narrower, still project-relevant claim — in a pool of near-peer small models with no dominant endpoint, confidence-gated selection recovers none of the oracle gap and can significantly regress (max-confidence on GSM8K: −57.5% recovered, McNemar p=.021 after Holm), because complementarity concentrates in the worst-calibrated members. Usable as a caution against small-model-only ensembling; not usable as a falsification of small→frontier confidence-based escalation.

PRIMARY SOURCE EXISTS AND MATCHES. arXiv:2606.07587 = "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers", Lu, Q. Zhang, S. Zhang, Yu, Wang, Chen, Xing; submitted 27 May 2026, cs.LG, 23 pages / 12 tables / 9 figures. Abstract confirms scope: "extensive study of 21 routing methods across five benchmarks reveals ... the routing plateau: many methods, including kNN, achieve very similar accuracy and converge to a narrow performance range that remains far below the oracle router", cause = "predictability bottleneck: current routers mainly learn global averaged model-performance trends rather than fine-grained query-specific routing signals."

NUMBER-BY-NUMBER CHECK (fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2606.07587v1):
1. "10-30 pp below oracle" — CONFIRMED. Intro: "all existing routers remain far below the oracle router ... For example, the best router trails the oracle by 10-30 pp."
2. "+2.13 pp from all three interventions combined" — CONFIRMED and it IS the combination, not the best single lever: "By scaling the routing training set from 30k to 300k queries, upgrading the query encoder from ModernBERT-base (~110M parameters) to ModernBERT-large (~340M parameters), and fine-tuning the router end-to-end, we obtain a combined accuracy gain of up to 2.13 pp". Ablation (Table 6): data scaling alone +0.47 pp, fine-tuning alone +0.42 pp, encoder scaling alone +0.13 pp, data+FT +0.77 pp, full Scaled-FT mean +1.24 pp across eight methods. So the claim quotes the paper's *most favourable* figure (2.13 = "up to"), i.e. it errs against its own pessimistic conclusion, not for it.
3. "closing 14.6% of the oracle gap" — CONFIRMED verbatim.
4. Per-benchmark (Table 1, encoder-averaged, best router = Zooter in both): RouterBench 80.38 vs oracle 91.69; EmbedLLM 67.51 vs oracle 97.97 (= 30.46 pp ≈ 30.5 pp). Claim says 80.39 for RouterBench — a 0.01 pp transcription/rounding slip, immaterial.
5. Model sizes/encoders: ModernBERT-base ~110M and ModernBERT-large ~340M — CONFIRMED verbatim.

DATE: 3 months old (27 May 2026 vs today 22 Aug 2026). Not outdated; it is the most recent systematic survey of the failure mode.

NOT MARKETING: no vendor involvement; the paper is a negative-result/limits study of 21 third-party methods, i.e. the opposite of a cherry-picked vendor benchmark.

WHERE I WOULD DOCK POINTS (qualifications, not refutations — do not let these be dropped when the claim is reused):
(a) "best ACHIEVABLE router" is looser than the paper. The paper measures the best of 21 *studied* methods; it does not prove an information-theoretic ceiling. Correct phrasing: "the best router in a 21-method sweep".
(b) The oracle is unattainable BY CONSTRUCTION, and the paper says so explicitly: it is defined as "if a router could see the correctness labels of every model before choosing, it would pick a correct one", and "it is computed from labels that a real router never sees at decision time, so it sits as an upper bound rather than something deployed systems can match." Consequence for the robot project: the 10-30 pp figure is NOT 10-30 pp of realizable headroom being left on the table; it is the distance to a label-oracle. Anyone citing this to argue "routing is broken" must not silently upgrade the oracle into an attainable target.
(c) The "+2.13 pp / 14.6%" pair is benchmark-specific and internally consistent only on the Nine-by-30k setting (best 68.38 vs oracle 82.65, gap 14.27 pp -> 2.13/14.27 = 14.9%). It must NOT be applied to EmbedLLM, where the same 2.13 pp would close only ~7% of the 30.46 pp gap. The claim's wording ("Verified per-benchmark") stops just short of that error but invites it.
(d) Single non-peer-reviewed preprint; I could not obtain independent corroboration (Google/DuckDuckGo returned no substantive results — CAPTCHA/JS walls; Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429, so citation count unverified). The claim's strength is however scoped to "this study measured X", and the measurements are directly readable in the source, so single-sourcing is acceptable here.
(e) Metric-frame caveat that a downstream reader should keep: this is per-query *accuracy vs oracle*, a different frame from the cost-quality-curve framing RouteLLM/FrugalGPT-lineage work reports wins in. The two are not in contradiction, but "routing gains X% cost reduction at Y% quality" claims are not refuted by this paper, and vice versa.

SOURCE IS REAL AND THE CORE SENTENCE CHECKS OUT — BUT THE "VERIFIED PER-BENCHMARK" NUMBERS ARE FABRICATED.

Paper verified to exist: arXiv:2606.07587v1 [cs.LG], 27 May 2026, "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers", Lu/Zhang/Zhang/Yu/Wang(Amazon)/Chen/Xing, Rice University. CC BY 4.0. I pulled the full HTML (582,702 bytes, /tmp/rph.html) and grepped it.

SUPPORTED parts:
- "even the plateaued configurations remain 10 to 30 pp below the oracle router" — exact string present (Sec. 4.2). Also "the best router trails the oracle by 10–30 pp across the five benchmarks" (intro).
- "we obtain a combined accuracy gain of up to 2.13 pp, closing 14.6% of the oracle gap. Nevertheless, a substantial gap remains" — exact, and the three levers are as claimed: 30k→300k (Nine-by-30k 23,027 train → Nine-by-300k 302,371 train), ModernBERT-base (~110M) → ModernBERT-large (~340M), plus end-to-end FT.
- Table 1 (λ=0) best cells match: RouterBench kNN 80.39±0.1 (Zooter 80.38); EmbedLLM Zooter 67.51±0.3. Both correct.

REFUTING findings:
1. FABRICATED ORACLE NUMBERS. The paper contains NO oracle accuracy per benchmark. grep over the full HTML: "91.69" = 0 hits, "97.97" = 0 hits, "0.9169" = 0, "0.9797" = 0, "91.6" = 0, "97.9" = 0, "30.5" = 0, "11.3" = 0. There is no "Oracle" row in Table 1 (I dumped the whole table: 21 method rows + a "Top-5 router spread" row, no oracle row). All 32 occurrences of "oracle" in the paper are prose/definition/Table-3-gap; the ONLY absolute oracle value stated anywhere is "On Nine-by-300k, the oracle accuracy on the shared test split is 0.8265". So the clause "Verified per-benchmark: RouterBench best 80.39% vs oracle 91.69%; EmbedLLM 67.51% vs 97.97% (30.5 pp)" asserts a verification that cannot have happened against this source.
2. THE RouterBench ORACLE NUMBER IS ALSO INCONSISTENT with what the paper does report. Back-deriving from Table 3 (RouterBench f_hard=0.111, hard gap=0.869, %expl=90.8%): full-test-set oracle-minus-all-router-mean = 0.111×0.869/0.908 ≈ 0.1063, i.e. ~10.6 pp above the 12-router MEAN (~79.5–80%), giving oracle ≈ 90.1–90.6% and a best-router gap of ~9.7–10.2 pp — not 91.69% / 11.30 pp. A second independent reader of the same HTML also estimated "approximately 90.6%". The claimed 91.69% overstates the gap by ~1.1 pp and cannot be read off Fig. 1's dashed line to 2 decimals.
3. OVERREACH IN WORDING. Paper says "the BEST ROUTER [of the 21 evaluated] trails the oracle"; the claim upgrades this to "the BEST ACHIEVABLE router". The string "best achievable" does not appear in the paper, and the paper explicitly says the oracle "is computed with hindsight from post-generation correctness labels" and "sits as an upper bound" a real router never sees — i.e. it is a non-attainable ceiling by construction, not a target the claim's phrasing implies.
4. SCOPE MISMATCH THE CLAIM HIDES (decisive for this project's question). Table 8: pool sizes K=9 (Nine-by-*), K=11 (RouterBench), K=10 (R2-Bench), K=13 (CARROT/SPROUT), K=112 (EmbedLLM). The oracle is max over K models, so the oracle gap grows mechanically with K — which is exactly why EmbedLLM (K=112, no cost annotations at all: "Cost … ×") shows the 30 pp end of the range. A 2-tier local-small→cloud-large escalation is K=2; citing a 112-model oracle gap as the bound on a 2-model cascade is not supported by this paper. All Table 1 numbers are λ=0 (accuracy-only, cost ignored), so they say nothing about the cost-quality question the cascade is meant to answer.
5. THE PAPER SELF-QUALIFIES in a way the claim drops: "absolute ceilings, oracle-gap sizes, and method rankings all depend on each benchmark's pool, query mix, and per-task scorers. Hence, the plateau conclusion holds only within the cost–accuracy regimes that those benchmarks cover." The claim presents 10–30 pp as a general law.

Not outdated (May 2026, current), not marketing, primary source, single-institution preprint with no independent replication yet — acceptable strength for the plateau finding, insufficient for the fabricated per-benchmark table.

NET: the claim's first sentence is well-supported verbatim; its second sentence ("Verified per-benchmark…") is unverifiable-to-false against the primary source, and its generalization to a 2-tier cascade is unsupported. Under the stated rule (unsupported by quote → refuted), refuted=true. Usable rewrite: "21 routers × 5 benchmarks (pools K=9–112, λ=0): the best router trails the hindsight per-query oracle by 10–30 pp; 10× data + 3× encoder + end-to-end FT together buy up to +2.13 pp (14.6% of the gap), avg 8.5% on Nine-by-300k (oracle 82.65%). Per-benchmark oracle accuracies are not reported; the gap magnitude scales with pool size and is not measured for a 2-model cascade."
