SOURCE VERIFIED (primary, fetched directly, /tmp/p.pdf + arxiv.org/html/2606.07587v1): arXiv:2606.07587v1 [cs.LG], 27 May 2026, CC BY 4.0, "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers", Lu/Zhang/Zhang/Yu/Wang/Chen/Xing (Rice University + Amazon). Current (3 months old), not marketing, not a forum post.

NUMBERS CHECK: every figure matches verbatim. Table 3 confirms per-benchmark rows — RouterBench f_hard=0.111, spread 0.030, hard gap 0.869, easy gap 0.023, 38.5x, 90.8% expl.; CARROT/SPROUT 0.118/0.153/0.621/0.023/27.2x/69.9%; R2-Bench 0.138/0.219/0.671/0.020/34.0x/75.5%; Nine-by-30k 0.164/0.216/0.756/0.055/13.8x/86.1%; EmbedLLM 0.354/0.156/0.685/0.064/10.7x/79.3%. "spread ... only 3.0-21.9 pp" verbatim. "Routers concentrate on 2-3 LLMs regardless of difficulty" verbatim.

REFUTATION 1 (decisive — authors disclaim exactly this use). Appendix B, Limitations, verbatim: "Our study is restricted to single-shot routing over fixed model pools; cascades, ensembles, post-hoc rejection, and dynamically changing pools fall outside our scope and may scale differently." The project premise under attack IS a cascade with post-hoc deferral. The claim cites a paper that names cascades and post-hoc rejection as out of scope to "directly refute" a cascade. Related Work confirms: "Cascades, orchestration, and bandit-style routers ... sit at the edge of the single-shot setting and serve as reference points."

REFUTATION 2 (failure direction is inverted). Broader Impact, verbatim: "routers trained for aggregate accuracy tend to over-select the globally strongest model even on queries where it is wrong (Sec. 5.1, Fig. 4)". That is OVER-escalation, not failure to escalate. In a local-small -> cloud-large cascade, defaulting to the strongest model is the safe behavior. The claim's headline sentence "Routers fail specifically on the queries that require escalation" asserts the opposite of the mechanism the paper measured.

REFUTATION 3 (the hard-query gap is unrecoverable by ANY two-tier design, so it cannot measure escalation-detection). Sec 5.1 definition, verbatim: hard iff "n_correct(i)=1, or 1 < n_correct(i) <= max(8, ceil(K/2)) and the global top-1 model is incorrect on i", over SOLVABLE queries only. The second branch requires the router "to look beyond the strongest average-performing model." Where the global top-1 (the analogue of GPT-5.6 Sol) is wrong, escalating to it cannot help. The 0.621-0.869 gap therefore measures specialist-identification among a large pool, not "detect that the small model will fail." Pool sizes are K in [9,112] (Tab. 8) — a 1-of-9 to 1-of-112 identification task, versus the project's binary 1-of-2. Correspondingly, "they select from only 2-3 models regardless of difficulty" is vacuous in a 2-model pool.

REFUTATION 4 (claim misstates the definition). The claim renders hard as conjunctive "(few models answer correctly, global-best model wrong)". It is disjunctive: the n_correct=1 branch carries no global-best-wrong condition.

REFUTATION 5 (paper's own conclusion opposes an impossibility reading). Title says "...and Breaking the Accuracy Limits". Abstract: "larger training datasets, stronger encoders, and end-to-end fine-tuning can further improve routing accuracy." Sec 6.2 is titled "Scaled Fine-Tuning Improves All Trained Routers." Sec 6.4: "Our proposed Scaled-FT narrows the gap to the oracle but does not close it. This gap is expected: the oracle is computed with hindsight from post-generation correctness labels." The paper frames the plateau as a limit of CURRENT query-only methods and names untried fixes ("lightweight lookahead signals from partial generation or confidence estimates") — i.e. it does not rule out a cheap deferral signal, it says nobody has built one from static query embeddings.

REFUTATION 6 (scope leakage). Fig. 4's "2-3 LLMs" caption is for the CARROT benchmark specifically; the claim states it as general. Limitations also says "the plateau conclusion holds only within the cost-accuracy regimes that those benchmarks cover" and that the analysis "assumes per-query correctness labels for every (query, model) pair ... harder to obtain for open-ended generation." The project's target loop is Chinese/Cantonese voice dialogue + ROS 2 tool-calling with no binary per-query correctness labels; the benchmark suite is English-dominant static QA (57 sources, MMLU/GSM8K/ARC-style with answer-extraction scorers).

MINOR: study is 21 routers across 5 benchmarks; Table 3's spread is over a 12-router subset. The claim's "the 12 routers" is faithful to Tab. 3 but reads as if it were the whole study.

SURVIVING WEAKER CLAIM (what should be reported instead): "Across 21 routing methods and 5 benchmarks (arXiv:2606.07587, May 2026), query-only routers plateau far below oracle; 69.9-90.8% of the oracle gap sits on 11.1-35.4% hard queries, and routers over-select the globally strongest model even when it is wrong. This is evidence that predicting per-instance correctness from the query alone is unsolved, but the authors explicitly exclude cascades and post-hoc rejection from scope, so it does not settle whether a cheap escalation detector is buildable."

Search caveat: WebSearch was not available in this environment; I verified against the primary artifact (PDF + full HTML) rather than secondary commentary, so no independent replication/critique of this 3-month-old v1 preprint was located either way. That absence is itself a source-strength problem for a claim phrased as "directly refutes."

I pulled the primary source and extracted Table 1 verbatim (pdftotext of arXiv:2606.07587, "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers", Lu/Zhang/Zhang/Yu/Wang/Chen/Xing, preprint, submitted 2026-05-27; local text at /tmp/rp.txt line 230).

WHAT CHECKS OUT (numbers are exact, not misquoted):
- HybridLLM [15]: 71.67±0.0 / 60.46±0.0 / 46.87±0.0 / 73.99±0.0 / 77.62±0.0, Avg 66.12 — matches the claim digit-for-digit.
- Zooter 77.01 top, kNN 76.95, Elo 76.93; 77.01 − 66.12 = 10.89 pp. "Roughly 11 pp" and "lowest Avg in the table" are correct (OptLLM has no Avg because EmbedLLM is "—", but its four reported cells all exceed HybridLLM's).

WHY THE CLAIM IS STILL REFUTED — its load-bearing sentence ("Confidence-based deferral is not merely at the plateau; it is measurably below it") is contradicted by the SAME table:
1. The paper's own taxonomy (App. §6.1, /tmp/rp.txt line 483) labels cp_router [56] and mess_plus [66] "confidence-cascade routers." Their Table 1 averages are CP-Router 76.64 and MESS+ 76.77 — i.e. 0.24–0.37 pp off the 77.01 leader, squarely ON the plateau. CP-Router is cited (line 704) as "CP-Router: An Uncertainty-Aware Router Between LLM and LRM, 2025" — a BINARY weak-vs-strong deferral router driven by output uncertainty, which is structurally at least as close to the user's small→large design as HybridLLM is. So the confidence-deferral FAMILY sits at the plateau; one member of it does not.
2. The paper explicitly attributes HybridLLM's deficit to a training/degeneracy artifact, not to the deferral principle: "the lowest-performing methods, such as MIRT, IRT-Router, and HybridLLM, either fail to train productively on some encoders or collapse to routing queries to a single fixed model" (lines 250–251). HybridLLM's ±0.0 cross-encoder std on all five benchmarks (vs ±0.0–1.1 for others) is the fingerprint of exactly that collapse — its score is encoder-invariant, i.e. it is effectively reporting one fixed model's accuracy, not a measurement of deferral quality.
3. Task/design mismatch inflates the gap: the benchmark metric is K-way "did the router pick a model that is correct," over pools of K ∈ [9, 112] (§4.1, Tab. 8). HybridLLM is a 2-model method forced into a ≥9-model selection task; the other 20 methods can exploit per-query choice among 9–112 models. An 11 pp deficit against 9–112-way routers is not transferable evidence about a K=2 architecture, which is the user's actual case.
4. The claim uses the λ=0 (quality-only, zero cost weight) table — the one regime where a cost-saving cascade has no reason to exist. In the cost-aware table (Tab. 2, λ=0.2/0.5/0.7/0.9, "16 calibrated methods"), HybridLLM is ABSENT entirely. The paper therefore contains NO measurement of HybridLLM in the cost-utility regime that motivates two-tier deferral in the first place.
5. Source-strength caveat: unrefereed arXiv preprint (v1, 2026-05-27), single group, no independent replication found; adequate for reporting its own Table 1, thin for the strong causal generalization the claim draws from it.

Correct residual finding (usable, weaker): in this preprint's λ=0 K-way routing-accuracy setting, one specific 2018-style binary small/large router (HybridLLM) degenerates and lands 10.89 pp below the plateau, and the paper diagnoses it as collapse-to-one-model. That is evidence that naive binary deferral routers can fail degenerately — NOT evidence that confidence-based deferral as a class is below the plateau (CP-Router 76.64 / MESS+ 76.77 falsify that), and not evidence about the user's K=2 latency-motivated design.

result.evidence:
The NUMBERS are verified verbatim, but the claim's two load-bearing assertions — that HybridLLM is "a confidence-based binary small-vs-large deferral router" and therefore that "confidence-based deferral is measurably below the plateau" — are both refuted.

VERIFIED (supported): arXiv 2606.07587 "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers" (Lu, Zhang, Zhang, Yu, Wang, Chen, Xing; submitted May 2026) is real. Table 1 (Sec. 4.2, test routing accuracy at lambda=0, averaged across encoders, %) contains exactly: HybridLLM 71.67±0.0 / 60.46±0.0 / 46.87±0.0 / 73.99±0.0 / 77.62±0.0 / avg 66.12; Zooter 80.38/68.38/67.51/82.12/86.64/77.01 (highest); kNN 80.39/68.36/67.16/82.08/86.78/76.95. 77.01-66.12 = 10.89 pp, so "roughly 11 pp" is right, and HybridLLM is the only method below 70 among the rows with a computed average.

REFUTATION 1 — mechanism misattribution (fatal). HybridLLM = Ding et al., arXiv 2404.14618, "Hybrid LLM: Cost-Efficient and Quality-Aware Query Routing." Its own abstract: "a router that assigns queries to the small or large model based on the predicted query difficulty and the desired quality level." It is a PREDICTIVE pre-hoc router (trained DeBERTa quality-gap predictor) that decides BEFORE any generation. It is NOT confidence-based, and it is NOT a deferral/cascade — the small model never runs prior to the decision, so no confidence signal from the small model exists. The user's proposed architecture is the opposite topology: run local Qwen3, measure confidence, then escalate to GPT-5.6 Sol. Calling HybridLLM "the routing method most structurally similar" to that cascade, and generalizing its score to "confidence-based deferral," measures a mechanism the row does not contain. The paper itself files HybridLLM under the "expert-orchestration and cascade routers" family and notes cascades/orchestration/bandit routers sit "at the edge of the single-shot setting" it evaluates — i.e. an acknowledged framework mismatch, not a clean verdict on deferral.

REFUTATION 2 — the paper's own diagnosis contradicts the claim's causal reading. Verbatim from the paper: "the lowest-performing methods, such as MIRT, IRT-Router, and HybridLLM, either fail to train productively on some encoders or collapse to routing queries to a single fixed model." The authors attribute 66.12 to training failure / degenerate collapse in THEIR harness, not to an intrinsic ceiling of the paradigm. The ±0.0 standard deviation on all five benchmarks is consistent with exactly that collapse (a router that always emits one fixed model is encoder-invariant and deterministic), which makes 66.12 approximately a best-single-model baseline rather than a measurement of deferral quality. The claim's sentence "Confidence-based deferral is not merely at the plateau; it is measurably below it" converts a reported implementation pathology into a design-space law.

REFUTATION 3 — metric is off-axis for the claim's use. Table 1 is routing accuracy at lambda=0, i.e. pure accuracy maximization with the cost term zeroed. HybridLLM's stated objective is cost-efficiency at a target quality level; evaluating it with cost weight 0 scores it on the only axis it does not optimize. For the user's question — is a two-tier setup worth it for cost/latency — a lambda=0 accuracy ranking is not the relevant quantity.

MINOR: "WORST of all 21 methods" is imprecise. Only 20 of the 21 rows have a computed average; OptLLM's row is "OptLLM [36] 76.68±0.3 66.61±0.1 — 80.43±0.3 85.12±0.2 —" with the average shown as an em dash (missing EmbedLLM), so it is excluded from the ranking rather than beaten. Also unresolved: repeated fetches returned inconsistent candidate-pool sizes (K in [9,112]; one pass attributed K=112 to RouterBench, another to CARROT/SPROUT), and the paper does not describe how a natively BINARY router was adapted to K-way pools. If the 46.87 outlier is the large-K benchmark, that row partly measures "binary router in an N-way selection task" — a penalty that would NOT apply to the user's genuinely two-model setup. I flag this as unverified rather than asserting it.

SOURCE QUALITY: primary and correctly quoted, but an unreviewed ~3-month-old preprint whose own authors flag training failure for the exact row being used as the claim's linchpin. No third-party reproduction or critique found (Google search returned nothing on this paper). Adequate for the raw numbers; insufficient to support the strong generalization about confidence-based deferral.

result.evidence:
VERIFIED PART: the source is real and every number checks out. arXiv:2606.07587 "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers" (Lu, Zhang, Zhang, Yu, Wang, Chen, Xing; submitted 2026-05-27) contains verbatim: "the spread among the 12 routers on hard queries is only 3.0-21.9 pp, indicating that routers share the failure of routing hard queries", plus 11.1%-35.4% / 69.9%-90.8% / 0.621-0.869 vs 0.020-0.064 / 10.7-38.5x, and "routers concentrate on 2-3 LLMs regardless of difficulty". So the descriptive statistics are NOT refuted.

WHAT IS REFUTED IS THE CLAIM'S OPERATIVE CONCLUSION ("this directly refutes the premise that a cheap mechanism can reliably detect I-do-not-know-this-one"). Four independent grounds:

(1) DEFINITIONAL INVERSION - fatal for the two-tier use case. Verbatim definition from the paper: "We call a solvable query i hard if either ncorrect(i)=1, or 1<ncorrect(i)<=max(8,ceil(K/2)) and the global top-1 model is incorrect on i... All remaining solvable queries are labeled easy." Both branches require the globally strongest model to be wrong (or to not be the single correct one). In a local-small -> cloud-large escalation, those queries are exactly the ones where escalating does NOT help, by construction: the big model is wrong too. The escalation-relevant subset (small model wrong, big model right => global top-1 correct) falls into the paper's EASY bucket, where the router-to-oracle gap is only 0.020-0.064, i.e. routers are already near-oracle there. Read against the two-tier question, the paper is evidence FOR cheap routing on the subset that matters, not against it. The 69.9%-90.8% gap share is an artifact of a K-way model-picking oracle (K=9 up to K=112 models across the five benchmarks), which credits "find the one idiosyncratic weak model that happened to be right" - a term that simply does not exist in a 2-model cascade.

(2) MECHANISM MISMATCH. The paper's failure mode is explicitly a "predictability bottleneck" of pre-hoc routers scoring "static query embeddings" before any generation. The project's design runs the small model first and inspects its actual output (post-hoc deferral), which the paper does not test. Newer/credible work on that mechanism contradicts the universal claim: arXiv:2607.25018 "Conformal Cascade" (v3, 2026-07-31, i.e. AFTER the plateau paper) reports distribution-free accuracy guarantees for multi-tier deferral using prediction-set size and "improvements over confidence-threshold baselines across 18 benchmarks"; arXiv:2509.21837 (semantic-agreement cascades) reports "match or surpass target-model quality at 40% of the cost and reduce latency by up to 60%"; arXiv:2604.23577 (RouteNLP) reports 58% cost reduction in a production enterprise deployment at maintained acceptance rate. Most directly, arXiv:2605.06350 "Is Escalation Worth It? A Decision-Theoretic Characterization of LLM Cascades" (2026-05-07) concludes that cascade frontiers are limited by "structural costs rather than routing limitations" - the opposite causal attribution to the claim's.

(3) THE PRIMARY SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE CLAIM'S FRAMING. The title is "Understanding and BREAKING the Accuracy Limits"; the abstract ends "larger training datasets, stronger encoders, and end-to-end fine-tuning can further improve routing accuracy... actionable directions." The authors demonstrate +1.24 pp combined (data 30k->300k +0.47 pp, fine-tuning +0.42 pp, encoder +0.13 pp), closing 14.6% of the oracle gap. That is a modest, not an impossibility result; citing it as "directly refutes" misreports the authors' own stance. (The 14.6% figure does support a weaker claim: the plateau is real and hard to move.)

(4) OVERREACH IN WORDING + SCOPE. "spread is only 3.0-21.9 pp, i.e. they share the same failures" - a 21.9 pp spread at the top of the range is not "the same failures"; the word "only" is unsupported at the upper bound. Scope: one un-peer-reviewed preprint ~3 months old, no replication, English single-turn static text QA (RouterBench, R2-Bench, EmbedLLM, CARROT/SPROUT, Nine-by-30k/300k), and confirmed NO evaluation of tool-calling, no Chinese/multilingual, no latency - none of the three axes that decide this T4 voice+ROS2 project. Extraordinary strength ("directly refutes") is not matched by a single-preprint, wrong-setting evidence base.

USABLE RESIDUE for the report: cite 2606.07587 only for the narrow, supported claim "pre-hoc embedding-based K-way routers plateau far below oracle and concentrate on 2-3 models", and pair it with 2605.06350 / 2607.25018 for the cascade case. Do not use it to assert that binary local->cloud deferral is an unsolved problem.

A Decision-Theoretic Characterization of LLM Cascades" (2026-05-07, finds structural costs not routing limitations bind); arXiv:2607.25018v3 "Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference" (2026-07-31, deferral with formal guarantees beating confidence thresholds on 18 benchmarks); arXiv:2509.21837v3 semantic-agreement cascades (target-model quality at 40% cost, up to 60% lower latency); arXiv:2604.23577 RouteNLP (58% production cost reduction); and the primary source itself (arXiv:2606.07587 hard-query definition requiring the global top-1 model to be incorrect, plus its own +1.24 pp / 14.6%-of-gap improvement results)

NUMBERS VERIFIED, INTERPRETATION REFUTED.

Verified: arXiv 2606.07587 is real — "The Routing Plateau: Understanding and Breaking the Accuracy Limits of LLM Routers" (Lu, Zhang, Zhang, Yu, Wang, Chen, Xing). I pulled https://arxiv.org/html/2606.07587v1 and stripped it to text. Table 1 ("Test routing accuracy at λ=0", encoder-averaged, 21 rows) reads verbatim: HybridLLM [15] 71.67±0.0 / 60.46±0.0 / 46.87±0.0 / 73.99±0.0 / 77.62±0.0 / 66.12; Zooter 80.38/68.38/67.51/82.12/86.64/77.01; kNN 80.39/68.36/67.16/82.08/86.78/76.95. So the digits and the ~10.89 pp gap are correct, and HybridLLM is lowest of the 20 rows that have an Avg (OptLLM has no Avg due to a missing EmbedLLM cell, but OptLLM beats HybridLLM on all 4 shared benchmarks). That part survives.

REFUTATION 1 — the same table contradicts the claim's thesis. The paper's own taxonomy (Sec. on encoder fine-tuning) names its "confidence-cascade routers" explicitly: "confidence-cascade routers (cp_router [56], mess_plus [66])". Their Table 1 averages are CP-Router 76.64 and MESS+ 76.77 — i.e. 0.24–0.37 pp below best-in-class Zooter (77.01) and ABOVE trivial kNN's benchmark on two of five columns. So "Confidence-based deferral is not merely at the plateau; it is measurably below it" is falsified by the very table cited: the paper's actual confidence-cascade family sits AT the plateau. HybridLLM is a single outlier, not the family.

REFUTATION 2 — HybridLLM is not structurally the user's design. Ding et al. (arXiv 2404.14618) route "based on the predicted query difficulty and the desired quality level" — the decision is made from the query BEFORE any model runs. It never runs the small model first and never consults small-model confidence. The user's proposal (small model answers, self-assesses, escalates) is a post-hoc cascade. Calling HybridLLM "the routing method most structurally similar to the user's proposed two-tier small→large deferral" and "confidence-based" misassigns the mechanism.

REFUTATION 3 — the paper attributes 66.12 to degeneracy, not to deferral. Sec. 4.2: "the lowest-performing methods, such as MIRT [55], IRT-Router, and HybridLLM [15], either fail to train productively on some encoders or collapse to routing queries to a single fixed model." HybridLLM's std is ±0.0 on all five benchmarks across six encoders — zero variance, the signature of a collapsed deterministic router. Its worst cell is EmbedLLM (46.87 vs 67.51 plateau, −20.6 pp), the benchmark with the largest model pool; Nine-by-30k has 9 models and RouterBench 11, so a 2-model method is handicapped by pool size, not by its confidence signal.

REFUTATION 4 — the paper disclaims this number as out of scope. Limitations: "Our study is restricted to single-shot routing over fixed model pools; cascades, ensembles, post-hoc rejection, and dynamically changing pools fall outside our scope and may scale differently." And Sec. 2: "Cascades, orchestration, and bandit-style routers [15, 73, 74, 66, 32] sit at the edge of the single-shot setting and serve as reference points." HybridLLM is citation [15] — included as a reference point, expressly not as an in-scope measurement of cascade quality.

Net: source quality is high (primary, current — 2026), the quoted digits are exact, but the claim commits three overreaches: it generalizes one collapsed router to a mechanism verdict, mislabels a pre-execution difficulty router as confidence-based small-first deferral, and ignores that the paper's real confidence-cascade entries (CP-Router 76.64, MESS+ 76.77) are on the plateau. Usable downgraded form: "in a 9–11-model single-shot pool, a binary small/large query-difficulty router collapsed to one fixed model and lost 10.9 pp; the paper treats cascades as out of scope." The strong form — that confidence-based deferral is measurably below the plateau — is not supported.

result.evidence:
The source paper is real (arXiv:2605.07395v1, "Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts", Garg & Sagtani, submitted 2026-05-08, 12 pages / 14 tables, cs.LG+cs.AI+cs.CL, no venue, no affiliations listed, no citing works found, no other arXiv listing for the first author). The quote is verbatim. But the CLAIM built on it is refuted on four independent grounds:

(1) OVERREACH — the paper measures no cost at all. Full-text extraction: "The paper does not measure actual cost savings in dollars or tokens. It measures routing 'headroom' (quality gradients between tiers)... No cascade cost-benefit analysis is provided." The abstract's phrase is "existing routing HEADROOM estimates are substantially inflated" — headroom = the oracle quality gap that ideal routing could recover. The claim silently converts that into "published cost-savings estimates for small-model-first cascades are inflated." That inference is not in the paper, and no cascade cost figure (FrugalGPT, RouteLLM, AutoMix, Hybrid-LLM) is re-measured or disputed anywhere in it.

(2) DIRECTION INVERSION — the paper's finding pushes the opposite way from the claim's second sentence. Lower true unsolvability means small models solve MORE than benchmarks credited, i.e. a cheap first tier can own MORE queries. The paper's own data says exactly that: smallest tier (Gemma 4 E2B, ~2B) is the optimal tier for 50.3% of queries under judge evaluation, and the abstract's collapse finding is "~79% smallest-tier optimal" as the majority class. A dataset in which the cheapest 2B tier is optimal for 50-79% of queries is evidence FOR, not against, "a cheap first tier has a large set of queries it can own." What the paper actually shows is that routers cannot IDENTIFY the residual ~21% needing escalation (collapse to majority-class prediction, verified by random-feature and shuffled-label controls, 13-17 pp opportunity cost). That is a deferral-signal finding, not a "no cheap-tier set exists" finding.

(3) THE PAPER'S OWN NUMBERS DON'T SUPPORT "SUBSTANTIALLY AN ARTIFACT" UNIFORMLY — corrections run in opposite directions by task: MMLU judge-reported 20.5% unsolvable → exact-match-implied ~17.9% (down), but MedQA 3.0% → ~16.7% (UP 5.6x). So artifact correction increased measured unsolvability on one of two verifiable benchmarks. There is also an internal inconsistency between the abstract (~79% smallest-tier optimal) and the body (50.3%).

(4) SELF-INFLICTED ARTIFACT + AUTHOR-STATED NON-GENERALITY — verbatim Limitations: "4,096-token context limit. Inflates truncation rates for MMLU (65%) and MedQA (57%)"; "Thinking mode disabled... would likely change the quality gradient, optimal tier distribution, and unsolvability ceiling"; "Judge model overlap. The judge shares weights with the 26B-A4B inference tier"; "All routing collapse findings are specific to Gemma 4 under the reported conditions; the label imbalance will differ across families and deployment mixes." Truncation — one of the three headline artifacts — is thus produced by the authors' own generation budget, not demonstrated in the routing literature they say is inflated, and the judge is weight-contaminated with a tier it grades.

RELEVANCE TO THIS PROJECT'S QUESTION: the model pool is Gemma 4 (E2B/E4B/26B-A4B/31B) plus Llama-3.1-8B/70B — no frontier model, so it does not test a local-small → GPT-5.6-Sol/Sonnet-5 cascade. Benchmarks are MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT: English-only, zero non-English, zero tool-calling/agentic tasks. It therefore says nothing about Chinese/Cantonese degradation or ROS 2 function-calling reliability, the two decisive axes here.

Table 15 sanity checks: "Balanced classifier (positive ctrl) 41.60% acc, Recall[non-E2B] 9-55% → **Task is learnable; collapse is objective-specific**." Body text: "A balanced classifier (class_weight='balanced') achieves 41.6% accuracy but non-zero recall across all tiers (E2B 47.1%, E4B 13.3%, 26B-A4B 9.3%, 31B 54.8%), **demonstrating the task is learnable under cost-sensitive objectives**." Sec 8.5: collapse is attributed to (a) prior-dominated decision, (b) cross-entropy objective mismatch, (c) length shortcut — all fixable artifacts of label marginal + loss function, NOT absence of signal. Sec 9.2 then prescribes fixes (class-weighted/focal loss, minority oversampling, domain pre-filter, exact-match-grounded labels). The claim converts "routers collapse when you train cross-entropy on judge-derived labels with a 79% majority class" into "routers cannot learn difficulty" — a causal misread.

REFUTATION 3 — "standard routers" is a euphemism for three toy baselines on one dataset. Sec 3.4: the only routers trained are feat_lr (logistic regression on 13 hand-crafted surface features: character length, token length, punctuation counts, question-word presence), feat_mlp (2-layer MLP on the same features), and distilbert (DistilBERT-base-uncased fine-tune). Train = Alpaca train split n=12,000; test = Alpaca test split n=3,000. Labels come from an LLM judge that the same paper shows is broken (verbosity bias; 4,096-token cap causing 65% truncation on MMLU, 57% on MedQA; judge shares weights with the 26B-A4B inference tier). No RouteLLM-style preference-trained router, no matrix factorization, no embedding router, no LLM-as-router was tested. Table 14: majority 79.3%, feat_lr 79.27%, feat_mlp 79.30%, distilbert 79.40% (and distilbert does get 3.6% recall on the 26B tier, so "always predicting the cheapest tier" is not literally true for all three).

REFUTATION 4 — the 79% number is a dataset+pool-specific label prevalence, not a property of routing. Sec 3.4: "Label distribution: E2B 79.3%, E4B 10.0%, 26B-A4B 6.5%, 31B 4.2%, **partly reflecting genuine model differences, partly reflecting the judge's tendency to assign score <2 to larger-model responses on knowledge tasks even when those responses select the correct letter**." The tier pool is four local Gemma-4 models (2B→31B) on Alpaca instruction-following. This is not transferable to the project's setting (Qwen3-4B local vs GPT-5.6 Sol via Bedrock), where the capability gap and therefore the label marginal are far larger — the paper itself says the imbalance "will differ across families and deployment mixes."

REFUTATION 5 — contradicting evidence, cited inside the same paper. Sec 10 Related Work: "Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing achieves ~30% cost reduction within model families"; RouteLLM "proposed training binary routers on human preference data"; Hybrid-LLM and Zooter "explored BERT-based routing with synthetic labels"; RouterArena/RouterBench provide router comparisons. The paper does not reproduce and fail any of these; it never claims their routers collapse. So "trained routers do not learn a genuine signal" is contradicted by the prior work this paper itself treats as valid, and the paper's actual thesis is narrower: reported routing HEADROOM (the unsolvability ceiling) is inflated by evaluation artifacts.

WHAT SURVIVES (usable, narrow form): "In Garg & Sagtani 2026 (arXiv:2605.07395, preprint, Gemma-4 tier pool, Alpaca n=12k train/3k test, judge-derived labels with 79.3% smallest-tier-optimal), three cross-entropy-trained routers (LR/MLP on surface features, DistilBERT) all landed within 0.1 pp of the 79.3% majority baseline with ~0% recall on larger tiers; random-Gaussian-feature and shuffled-label controls reproduced this exactly, and a class-weighted classifier recovered 9-55% minority recall — so the collapse is an artifact of label imbalance plus objective choice, and is fixable, not evidence that difficulty is unlearnable." Note that even this narrow form supports a warning relevant to the project: naive router training on judge labels silently degenerates, and the paper's under-routing asymmetry (621 under-routing errors vs 1 over-routing error on MedQA; router accuracy dropping 78.7%→39.2% under distribution shift, 40 pp range) is a real, quantified hazard for a robot loop. But that is a "your labels and objective will betray you" claim, not the claim under review.

SOURCE IS REAL, QUOTE IS REAL, GENERALIZATION IS NOT. arXiv:2605.07395 exists (Garg & Sagtani, "Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts", submitted 8 May 2026, 11 pp, cs.LG; abstract verified verbatim: "standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost"). I pulled the full PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.07395, 285,719 B) and verified Tables 14/15. The narrow numbers hold: majority baseline 79.3%; feat_lr 79.27%, feat_mlp 79.30%, distilbert 79.40%; recall on non-E2B tiers 0% (distilbert 3.6% on one tier); random Gaussian features 79.30% / 0% recall; shuffled labels 79.30% / 0% recall.

REFUTED BY THE SOURCE'S OWN POSITIVE CONTROL. Table 15 row 4: "Balanced classifier (class_weight='balanced') achieves 41.6% accuracy but non-zero recall across all tiers (E2B 47.1%, E4B 13.3%, 26B-A4B 9.3%, 31B 54.8%), demonstrating the task is learnable under cost-sensitive objectives." The paper's own interpretation column reads "Task is learnable; collapse is objective-specific" (p.txt L1024-1025). Section 8.5 names the mechanisms as (a) prior-dominated decision at a 79.3% label prior and (b) "Objective mismatch. Cross-entropy optimizes accuracy, not recall... changing the objective alone recovers non-zero recall." So the paper claims a fixable label/objective pathology, NOT the claim's universal "trained routers do not learn a genuine 'can the small model handle this?' signal." The claim inverts the paper's thesis: the 79.3% skew is itself an artifact ("Oracle labels derived from judge-scored data reach 79.3% E2B-optimal BY CONSTRUCTION"), driven by judge/exact-match divergence of 10-24 pp on MMLU, 65% truncation on MMLU / 57% on MedQA under a 4,096-token cap, and 5.4-12.4% parse failures — and the paper's remedies (dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, cost-sensitive objectives, MoDEM-style domain pre-filter) presuppose the signal is recoverable.

WHAT "STANDARD ROUTERS" ACTUALLY MEANS HERE. The three routers are (i) logistic regression on 13 hand-crafted surface features (char length, token length, punctuation counts, question-word presence), (ii) a 2-layer MLP on the same features, (iii) DistilBERT — trained on Alpaca only (12,000 train / 3,000 test). SHAP shows char_len/token_len dominate: "routing functions as length-based triage rather than difficulty-based triage." That is a statement about length-feature baselines on one instruction-following split, not about trained routers in general.

EXPLICIT SCOPE LIMIT IN THE PAPER. Limitations: "Single primary model family. All routing collapse findings are specific to Gemma 4 under the reported conditions; the label imbalance will differ across families and deployment mixes." Also "Judge model overlap. The judge shares weights with the 26B-A4B inference tier." Tiers are self-hosted Gemma-4 E2B/E4B/26B-A4B/31B on H100 — no local-vs-cloud pairing, no tool-calling/agentic evaluation, no Chinese/Cantonese, no latency-based deferral, thinking mode disabled, greedy decoding.

EXTERNAL CONTRADICTION. RouteLLM (arXiv:2406.18665, Ong et al.) — extracted PDF text — reports learned routers significantly beating the feature-free/random baseline: "routers performing significantly better than the random router across all metrics... matrix factorization requires half the number of GPT-4 calls as compared to random to achieve a PGR of 50%"; with augmented training data "the BERT classifier achieving an APGR improvement of over 50% as compared to random"; on transfer to a new model pair "still significantly stronger than random, with our routers requiring up to 30% less GPT-4 calls than random to achieve CPT(80%)". RouteLLM also shows the failure is label-dependent, matching the fix framing: "On MMLU, all routers perform poorly at the level of the random router when trained [on Arena data]" until augmented, after which they need ~20% fewer GPT-4 calls than random. The source paper's own Related Work concedes third-party positives it does not refute: Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing "achieves ~30% cost reduction within model families", and MoDEM's BERT domain classifier is cited as "empirical support for our recommendation that domain detection as a pre-filter is the most promising direction for breaking routing collapse."

SOURCE-STRENGTH MISMATCH. A universal negative about router learnability is an extraordinary claim; the only support is a single unrefereed 11-page arXiv preprint (no venue/comments field), 2 authors, one model family, one training split, three shallow router variants — and that preprint's own positive control contradicts the universal reading.

NARROW VERSION THAT SURVIVES: "Under judge-derived oracle labels with a 79.3% cheapest-tier marginal (Gemma-4 tiers, Alpaca, 4,096-token cap), unweighted cross-entropy routers on surface features collapse to the majority class (79.27-79.40% acc, ~0% non-cheapest recall; reproduced by random features and shuffled labels), costing 13-17 pp versus a dual-judge/cost-sensitive ceiling." As written, the claim is an overreach and is contradicted both internally and externally.

SOURCE IS REAL, THE FRAMING IS NOT. arXiv 2605.07395 exists (Garg & Sagtani, "Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts", submitted 2026-05-08, 12pp). Verbatim abstract confirms the quote: "standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost." The claim's "versus an oracle/cost-sensitive router" is also the paper's own wording (Introduction): "The opportunity cost (routing performance achievable with dual-judge oracle labels and cost-sensitive objectives versus collapsed routers) is 13-17 percentage points across knowledge-intensive benchmarks." So the citation is not fabricated.

REFUTATION 1 — METRIC MISREAD: the claim calls it "end-to-end quality". The paper's metric is ROUTER CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY (which tier to pick), not downstream answer quality. The 79.3% figure the gap is measured from is the majority-class rate of the tier-selection classifier on Alpaca. A router that picks the wrong tier usually still produces a correct answer — over-escalation costs dollars and latency, not quality. Converting 13-17pp of tier-selection accuracy into "13-17pp of end-to-end quality left on the table" is a category error and inflates the stake.

REFUTATION 2 — NOT A MEASURED NUMBER, SO NOT "CONCRETE FALSIFIABLE": no cost-sensitive router was ever trained and shown to beat the collapsed router by 13-17pp. Section 8.2 derives it additively: "The MMLU gap under exact-match is 13 pp larger than judge-reported routing gain suggests; when truncation effects on both benchmarks are included, the total opportunity cost reaches 13-17 percentage points." Table 14 shows all three learned routers (feat_lr, feat_mlp, distilbert) sitting exactly at the 79.3% majority baseline; the only non-collapsed variant is a "Balanced classifier (positive ctrl)" at 41.60% — i.e. WORSE accuracy, included only to show "Task is learnable; collapse is objective-specific". Cost-sensitive objectives appear in Section 9.2 as RECOMMENDATIONS ("Use class-weighted objectives, focal loss, or minority oversampling"), not results. The 13-17pp is a theoretical upper bound from artifact decomposition, never empirically realized.

REFUTATION 3 — INTERNAL TENSION: the paper's own thesis is that "existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated" and that router training signals are DISTORTED by judge bias/truncation/format artifacts. Quoting a headroom figure computed from those same distorted measurements as a firm target inverts the paper's caution. The paper also reports a separate 28-44pp gap-to-oracle-ceiling, so 13-17 is only the artifact-attributable slice, not "the" opportunity cost.

REFUTATION 4 — OUT OF SCOPE for the research question: pool = Gemma 4 + Llama 3.1 families; benchmarks = MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT — all single-turn static text. Zero tool-calling, zero multi-step agent loop, zero latency measurement, zero Chinese/Cantonese, zero robotics. Stated limitations (Sec 9.4): "Thinking mode disabled... 4,096-token context limit... Judge model overlap... Single primary model family." Nothing here transfers to a voice + ROS 2 escalation loop, and the 4,096-token cap plus disabled thinking mode are precisely the truncation conditions the paper blames for the artifacts.

REFUTATION 5 — SOURCE STRENGTH: 12-page 2-author arXiv preprint, no venue, not peer reviewed, ~3.5 months old, no citations located (Semantic Scholar returned no record). Adequate to say "one preprint estimates", inadequate to carry a load-bearing "quantified... concrete falsifiable number" in a design decision.

SALVAGEABLE RESTATEMENT: "A single 2026 preprint (arXiv 2605.07395, n=206k query-model pairs, Gemma 4 / Llama 3.1, six static benchmarks) measured learned tier-routers collapsing to the ~79% majority class, and ESTIMATES — without training the corrective router — a 13-17pp gap in ROUTER TIER-SELECTION ACCURACY attributable to evaluation artifacts." That is a much weaker statement than the claim under review.

result.evidence:
MISREAD OF THE QUANTITY. The paper defines 13-17 pp explicitly in §5.1, and it is NOT a router-vs-oracle quality gap: "The judge-reported routing gain on MMLU (E2B->31B) is 58.3-42.4=15.9 pp. Under exact-match: 82.1-53.2=28.9 pp, 13 pp larger... The exact-match-verified MedQA routing gain is +40.4 pp vs. judge-derived +50.7 pp (10.3 pp overestimate). The combined metric-disagreement-induced distortion spans 10.3-13 pp, rising to 13-17 pp when truncation effects are included." So 13-17 pp is a MEASUREMENT-DISTORTION magnitude — how much an LLM-judge metric mis-states routing gain, plus truncation — not "end-to-end quality a naive learned escalation policy leaves on the table."

THE PAPER'S ACTUAL ORACLE GAPS ARE DIFFERENT NUMBERS. §8.2: "The within-distribution oracle ceiling on Alpaca is 86.6%; the collapsed router achieves 78.7% (-7.9 pp). On MMLU, the router achieves 54.1% vs. an exact-match-verified ceiling of ~82.1% (-28 pp). On MedQA, 39.2% vs. ~83.3% (-44 pp)." None of -7.9 / -28 / -44 is 13-17. §8.2's own closing sentence ("total opportunity cost reaches 13-17 pp across knowledge-intensive scenarios") directly contradicts the -28 and -44 pp it states two sentences earlier for the only two knowledge-intensive benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA). The abstract's phrase quoted in the claim is the paper's own sloppy relabeling of a §5.1 metric-divergence number; the claim inherits and amplifies it.

"versus ... COST-SENSITIVE ROUTER" IS UNSUPPORTED AND SIGN-FLIPPED. The only cost-sensitive router in the paper is the §8.3 positive control: "A balanced classifier (class_weight='balanced') achieves 41.6% accuracy" vs. the collapsed router's 79.27%. Against that baseline the collapsed router is +37.7 pp on the reported metric, not 13-17 pp worse. The paper never measures end-to-end quality of a cost-sensitive router at all; §9.2 only claims the 13-17 pp is "reducible."

THE 17 UPPER BOUND IS A SELF-INFLICTED ARTIFACT, NOT A PROPERTY OF ESCALATION. The truncation component comes from §5.2's "MMLU has a 65% and MedQA a 57% response truncation rate," caused by the authors' own 4,096-token cap, which §9.4 lists as a limitation and §5.2 recommends replacing with budgets achieving "<5% truncation." Remove the authors' own configuration defect and the number changes.

NOT VERIFIABLE / NO SUPPORTING TABLE. 13-17 pp appears only in prose (6 occurrences, abstract + §5.1 + §8.2 + §9.2); there is no table, formula, or per-benchmark decomposition showing how truncation is combined with 10.3-13 pp to reach 13-17. It is therefore not the "concrete falsifiable number" the claim advertises.

SOURCE STRENGTH BELOW CLAIM STRENGTH. arXiv v1 only, no peer-reviewed venue, citationCount=1, both authors independent researchers. Self-declared limitations gut generality: thinking mode disabled, judge shares weights with the routed 26B-A4B tier, "All routing collapse findings are specific to Gemma 4." The "routers" are logistic regression / small MLP / DistilBERT over 13 features with plain cross-entropy on a 79.3% majority class, and §8.3 shows random Gaussian features and shuffled labels reproduce the collapse exactly — i.e. a textbook class-imbalance failure of a toy classifier, not evidence about learned escalation policies in general, and nothing like a Qwen3-on-T4 -> GPT-5.6-Sol cascade where the capability gap and label marginal differ entirely.

The paper is real (arXiv:2605.07395v1, "Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts", Garg & Sagtani, 2026-05-08) and the quoted sentence is verbatim from its abstract. The NUMBERS are supported; the CLAIM built on them is an overreach that the paper's own text contradicts on four counts. Full text extracted from the PDF (/tmp/router_paper.txt).

1) REFUTED BY THE PAPER'S OWN POSITIVE CONTROL. The claim's parenthetical — "the router performs no better than a feature-free majority baseline" generalised into "trained routers do not learn a genuine 'can the small model handle this?' signal" — is directly denied in Section 8.3: "A balanced classifier (class_weight='balanced') achieves 41.6% accuracy but non-zero recall across all tiers (E2B: 47.1%, E4B: 13.3%, 26B-A4B: 9.3%, 31B: 54.8%), demonstrating the task is learnable under cost-sensitive objectives." Table 15's own interpretation column reads: "Task is learnable; collapse is objective-specific". Section 9.2: cost-sensitive objectives are "sufficient to recover non-zero recall." The paper diagnoses a *fixable label-marginal + cross-entropy objective* pathology, not an absence of learnable signal. The claim converts a conditional, remediable engineering failure into an intrinsic impossibility.

2) THE 79.3% IS MISQUOTED IN SCOPE. The claim says "~79% of queries labelled smallest-tier-optimal". Table 5 gives the oracle distribution over ALL queries as E2B 50.3% / E4B 14.0% / 26B-A4B 13.1% / 31B 5.5%; the caption specifies "79.3% of solvable queries". And 79.3% is the label prevalence of ONE dataset split — Section 3.4: routers trained on "the Alpaca train split (n=12,000)", evaluated on "the Alpaca test split (n=3,000)", label distribution "E2B 79.3%". Alpaca is English single-turn instruction-following, where a 2B model genuinely suffices most of the time. Off-distribution the router does NOT sit at the majority level: "Router accuracy collapses by 39.5 pp on MedQA (78.7% in-distribution -> 39.2%)".

3) THE COLLAPSE IS PARTLY AN ARTIFACT OF A DELIBERATELY CRIPPLED SETUP. Section 9.4 Limitations: "Thinking mode disabled"; "4,096-token context limit. Inflates truncation rates for MMLU (65%) and MedQA (57%)"; "Judge model overlap. The judge shares weights with the 26B-A4B inference tier"; and decisively "Single primary model family. All routing collapse findings are specific to Gemma 4 under the reported conditions; the label imbalance will differ across families and deployment mixes." The 79.3% label skew is stated to be "79.3% E2B-optimal by construction" of judge-scored data.

4) "STANDARD ROUTERS" = THREE TOY MULTI-CLASS MODELS, NOT THE LITERATURE'S ROUTERS. Section 3.4: feat_lr (logistic regression on char length, token length, punctuation counts, question-word presence), feat_mlp (2-layer MLP on the same features), distilbert (DistilBERT-base-uncased). They predict one of 4 same-family Gemma-4 tiers — not the binary "can the small model handle this" question the claim frames. The paper's own Related Work cites the binary formulation as working: "RouteLLM [Ong et al., 2025] introduced a training framework for binary routers using human preference data, achieving over 2x cost savings on standard benchmarks"; "FrugalGPT ... reduce cost by up to 98%"; "Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing achieves ~30% cost reduction within model families"; "MoDEM [Simonds et al., 2024] uses BERT-based domain classification before tier prediction, providing empirical support for our recommendation that domain detection as a pre-filter is the most promising direction for breaking routing collapse." The paper never reproduces or refutes RouteLLM/RouterBench; it does not claim routers in general fail.

MINOR ALSO: "always predicting the cheapest tier" overstates Table 14 — distilbert reaches 79.40% with R[26B]=3.6%, not literally 0% everywhere.

WHAT SURVIVES (narrow version): on Alpaca with Gemma-4 judge-derived labels at 79.3% E2B prevalence, three unweighted cross-entropy routers score 79.27/79.30/79.40% vs a 79.3% majority baseline with ~0% minority recall, and random Gaussian features (79.30%) and shuffled labels (79.30%) reproduce it exactly; final training loss 1.484 vs log(4)=1.386 floor; SHAP shows char_len/token_len dominant, i.e. "length-based triage rather than difficulty-based triage". That is a real cautionary result about naive label construction — it is NOT evidence that a router cannot learn deferral.

SOURCE QUALITY vs CLAIM STRENGTH: single un-peer-reviewed 12-page preprint, 2 authors, no venue, no citations found (Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429, no corroborating citations located), zero non-English data, zero tool-calling/agentic/multi-turn routing, no local-small->cloud-large cross-vendor two-tier setting, no voice or robotics latency dimension. Insufficient to carry an unconditional claim about what trained routers can learn — especially for this project's Qwen3-on-T4 -> GPT-5.6 Sol two-tier Chinese/Cantonese voice+ROS 2 case, which shares none of the paper's conditions.

The "hindsight" sentence is verbatim (p.7). So: numbers real, source is the primary paper, dated 3 months ago (current), not marketing (academic preprint, code at github.com/RaghuHemadri/r2v-agent). No third-party critique or reproduction found (Google search for the arXiv ID returns nothing; Semantic Scholar API rate-limited). Appendix D.1 confirms NO individual backbone reaches LLM-only: best TextWorld 98.4 (vs 98.7), best TerminalBench 95.7 at 16.3% escalation (vs 98.1). So the load-bearing conclusion — a purpose-built calibrated step-level router does not reach frontier quality, on point estimates, on all three benchmarks, for all four backbones — survives.

THREE MATERIAL OVERREACHES the claim must be corrected for before use:

(1) "strictly worse end-to-end on all three benchmarks" is rhetorically inverted relative to the source. On TextWorld the gap is 0.5 pts and the paper's own words are "R2V reaches 98.2% SR with 41.7% LLM calls, within 0.4 points of the hindsight oracle's 98.6% SR and within 0.5 points of LLM-only execution." Figure 3 plots 95% bootstrap CIs but Table 2 reports NO CIs, SDs, or significance test; a 0.5-pt difference over 250 ALFWorld test episodes (single split, seed 42, 5 perturbation seeds) is almost certainly inside the CI. The paper's Conclusion says the opposite of the claim's framing: "efficient agents do not need to choose between cheap but brittle SLM execution and expensive full LLM execution; calibrated step-level routing provides a practical middle ground." Honest restatement: gap is 4.5 pts on HumanEval+ (at 0.6% escalation, i.e. ~99% cost cut), ~0.3-0.5 pts and probably not significant on TextWorld, 2.4-4.8 pts on TerminalBench depending on backbone/λ_cons.

(2) The hindsight attribution is mis-scoped. The paper attributes the remaining gap TO THE ORACLE, on TerminalBench (shell tasks) ONLY — not the gap to LLM-only, and not on all three benchmarks. Note the oracle itself never reaches LLM-only (98.6<98.8, 98.6<98.7, 97.8<98.1), so hindsight-identifiability is NOT the full explanation; the claim's version actually understates the structural case against cascades.

(3) Transfer to this T4 robot project is limited and the claim doesn't say so. The SLMs are Gemma-9B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B (not Qwen3), each BENCHMARK-SPECIFICALLY DISTILLED via BC on 800-820 teacher trajectories (Gemini 3 Flash Preview / Claude Opus 4.6 / GPT-5 / Gemini 3.1 Pro) plus verifier-guided DPO, plus a hand-built per-benchmark programmatic process verifier (smoke tests / ALFWorld goal state / terminal output signatures), plus a trained 15-feature MLP router with Brier calibration + temperature scaling. None of that exists for a Cantonese/Mandarin voice-dialogue + ROS 2 loop, which has NO programmatic step verifier — the precondition R2V's router depends on ("R2V still depends on the quality of the verifier and the risk features"). Feature-group ablation (Qwen2.5-7B, noisy eval), TextWorld/TerminalBench SR and LLM%: "Entropy only" = 64.6/2.4% and 87.6/18.7%, but "Log-prob only" = 96.5 SR at 64.3% escalation on TextWorld and 91.0 SR at 5.4% escalation on TerminalBench. Log-prob-only routing therefore lifts TextWorld from 64.6% to 96.5% — within 1.8 points of the full 15-feature R2V router (98.3) — and on TerminalBench beats entropy-only on BOTH axes (91.0 vs 87.6 SR at 5.4% vs 18.7% escalation). The claim's headline "token-level logprob/entropy confidence ... is an unusable escalation signal" lumps together two signals whose measured behaviour in this very paper diverges by ~32 SR points on the flagship benchmark. Only the single scalar entropy threshold fails; logprob features are demonstrably usable.

(2) The 0.0% escalation is an artifact of the paper's own SLM training, not a property of entropy. Sec. 5.1: "The entropy router escalates using a validation-calibrated token-entropy threshold" and "All deployable methods share the same distilled SLM". That shared SLM was trained with DPO plus a consistency regularizer that explicitly minimizes JSD(pi(.|x^z) || pi(.|x^z')) across perturbation seeds (Eq. 4) — i.e. the training objective deliberately makes the action distribution invariant to exactly the observation perturbations the entropy router is being asked to detect. Entropy was engineered flat by construction. No entropy-threshold sweep on TextWorld is reported, so "stayed at exactly 64.6%" is a tautology of a threshold that never fired once, not a demonstration that no threshold works. This finding does not transfer to an off-the-shelf, non-consistency-regularized Qwen3 policy, which is what this project would deploy.

(3) Domain extrapolation, not "direct evidence". The tasks are a synthetic text game (TextWorld) and a shell benchmark (TerminalBench); "noisy" means injected textual perturbations (truncated logs, tool flakiness, prompt corruption, and the TerminalBench verifier literally "strips perturbation noise" from output blocks). Nothing in the paper involves ASR error, audio, vision, or ROS 2. Calling it "direct evidence ... for a robot/voice loop with noisy observations" is an analogy on the word "partially observable".

Additional source-quality flags: unrefereed v1 preprint, 3 months old, zero independent replication, and the entropy router is a baseline built by the authors of the method it loses to (self-serving-baseline risk). Internal red flag on the very table the claim cites: Appendix Table 4 gives the paper's process verifier a TerminalBench AUROC of 0.508 with near-identical mean scores on successful (0.406) vs failed (0.398) steps — i.e. chance-level — yet verifier-dependent R2V still reports 93.3% there, which is hard to reconcile.

VERIFICATION OF THE NUMBERS: all of them check out verbatim against the primary source. arXiv:2605.16604 exists ("R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help", Raghu Vamshi Hemadri et al., v1 submitted Fri 15 May 2026, cs.LG). From the full HTML (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.16604v1): Table 4 gives "TerminalBench 55.55% / 44.45% / 0.406 / 0.398 / 0.508"; Appendix C.2 gives "episode-level AUROC 0.508 and Brier score 0.276, reflecting near-chance separation"; HumanEval+ verifier "AUROC 0.856 and Brier 0.172"; TextWorld "AUROC ~0.78"; Table 9 gives TerminalBench Full ECE 0.162 / No-entropy ECE 0.238. So the claim is NOT a fabrication and the quote is accurate. It is refuted on OVERREACH and EXTERNAL VALIDITY, on four independent grounds:

(1) THE CONCLUSION INVERTS THE PAPER'S OWN HEADLINE RESULT ON THAT EXACT BENCHMARK. The claim concludes routing/difficulty estimation is "unreliable in the most heterogeneous, tool-noisy setting". The paper's Table 2 says the opposite for the same setting: TerminalBench SLM-only 81.1% SR -> R2V 93.3% SR at 33.9% LLM calls, versus a heuristic router needing 66.0% escalation for comparable reliability, and the paper itself labels TerminalBench "the most heterogeneous setting". The claim cherry-picks appendix diagnostics (Table 4, C.2, Table 9 ablations) and drops the main table that contradicts it.

(2) THE "NEAR-CHANCE" OBJECT IS NOT A DIFFICULTY ESTIMATOR. The 0.406/0.398/0.508 figures are the *mean-aggregated score of a hand-written rule table*, not a learned calibrated estimator: per C.2 the TerminalBench verifier "operates without Docker or subprocess execution", assigning "clean bash prompt yields 0.68, no signal yields 0.55, image_read returns 0.52, and unrecognized actions return 0.40". The paper explicitly says this is by design: "This is expected: individual step scores encode local command quality rather than complete episode outcome, and the router learns to bridge this local-to-global gap." The router's own TerminalBench Brier is 0.185, materially better than the verifier's 0.276. Generalizing a crude non-executing heuristic's failure into "calibrated difficulty estimation is unreliable" is an unsupported leap.

(3) THE ENVIRONMENT IS A REPLAY SURROGATE, SO "CLOSEST TO A ROS 2 ROBOT" IS THE LEAST SUPPORTED PART. The paper's "TerminalBench" is 89 tasks replayed from the yoonholee/terminalbench-trajectories HuggingFace dataset, split ~62/13/14 tasks (only ~14 held-out tasks), with no Docker or subprocess execution anywhere in the verifier. Its reported success rates are impossible in the real harness: the paper reports LLM-only 98.1% and distilled 7B-14B SLM-only 81.1% on "TerminalBench", while the live Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard (tbench.ai, checked 2026-08-22) tops out at NexAU-AHE/GPT-5.5 84.7% +/- 2.1, LemonHarness 84.5%, Codex CLI 82.2%. A distilled Qwen2.5-7B scoring 81.1% and any system scoring 98.1% is not the real benchmark. The ECE 0.162/0.238 the claim leans on are therefore measured in simulated tool noise, which is the opposite of the "tool-noisy real world" the claim invokes.

(4) MATERIAL OMISSION THAT REVERSES THE DEPLOYMENT IMPLICATION. The claim says ECE degrades "to 0.238 when token log-probabilities are unavailable (closed-API case)" and stops there. Table 9 also shows the paper's own fix: pseudo-entropy over verifier scores restores TerminalBench to 92.8% SR with ECE 0.181 (vs full 0.162), and on TextWorld to 98.1% SR / ECE 0.054 — with the paper concluding "black-box deployment is practical for code and navigation tasks". Worse, the constraint is irrelevant to the project it is cited against: a locally hosted Qwen3 exposes logprobs, so the 0.162 column, not 0.238, is the applicable one.

SOURCE-STRENGTH MISMATCH: single un-peer-reviewed v1 preprint (no journal/conference comment field), one group, single seed 42, single 70/15/15 split, ~14 test tasks with episodes clustered within tasks, and no confidence intervals on any AUROC/ECE/Brier figure — an AUROC of 0.508 from ~14 tasks is not distinguishable from a wide band around chance in either direction. Internal sloppiness signals: the teacher pool is "Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro" in Sec 5.1 but "Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and others" in Appendix C.1; backbone listed as "Gemma-9B" (no such model; Gemma-2-9B). Not marketing, not outdated (3 months old), but far too thin to carry a load-bearing architectural verdict.

SALVAGEABLE NARROW CLAIM: "In R2V-Agent (arXiv:2605.16604), a hand-coded non-executing process verifier separates success from failure episodes at AUROC 0.856 on HumanEval+, ~0.78 on TextWorld, and 0.508 on a 89-task replayed TerminalBench surrogate, and the learned router's ECE on that surrogate is 0.162 (0.238 without logprobs, 0.181 with a logprob-free proxy) versus 0.052-0.067 elsewhere — i.e. verifier quality and router calibration are benchmark-dependent." What must be dropped: "therefore unreliable" (the paper shows 81.1%->93.3% there), "badly calibrated" (unqualified), and "the setting closest to a ROS 2 robot" (a replay dataset with no execution, no embodiment, no real-time constraint, and success rates above real-harness SOTA).

Paper = "R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help", submitted 15 May 2026, cs.LG, authors Hemadri, Mohammed, Maheshwary, Daruru, Davasam, Yadav, Sunkara, Rajeswar. Table 2 verbatim: SLM-only 91.9/0.0% | 64.6/0.0% | 81.1/0.0%; Entropy Router 92.9/0.8% | 64.6/0.0% | 87.4/4.1%; R2V 94.3/0.6% | 98.2/41.7% | 93.3/33.9%; Oracle 98.6/8.1% | 98.6/35.4% | 97.8/18.4%; LLM-only 98.8/100% | 98.7/100% | 98.1/100%. The supporting quote is verbatim from Sec 5.2 "TextWorld." So: no fabrication, no misquote, primary source, 3 months old, not marketing. WHAT FAILS IS THE CLAIM'S STRENGTH AND SCOPE, on four specific grounds.

(1) The load-bearing row is the authors' OWN baseline at a SINGLE operating point, and 0.0% escalation is a degenerate threshold, not a measured curve. The paper says only "the entropy router escalates using a validation-calibrated token-entropy threshold." A firing rate of exactly 0.0% means the threshold never triggered on TextWorld — that is one miscalibrated scalar, not a demonstration that the signal carries no information. The paper sweeps its own method's hyperparameters extensively (Table 7 CVaR sweep: (0.05,0.02)→98.05/56.63; (0.20,0.15)→95.29/21.11) but reports NO threshold sweep or Pareto curve for the entropy baseline. Asymmetric tuning effort in favour of the proposed method is exactly the bias pattern that inflates "baseline X is unusable" conclusions.

(2) The apparently corroborating ablation is methodologically invalid as independent evidence. Table 3 shows "Features / entropy only → TextWorld 64.6/2.4", which looks like a learned entropy-only router also failing. But both Table 3 and Table 8 captions state: "Feature ablations are applied at inference time without retraining" / "Feature masking is applied at inference time without retraining." That is a router TRAINED on all 15 features then run with 14 of them zeroed — a broken model, not a router trained on entropy alone. So there is exactly ONE piece of evidence for the claim in this paper, not two.

(3) The same table contains omitted counter-evidence against the word "unusable." TerminalBench: entropy escalation bought +6.3 SR points (81.1→87.4) for 4.1% LLM calls = 1.54 SR points per 1% escalation, versus R2V's 12.2/33.9 = 0.36 and the heuristic router's 13.9/66.0 = 0.21. On the paper's own cost-efficiency metric, the entropy router is the MOST escalation-efficient row in Table 2. On HumanEval+, Table 3's entropy-only variant reaches 96.0 SR — ABOVE full R2V's 94.3. The claim's framing "87.4% vs LLM-only 98.1%" silently switches the comparator from the SLM baseline (which entropy beat) to the ceiling. For a T4 project whose whole constraint is cost/latency, "+6.3 points for 4.1% of calls" is not "unusable."

(4) "Direct evidence ... for a robot/voice loop with noisy observations" is an extrapolation, not direct evidence. The paper contains zero robotics, zero speech/ASR, zero non-English data; benchmarks are HumanEval+, TextWorld (a text game), TerminalBench. Backbones are 2024-era Gemma-9B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B — not Qwen3, which is the project's candidate. Also, "the 35.4% of steps belonging to failed episodes" is the claim's own inference from the Oracle Router's TextWorld LLM% (the paper states the analogous 8.11% only for HumanEval+); defensible, but it is the reviewer's arithmetic being presented as the paper's finding.

Prior literature further qualifies the blanket version: Gupta et al., "Language Model Cascades: Token-level uncertainty and beyond" (arXiv 2404.10136, ICLR 2024) finds that naive sequence-level uncertainty is length-biased and weak, but that "incorporating token-level uncertainty through learned post-hoc deferral rules can significantly outperform such simple aggregation strategies" on FLAN-T5 NLP benchmarks. That is a single-turn setting and does not overturn the TextWorld result, but it does refute "token-level logprob/entropy confidence is an unusable escalation signal" as a general statement.

WHAT SURVIVES (the narrow version the project should record instead): "On TextWorld under noisy evaluation, a single validation-calibrated token-entropy threshold escalated 0.0% of steps and left success rate at the SLM-only 64.6%, while verifier-based features carried nearly all the routing signal (Table 8: verifier-only 97.9% SR vs entropy-only 64.6%). Single arXiv preprint, unreplicated, entropy baseline tuned at one operating point only." That version is CONFIRMED. The version under review — "unusable," "direct evidence for a robot/voice loop," with the TerminalBench gain reframed as a failure — is an overreach and should not be cited at its current strength.

I downloaded the primary source (arXiv 2605.16604v1, "R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help", Hemadri et al., submitted 2026-05-15, cs.LG; full HTML at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.16604v1, extracted to /tmp/r2v.txt). Every quoted figure is real: Table 2 "Heuristic Router 97.4 26.6% | 98.4 99.9% | 95.0 66.0%"; Table 3/8 "w/o verifier 62.6/19.8", "w/o entropy 62.6/31.8", "entropy only 64.6/2.4"; R2V TextWorld 98.2/41.7; SLM-only TextWorld 64.6. So the claim is not fabricated. It is refuted as an overreach, contradicted by the same paper's own tables on four counts:

(1) "Cheap non-learned escalation rules degenerate to 'always call the big model'" is a 1-of-3-benchmark result stated as a law. On HumanEval+ the SAME hand-written verifier-rule router scored 97.4% SR at 26.6% escalation — no collapse, and 3.1 SR points ABOVE the learned R2V router (94.3%). On TerminalBench it scored 95.0% vs R2V's 93.3%. The heuristic router is quality-dominant on 2 of 3 benchmarks; it only loses on escalation fraction. The paper also reports no threshold sweep for the heuristic baseline (it sweeps only R2V's alpha/epsilon, Table 7, 8 settings), so 99.9% is one un-tuned operating point of one rule, not a property of non-learned rules.

(2) "The learned router requires BOTH verifier scores AND token-entropy features" is directly contradicted by Table 8 (same paper): on TextWorld "Verifier only" = 97.9 SR / 78.5% LLM and "Log-prob only" = 96.5 SR / 64.3% LLM — both single-feature-family routers land ~33 points above SLM-only (64.6). Single families work for quality; they cost more escalation. The claim conflates the "w/o verifier"/"w/o entropy" rows with "X only" rows.

(3) "Entropy-only yields no gain" holds only on TextWorld. On HumanEval+ entropy-only = 96.0 SR at 20.4% escalation, which BEATS the full learned router (94.3) and SLM-only (91.9); on TerminalBench entropy-only = 87.6 vs SLM-only 81.1. Two of three benchmarks show a cheap single-feature signal producing real gains.

(4) The 62.6% figures are methodologically unusable as evidence of feature necessity. Table 3/8 captions state feature masking "is applied at inference time without retraining", on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-7B). The results are non-monotone: "w/o verifier" (62.6 SR @ 19.8% escalation) scores BELOW its own feature subset "entropy only" (64.6 @ 2.4%) and below "step/context only" (70.4 @ 1.2%), and below SLM-only (64.6) despite handing 20% of steps to a teacher whose LLM-only SR is 98.7. A superset of features escalating 8x more while scoring worse than the subset measures MLP input-distribution shift, not which features are needed.

(5) "Cheap" is an equivocation the paper cannot ground. It states explicitly: "All deployable methods share the same distilled SLM and verifier and differ only in the routing decision." The heuristic router therefore runs the same learned process verifier plus K=5 candidate samples via vLLM — no baseline in the paper is a "feature-poor cheap detector". The paper's cost axis is fraction of steps escalated, never detector compute; "latency" appears twice, both in POMDP prose, and there are zero wall-clock/TTFT/tokens-per-second measurements. Meanwhile the learned alternative it recommends cost 360-576 H100 GPU-hours plus Gemini/OpenAI API spend (Appendix compute-budget section) — so the paper supports neither half of "no feature-poor detector both works and is cheap".

(6) Source strength vs claim strength: a universal negative ("there is no simple, feature-poor detector that both works and is cheap") rests on a single 3-month-old non-peer-reviewed preprint with no replication found (DuckDuckGo/Bing searches for "R2V-Agent" returned no independent discussion; arXiv API queries returned nothing). Adjacent literature cuts the other way on cheapness: Gupta et al., "Language Model Cascades: Token-level uncertainty and beyond" (arXiv 2404.10136, 2024) improves the cost-quality frontier with a post-hoc deferral rule over token logits alone — no process verifier.

(7) Transfer to this project's constraint is nil: benchmarks are HumanEval+/TextWorld/TerminalBench text agents; no latency, no Chinese/Cantonese, no voice or ROS loop, no T4-class hardware. The binding question here is whether a local TTFT beats the measured 900 ms Bedrock p50, which this paper never measures.

Usable residue: the specific TextWorld observation (a verifier-threshold rule hit 99.9% escalation while a calibrated router matched it at 41.7%) is real and worth citing as one datapoint that escalation-rate tuning is nontrivial on partially-observed tasks. The sweeping form of the claim is not supportable.

(2) "The learned router requires BOTH verifier scores AND token-entropy features — removing either drops TextWorld from 98.2% to 62.6%" — internally contradicted by Table 8 (Appendix D.2), which the claim's quote silently truncates. The explanation is stated in both captions: "Feature masking is applied at inference time **without retraining**" (Table 3 and Table 8 captions). WHAT CHECKS OUT (fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16604 + https://arxiv.org/html/2605.16604v1 — real paper, "R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help", Hemadri et al., submitted 15 May 2026, cs.LG, ServiceNow-affiliated authors). Every quoted figure is verbatim:

So the claim is NOT fabricated, and "benchmark-dependent" is the paper's own conclusion ("terminal-engineering agents benefit from true log-probability access").

REFUTATION 1 — the closed-API number is the wrong row. The paper's closed-API recommendation is pseudo-entropy (entropy over verifier scores), not "no entropy": Table 9 TerminalBench Pseudo-entropy = SR 92.8, LLM 33.1%, ECE 0.181, Brier 0.204. Paper text: "pseudo-entropy partially recovers performance and calibration". "No entropy" merely zeros the uncertainty dimensions with no substitute — a diagnostic ablation, not a deployment configuration. The claim's "degrading to 0.238 when token log-probabilities are unavailable (closed-API case)" therefore overstates the closed-API penalty by ~3x (0.162→0.181, not 0.162→0.238), and the SR penalty by ~5x (93.3→92.8, not 93.3→90.9).

REFUTATION 2 — the "near-chance" figure is an artifact the paper explicitly names, and the claim's own quote truncates the explanation. Full sentence continues: "...reflecting near-chance separation when local step scores are mean-aggregated. This is expected: individual step scores encode local command quality rather than complete episode outcome, and the router learns to bridge this local-to-global gap." Setup section: the verifier "provides local evidence rather than oracle supervision." So 0.508 measures a mean-aggregation baseline the authors deliberately reject, not the router's difficulty signal. Calling it "the 'do I know this?' evidence source" being near-chance recasts a by-design local feature as a failed global predictor.

REFUTATION 3 — "unreliable" contradicts the same paper's end-to-end TerminalBench result. With ECE 0.162 the router still reaches 93.3% SR at 33.9% LLM calls, "roughly half the heuristic-router cost" (abstract), and even the crippled no-entropy variant holds 90.9% at 25.6% escalation. Poorly calibrated absolute probabilities coexisted with a strictly better reliability-cost frontier; the claim conflates calibration error with decision usefulness and draws the opposite conclusion from its own source.

REFUTATION 4 — n is far too small for a strong generalization, and no CIs exist. Appendix C.1: TerminalBench = 89 tasks, task-level 70/15/15 split → "approximately 62/13/14 train/validation/test tasks." So AUROC 0.508 rests on 14 held-out tasks and ECE 0.162/0.238 on the 13-task router validation split (averaged over 4 backbones). At 14 tasks, 0.508 is not statistically separable from moderate discrimination; the paper reports no confidence intervals or seed variance for these diagnostics, and has no limitations section.

REFUTATION 5 — non-standard harness inflates external-validity risk. It is not the official Terminal-Bench harness: tasks are replayed from the yoonholee/terminalbench-trajectories HF dataset (URL live, HTTP 200). 93.3% SR versus public Terminal-Bench SOTA in the 50-60% range indicates a substantially easier replay setup, so neither the optimistic nor the pessimistic TerminalBench numbers transfer. REFUTATION 6 — the robotics bridge is unsupported. "the setting closest to a ROS 2 robot" appears nowhere in the paper; there is zero robotics, ROS, real-time, or continuous-control evaluation. Benchmarks are HumanEval+/EvalPlus (164 tasks), ALFWorld text-embodied (250 tasks), and replayed shell tasks. SOURCE CHECK (arXiv:2607.24440 exists; abstract fetched verbatim). Title: "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation", single author (M M Asif Ferdous), submitted 2026-07-27, comments "12 pages, 4 figures", categories cs.CV/cs.CL/cs.LG — a solo, non-peer-reviewed preprint with no venue.

1) NUMBERS QUOTED CORRECTLY, SCOPE MISREPRESENTED. The abstract says: "two confidence signals in the Qwen2-VL family: the confidence a model states in natural language, and its own mean token probability over the answer ... Across 5,700 predictions spanning six realistic photographic degradations at three severities ... scale sharply improves the model's internal uncertainty signal (mean error-detection AUROC 0.80 to 0.98 from 2B to 7B) while its verbalized confidence stays weak and often at chance (mean 0.61 to 0.69)". So the study is: ONE model family (Qwen2-VL, a 2024 VLM generation — not Qwen3), TWO scale points (2B, 7B), ONE modality (VQA on synthetically degraded photographs), internal signal = mean token probability of the emitted answer. The claim restates this as a property of "small open-weight models" and of text-based deferral in a voice-dialogue/tool-calling agent loop. n=2 sizes in one family cannot establish "barely improves with scale" or that "the gap widens with size" as a scaling law; and image-degradation-induced errors are precisely the error type that answer-token probability detects best (blur/noise → low visual evidence → flat token distribution), which structurally inflates the 0.98 and makes it non-transferable to "is this user request beyond my competence?" routing.

2) DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED ON THE PRESCRIPTIVE HALF ("must be read from logits, not words"). Tian et al., "Just Ask for Calibration", EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.14975, Stanford; Mitchell, Rafailov, Finn, Manning): "verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities", with ~50% relative ECE reduction across TriviaQA/SciQ/TruthfulQA for RLHF-tuned models — the exact opposite ordering, and RLHF/instruction-tuned chat models are what a local Qwen3 deployment would be. Xiong et al., "Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?", ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.13063): white-box (logit) methods beat verbalized, but "the gap is narrow, e.g., 0.522 to 0.605 in AUROC" — i.e. on text QA the LOGIT signal reaches only ~0.605 AUROC, nowhere near 0.98. So switching the local deferral signal from words to logits does not buy a usable detector in the text setting this project actually needs; the claim's remedy is unsupported by the text-domain literature.

3) THE SOURCE'S OWN HEADLINE FINDING UNDERCUTS THE REMEDY UNDER THIS PROJECT'S T4 CONSTRAINT. Same abstract: "4-bit quantization is nearly free for accuracy (-1.6 points) but expensive for the confidence signal (internal AUROC 0.95 to 0.80, and the verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses from 99% to 64%)". With only ~9–11 GB free VRAM on the T4, any local Qwen3 of useful size is 4-bit — the regime where the paper itself reports the internal signal degrading to 0.80 and verbalized output becoming unparseable 36% of the time. The claim cites the 0.98 figure (7B full/4-bit best case on a vision task) as if it were the available operating point.

4) PARTIAL SUPPORT ACKNOWLEDGED, NOT ENOUGH. Verbalized confidence being systematically overconfident IS corroborated independently (Xiong et al.: models "tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns"). So the direction "don't trust a small model's spoken confidence" is defensible; the specific quantitative claim (0.61→0.69 vs 0.80→0.98 as a general small-model property) and the strong conclusion ("directly refutes", "must be read from logits") are an overreach from a single non-peer-reviewed vision preprint, and the logit prescription is contradicted by two peer-reviewed text-domain papers (EMNLP 2023, ICLR 2024).
