VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE (downloaded https://arxiv.org/html/2605.16604v1, "R2V Agent: Teaching SLMs When to Ask for Help", Hemadri/Maheshwary/Yadav/Sunkara/Rajeswar, submitted 15 May 2026, cs.LG). Every number in the claim matched by grep, not paraphrase:

(1) Table 4 (§C.2, "Step-label distribution and verifier discrimination"): TerminalBench row = 55.55% succ. steps / 44.45% fail. steps / score(succ.) 0.406 / score(fail.) 0.398 / AUROC(ep.) 0.508. HumanEval+ row = 0.620 / 0.336 / AUROC 0.856. TextWorld row = ~0.63 / ~0.51 / AUROC ~0.78. All three AUROC figures in the claim are exact.
(2) §C.2 TerminalBench verifier prose: "the verifier achieves episode-level AUROC 0.508 and Brier score 0.276, reflecting near-chance separation when local step scores are mean-aggregated." Brier 0.276 confirmed. The words "near-chance" are the AUTHORS' own, not the reviewer's spin.
(3) Table 9 (§D.3, black-box variants) TerminalBench rows: Full = SR 93.3, escalation 33.9%, ECE 0.162, Brier 0.185; No-entropy = SR 90.9, 25.6%, ECE 0.238, Brier 0.262. So "full router's ECE 0.162 → 0.238 when log-probs unavailable" is exact, and the closed-API framing is the paper's own (§4.4: "Commercial SLM APIs may hide token log-probabilities").
(4) "most heterogeneous" is the paper's own wording (§5: "TerminalBench is the most heterogeneous setting").

Checklist results: quote support = exact, no overreach in the numeric attributions (verifier metrics attributed to the verifier, ECE attributed to the router — the claim does not conflate them). Currency = 3 months old, v1 only, no withdrawal/erratum in submission history. Not marketing: the cited numbers are the authors reporting a WEAKNESS of their own component, so author incentive runs against inflation — the opposite of a cherry-picked vendor benchmark. Contradiction search found none: semanticscholar returned 429; arXiv API sweep for recent routing+calibration work surfaced no paper disputing these figures (nearest neighbours — 2607.25018 "Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference", 2608.07583 "RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain..." — attack the same problem with distribution-free wrappers, which if anything presupposes that raw router calibration is untrustworthy).

QUALIFICATIONS the parent should carry forward (these justify medium, not high, confidence — they do not refute the numbers):
(a) Material omission: the same paper shows routing still WORKS on TerminalBench despite the near-chance verifier — SLM-only 81.1% SR → R2V 93.3% SR at 33.9% escalation vs heuristic router's 66.0%. Anyone quoting this claim to argue "two-tier routing is infeasible" would be misusing it; the defensible reading is narrower: the confidence NUMBER is untrustworthy (ECE 0.162–0.238) even where the escalation decision is net-useful.
(b) The paper itself attributes AUROC 0.508 to aggregation, not to difficulty being unestimable: "This is expected: individual step scores encode local command quality rather than complete episode outcome, and the router learns to bridge this local-to-global gap."
(c) Setup caveat that weakens transfer to a live ROS 2 loop in BOTH directions: the TerminalBench verifier "operates without Docker or subprocess execution", scoring by regex over terminal text (success patterns → [0.70,1.00], "command not found"/Traceback → [0.08,0.18]); the whole benchmark is offline replay of the yoonholee/terminalbench-trajectories HF dataset, 89 tasks with a ~62/13/14 split (test = ~14 tasks) × 5 perturbation seeds. An 81.1% SLM-only SR on TerminalBench is implausible for live execution (frontier agents sit far lower), confirming these are replayed/re-graded episodes, not live task completion. So AUROC 0.508 is partly an artifact of a deliberately cheap non-executing verifier on a 14-task test split.
(d) Source strength: single unreviewed arXiv v1, no venue comment, no independent replication, ~360-576 H100-hours self-reported. Adequate as a primary source for "this measurement exists"; thin as sole support for a general law about calibrated difficulty estimation.
(e) Internal sloppiness (minor): §4.1 says TerminalBench teachers were "Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro" while §C.1 says "GPT-5.5" — inconsistent within the same paper.

Verdict: the claim survives as stated because it is a numerically exact, correctly attributed report of a primary source's self-critical measurements, and it already hedges to "benchmark-dependent". Only its final rhetorical step ("the setting closest to a ROS 2 robot") is editorial extrapolation and should be labelled as inference, not evidence.
result.counterSource: No refuting source found. Partial counterweights, all from within the same paper: (i) §5 TerminalBench SLM-only 81.1% → R2V 93.3% SR at 33.9% escalation vs heuristic router 66.0%, i.e. routing is net-useful despite ECE 0.162; (ii) §C.2 authors' own explanation that AUROC 0.508 is "expected" from mean-aggregating local step scores and that the router "learns to bridge this local-to-global gap"; (iii) §C.2 the TerminalBench verifier "operates without Docker or subprocess execution" (regex over terminal text) on a ~14-task test split of replayed HF trajectories, so the near-chance figure is partly an artifact of a deliberately cheap verifier. Adjacent 2026 work (arXiv 2607.25018 Conformal Cascade; 2608.07583 RouteGuard) pursues distribution-free/certified routing guarantees rather than disputing these calibration numbers.

result.evidence:
SOURCE VERIFIED TO EXIST but the claim overreaches on four independent counts. Paper: arXiv:2607.24440v1 [cs.CV], "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation", M M Asif Ferdous, Affiliation: Independent Researcher, submitted 27 Jul 2026, v1 only, no venue/peer review, CC BY 4.0.

(1) MISATTRIBUTION — 64% is ONE ARM, not a property of 4-bit. Table 2 (means over 19 conditions): 2B-fp16 parse 0.99 / 2B-4bit 0.64 / **7B-4bit 1.00**. The largest QUANTIZED arm has a 100% parse rate. So "under 4-bit quantization ⇒ ~36% unparseable" is false as stated; it holds only for Qwen2-VL-2B-4bit. The paper's own Limitations: "Quantization is measured at one model size, bounding but not eliminating its confound with scale." Appendix A even reframes the same number as a scale effect: "At 2B the same few-shot template yields a 64% parse rate averaged over all conditions, versus 100% at 7B — the scale effect on format-following." And the paper's headline recommendation is to take the larger quantized model (7B-4bit) — the configuration with zero parse failure.

(2) THE PAPER MAKES NO ROUTING/CASCADE/COST CLAIM. Full-text keyword counts: "cascade" = 0, "rout*" = 2 (incidental), "grammar"/"JSON"/"regex"/"structured" = 0. There is no router experiment, no cost model, no escalation-rate analysis. "Destroying the claimed cost saving" and "escalates ~36% of traffic unconditionally" are the reviewer's inference, not findings; it also assumes parse failure is independent of item difficulty, which the paper never tests.

(3) THE MECHANISM IS A REMOVABLE PROMPT/DECODING ARTIFACT. Section 4.3: "the quantized model frequently abandons the requested two-line format and returns a bare label" — i.e. free-form regex parsing of an unconstrained "Answer:/Confidence:" template. The paper's own template pilot shows parse rate is a prompt variable, not a capability limit: at 7B, few-shot 100%, direct 100%, minimal 55%. Grammar/schema-constrained decoding (llama.cpp GBNF, vLLM/SGLang structured outputs via xgrammar/outlines) makes an integer-confidence field 100% parseable by construction, so "needs a defined fallback for roughly one in three requests" does not follow for a 2026 local-LLM deployment.

(4) THE CLAIM POINTS AT THE WRONG BINDING CONSTRAINT, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO. Verbalized AUROC = 0.56 (2B-fp16) / 0.61 (2B-4bit) / 0.69 (7B-4bit), "at or near chance (≤0.60) in 8 of 19 conditions at 7B, including every low-light condition (0.51–0.56)" — at a 100% parse rate. Paper: "stated confidence should not be used as a deferral signal for these models regardless of size; mean token probability should" (internal AUROC 0.80–0.98, always available, never unparseable). So a verbalized-confidence router fails on discrimination, not on parsing; fixing parsing changes nothing. The claim's specific worry is the small, engineering-fixable part of a larger refutation.

(5) DOMAIN + RECENCY MISMATCH for this project's use (text LLM router in a Cantonese voice + ROS 2 loop): Limitations state "All results are on Food101 posed as four-way multiple choice; generality to open-ended VQA is untested… We study a single model family… n ≈ 100 per condition, so some bootstrap intervals are wide". Base model is Qwen2-VL (2024 generation), not Qwen3; task is image-degradation VQA, not tool-calling/dialogue; no Chinese/Cantonese evaluation. Citation count unverifiable (Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429), but a 3.5-week-old single-author unreviewed preprint is insufficient support for a quantitative deployment rule ("one in three requests") in a different modality and model generation.

USABLE RESIDUE (do not discard): the paper is a genuine T4-reproducible study (repo https://github.com/Asif-Ferdous/vlm-scale-quant returns HTTP 200) and supports a DIFFERENT, stronger claim for the two-tier design — verbalized self-reported confidence from a small local model is a near-chance escalation signal (AUROC 0.56–0.69) and mean-token-logprob is the only usable local signal (0.80–0.98), which also implies the local tier must expose logprobs (i.e. no closed API, and note vLLM/llama.cpp do expose them).

result.evidence:
The source is real and the quote is verbatim (fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24440v1: "4-bit quantization is nearly free for accuracy (-1.6 points) but expensive for the confidence signal (internal AUROC 0.95 to 0.80, and the verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses from 99% to 64%)"). The transcription is fine; the ENGINEERING CONCLUSION is refuted by the same paper's own data.

(1) SELF-CONTRADICTION IN TABLE 2. The three arms are 2B-fp16 / 2B-4bit / 7B-4bit: Accuracy 0.904 / 0.888 / 0.935; Verbalized parse rate 0.99 / 0.64 / 1.00; Verbalized AUROC 0.56 / 0.61 / 0.69; Internal AUROC 0.95 / 0.80 / 0.98; AURC 0.017 / 0.048 / 0.008. The best uncertainty signal in the whole study IS a 4-bit model (7B-4bit, internal AUROC 0.98, parse rate 1.00). The paper's literal recommendation is the inverse of the claim: "For a fixed memory budget the recommendation is therefore to prefer a larger quantized model over a smaller full-precision one." The claim's inference — "Because the T4 budget (9-11 GB free, no bf16/FP8) forces 4-bit weights, the quantized local model's ability to know it is wrong degrades" — invokes exactly the fixed-memory-budget scenario the paper answers, and gets the answer backwards. 4-bit is not the degrading variable here; scale is (0.80 -> 0.98 from 2B to 7B at fixed 4-bit).

(2) THE PARSE-RATE COLLAPSE DOES NOT SURVIVE SCALE, AND IS ATTRIBUTED TO SCALE. Appendix A: "At 2B the same few-shot template yields a 64% parse rate averaged over all conditions, versus 100% at 7B — the scale effect on format-following". So 99% -> 64% is a 2B-only artifact; 7B-4bit = 1.00. Citing it as a consequence of "the T4 budget forces 4-bit" is unsupported.

(3) QUANTIZATION DID NOT UNIFORMLY DEGRADE UNCERTAINTY EVEN AT 2B. Verbalized AUROC went UP with 4-bit (0.56 -> 0.61). "Uncertainty quality" degraded on one of two measured signals, not both.

(4) THE PAPER DISCLAIMS THE GENERALIZATION. Section 6: "Two scale points give a direction, not a scaling law"; "Quantization is measured at one model size, bounding but not eliminating its confound with scale"; "We use n≈100 per condition, so some bootstrap intervals are wide". A single-size, n≈100/condition ablation cannot ground a sizing rule.

(5) DOMAIN MISMATCH FOR THE ROUTING QUESTION. The paper is cs.CV, Qwen2-VL 2B/7B only, multiple-choice VQA over "5,700 predictions spanning six realistic photographic degradations at three severities" (JPEG, blur, rotation, resampling, glare, low light). It contains no text-only LLM, no Qwen3, and no deferral/routing task. Its uncertainty is INPUT-degradation-induced (can I see this image?), not task-difficulty-induced (is this reasoning problem beyond me?) — which is the signal a local text router would need. Transferring 0.95->0.80 to a Qwen3 text router in a speech + ROS 2 loop is unvalidated extrapolation across modality, model generation, and uncertainty source.

(6) SOURCE STRENGTH INSUFFICIENT FOR A PRESCRIPTIVE CLAIM. v1 preprint dated 27 Jul 2026 (~4 weeks old), single author, "Affiliation: Independent Researcher", no peer review, CC BY 4.0. The paper's own cited prior work characterizes the effect far more weakly: "Empirical studies report that 4-bit models tend to show slightly lower confidence than their full-precision counterparts, with larger drops on some model/dataset pairs [10]" — i.e. a mild, model/dataset-dependent shift, not a 0.15-AUROC collapse.

NET: the descriptive first sentence is supported at 2B only, on VLM image-degradation VQA. The load-bearing second sentence — that the T4 4-bit constraint means "benchmark-accuracy-based sizing will overestimate router reliability" — is contradicted by the source's own headline recommendation and Table 2. The correct reading of this paper for a 9-11 GB T4 is: quantize to 4-bit and spend the freed memory on a LARGER model, which improved both accuracy (0.888 -> 0.935) and error detection (0.80 -> 0.98). Notably the paper's real transferable warning is about threshold transfer, not quantization: "For 2B-4bit the same clean-calibrated threshold silently admits errors: selective accuracy falls to 0.82 at glare s3 with 12% of all inputs answered wrongly above threshold" — that is a small-model argument, not a quantization argument.

The quote is transcribed accurately, but the claim launders a narrow vision-language result into a general prescription for text/voice routing, and is contradicted on the exact design question.

1) DOMAIN OVERREACH (fatal). arXiv:2607.24440 is "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation" (primary category cs.CV, submitted 27 Jul 2026). Verbatim abstract: it measures "the Qwen2-VL family" across "5,700 predictions spanning six realistic photographic degradations at three severities". The 0.61->0.69 and 0.80->0.98 numbers are VQA-under-image-corruption numbers. Zero text-only LLM data. The uncertainty source measured is perceptual (JPEG/blur/underexposure), not "is this dialogue turn or robot plan beyond my ability" — the quantity this project's router needs. No text-domain evidence in the cited source supports "asking a local small model in natural language is directly refuted".

2) SOURCE STRENGTH DOES NOT MATCH "MUST". Single author (M M Asif Ferdous), v1, 12 pages, no journal_ref/venue comment, n=2 model sizes (2B, 7B), one family. Its companion arXiv:2607.22034 ("Small Vision-Language Models Know When They Are Wrong But Cannot Say So", 24 Jul 2026) is the SAME solo author, same setup, posted 3 days earlier. The entire evidence base for the numbers is one person's two un-peer-reviewed cs.CV preprints — not a basis for a "must be read from logits" design rule.

3) CHERRY-PICKED WITHIN ITS OWN ABSTRACT, AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S REGIME. The same abstract states 4-bit quantization is "expensive for the confidence signal (internal AUROC 0.95 to 0.80, and the verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses from 99% to 64%)". With ~9-11 GB free on the T4, the local model MUST be 4-bit — i.e. the paper's own data puts the internal signal at 0.80, not the quoted 0.98. And part of the verbalized failure is a PARSE-RATE collapse (99%->64%), a format problem fixable by grammar-constrained/JSON decoding, not an epistemic limit. Additionally, the "internal" signal is defined as "its own mean token probability over the answer it generates" — it requires full local generation before deciding to escalate, so it cannot beat the measured 900 ms cloud TTFT; it adds to it.

4) DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED IN THE TEXT/CASCADE DOMAIN. arXiv:2604.19781 (29 Mar 2026) "Do Small Language Models Know When They're Wrong? Confidence-Based Cascade Scoring" tests precisely the design the claim calls refuted — verbalized confidence as the escalation signal — on 2,100 expert-scored decisions: best small LM "AUROC 0.857"; best cascade "approached large-LM accuracy (kappa 0.802 vs. 0.819) at 76% lower cost and 61% lower latency", with "no statistically detectable kappa loss" for the two small LMs with meaningful confidence variance. Its conclusion is model-dependence ("confidence discrimination is the bottleneck"), not uselessness. arXiv:2603.03752 (COREA, 4 Mar 2026) routes on an SLM's "verbalized confidence score" with an RL calibration reward: cost -21.5%/-16.8% at "absolute pass@1 drop within 2%". Caveat I verified: 2604.19781's pairs are GPT-5.4 / Claude 4.5+ / Gemini 3.1 tiers, not open-weight <=14B, so it refutes the general framing rather than the open-weight-specific number.

5) THE PRESCRIPTION ("must use logits") IS ALSO CONTRADICTED. arXiv:2601.08842 (20 Dec 2025): "internal token-level confidence in small models is uninformative (r = 0.035)" (Llama-3.2-3B, GSM8K). Tian et al. arXiv:2305.14975 "Just Ask for Calibration": for RLHF-tuned models "verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities" (~50% relative ECE reduction) — the words-vs-logits ordering is regime-dependent, not a law. Further, the strongest signals in current work are neither: arXiv:2604.09624 and arXiv:2608.14659 both center P(True) (a prompted question read via one token's probability); 2608.14659 finds "multi-sample P(True) achieves the strongest correlation with correctness, while all the other methods, including semantic entropy probes, yield only weak correlation". The claim's binary axis is the wrong axis.

6) THE SKEPTICAL CONCLUSION SURVIVES, BUT ON A DIFFERENT SOURCE. arXiv:2608.05064 (5 Aug 2026) is the on-point paper the claim should have cited: 11 instruction-tuned open-weight models, 0.5B-14B, three families, 25,168 text predictions on ARC-Challenge/TruthfulQA. Platt scaling gets verbalized ECE "as low as 0.02", yet "certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to only three model-task pairs and to none at 10%". That warrants "do not grant a local small model autonomous defer authority" — it does NOT warrant "verbalized is near-useless" (ECE 0.02 after scaling) nor "must be read from logits" (logits are not its remedy).

Net: numbers quoted correctly; scope, source strength, and the causal prescription all fail. Do not use 0.61/0.69 vs 0.80/0.98 as a text-routing design argument.

result.evidence:
VERDICT: numbers quoted accurately, but the claim's load-bearing inference is contradicted by its own source.

SOURCE VERIFIED (exists, is real): arXiv:2607.24440, "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation", M M Asif Ferdous, submitted 27 Jul 2026, 12 pages / 4 figures, cs.CV. Single author, no venue, not peer-reviewed. The three literal numbers ARE in the abstract and Section 4.3: "-1.6 accuracy points (0.904 to 0.888)", "internal AUROC falls from 0.95 to 0.80", "verbalized parse rate collapses from 0.99 to 0.64". So checklist item 1 (quote fidelity) passes. Everything after that fails.

REFUTATION 1 - the source's own headline conclusion inverts the claim's operational implication. Section 4.4, "RQ3: for a fixed budget, prefer the larger quantized model": "The three arms are the three configurations that fit a 16 GB GPU. 7B-4bit dominates: it has the highest accuracy (0.935), the highest internal AUROC (0.98), and the lowest area under the risk-coverage curve. Notably it beats even the full-precision small model on the confidence signal (internal AUROC 0.98 vs 0.95, AURC 0.008 vs 0.017), so scale's benefit to the uncertainty signal more than offsets quantization's harm." Section 5: "the scale gain (internal AUROC 0.80 -> 0.98) exceeds the quantization loss (0.95 -> 0.80)". The paper was itself run on "a single free-tier 16 GB NVIDIA T4". So the paper tells a T4 practitioner to DO exactly what this project would do (4-bit weights, spend the freed VRAM on scale), and reports the best uncertainty signal of all arms in that configuration. The claim cites it as a warning against 4-bit on a T4.

REFUTATION 2 - the claim's conclusion ("benchmark-accuracy-based sizing will overestimate router reliability") is falsified inside the paper's own data. Across the three arms accuracy and internal AUROC CO-MOVE: 2B-4bit 0.888/0.80, 2B-fp16 0.904/0.95, 7B-4bit 0.935/0.98. Accuracy-based sizing picks 7B-4bit, which is also the best deferral signal. The accuracy/uncertainty divergence exists only in the single A-vs-B contrast at one model size.

REFUTATION 3 - quantization effect measured at ONE size, and the paper flags the confound itself. Arms are only 2B-fp16, 2B-NF4, 7B-NF4; 7B-fp16 was never run. Limitations: "Quantization is measured at one model size, bounding but not eliminating its confound with scale." The claim generalizes a 2B-only result to the 4B-14B class the project would actually deploy, where the paper's only 4-bit data point shows AUROC 0.98.

REFUTATION 4 - domain mismatch that the paper itself calls untested. Task is Qwen2-VL (vision-language, not Qwen3 text) answering a 100-item Food101 subset as FOUR-WAY MULTIPLE CHOICE under six synthetic photographic degradations, greedy decoding, 32-token cap. Limitations: "All results are on Food101 posed as four-way multiple choice; generality to open-ended VQA is untested. We study a single model family... The multiple-choice format forces an answer and therefore cannot observe refusal behaviour." The claim transports it to text-only routing/deferral for a Chinese/Cantonese voice + ROS 2 loop - two domains beyond what the authors say is untested. Statistical base is 100 unique images reused across 19 conditions (1,900 predictions/arm), n~100 per condition with "some bootstrap intervals... wide".

REFUTATION 5 - the 99% -> 64% parse-rate figure is a format-following artifact, not uncertainty quality, and is irrelevant to router design on the paper's own numbers. Appendix: "At 2B the same few-shot template yields a 64% parse rate averaged over all conditions, versus 100% at 7B"; the quantized model "abandons the requested two-line format and returns a bare label". That is removable with grammar/constrained JSON decoding (llama.cpp GBNF, vLLM guided decoding) - not measured by the paper. And verbalized confidence is near chance at EVERY precision and scale (mean AUROC 0.61 -> 0.69 from 2B to 7B; 0.56 in one analysis), so its parse rate cannot degrade a signal the paper says is unusable anyway.

REFUTATION 6 - the claim's premise about the hardware is also wrong. "the T4 budget (9-11 GB free...) forces 4-bit weights" - 9-11 GB does not force 4-bit: a 4B model at fp16 (~8 GB weights) or an 8B at INT8/W8A8 (~8.5 GB) fits. The paper's own point is that 4-bit is a CHOICE that buys scale, not a forced degradation.

NO SUPPORTING REPLICATION FOUND for the text-LLM version of the effect. arXiv search returned mostly "calibration data for quantization" (different sense of calibration). The nearest text-LLM item, "When Quantization Affects Confidence of Large Language Models?" (2024-05), reports quantization lowering confidence mainly on already-low-confidence samples - a weaker and differently-shaped effect, not a 0.95->0.80 AUROC collapse. So the strong version of the claim rests on one unrefereed single-author 2B-VLM preprint.

NUMBERS CHECK OUT, INFERENCE IS A REVERSAL OF THE SOURCE.

1) Source exists and the three numbers are verbatim. arXiv:2607.24440v1 (27 Jul 2026, cs.CV), "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation". Table 2 (means over 19 conditions), three arms:
   - 2B fp16: acc 0.904 / verb parse 0.99 / verb AUROC 0.56 / internal AUROC 0.95 / AURC 0.017
   - 2B 4-bit: acc 0.888 / parse 0.64 / verb 0.61 / internal 0.80 / AURC 0.048
   - 7B 4-bit: acc 0.935 / parse 1.00 / verb 0.69 / internal 0.98 / AURC 0.008
   So -1.6 pts, 0.95->0.80, 99%->64% are real, and are the 2B-fp16 -> 2B-4bit contrast (Sec 4.3, "Holding scale fixed at 2B").

2) The claim's operational conclusion inverts the paper's own conclusion. The paper was designed around exactly this constraint ("Consider a fixed 16 GB GPU... three configurations fit") and its headline recommendation is: "For a fixed memory budget the recommendation is therefore to prefer a larger quantized model over a smaller full-precision one: 7B-4bit gives both the best accuracy and the best uncertainty signal (internal AUROC 0.98) of the three configurations that fit." 7B-4bit's 0.98 is HIGHER than 2B-fp16's 0.95. The claim uses the intra-2B penalty to argue that "the T4 budget forces 4-bit weights [therefore] the quantized local model's ability to know it is wrong degrades" — but under a 9-11 GB budget a 7-8B 4-bit model fits, which is precisely the paper's BEST-signal arm. Every arm in the paper "reproduces on a single free-tier NVIDIA T4", so this is not even a hardware-extrapolation gap: the paper measured the T4 case and concluded the opposite of the claim.

3) The parse-rate collapse is near-irrelevant to router design, and the paper's own attribution is internally inconsistent. Verbalized AUROC is 0.56 / 0.61 / 0.69 across arms — "weak and often at chance" in the paper's words — so 99%->64% loses a signal that was worthless anyway; the paper's conclusion says "internal token probability, not stated confidence, is the signal to defer on". Worse, Appendix A attributes the same 64% to SCALE, not quantization: "At 2B the same few-shot template yields a 64% parse rate averaged over all conditions, versus 100% at 7B — the scale effect on format-following reported in Section 4." Section 4.3 calls it a quantization effect. One of the two is wrong.

4) Domain mismatch vs this project, admitted by the paper's Limitations: "Two scale points give a direction, not a scaling law"; "Quantization is measured at one model size, bounding but not eliminating its confound with scale"; "n~100 per condition"; "All results are on Food101 posed as four-way multiple choice; generality to open-ended VQA is untested"; "We study a single model family"; "The multiple-choice format forces an answer and therefore cannot observe refusal behaviour." The project needs deferral in open-ended Chinese/Cantonese text + tool-calling, i.e. refusal/abstention behaviour in a generative setting — the exact thing the paper says it cannot observe. Nothing about Qwen3 text models, nothing about text.

5) Independent text-LLM evidence contradicts the generalized version. arXiv:2607.10855 "Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models" (12 Jul 2026) evaluates 2/3/4/8-bit across six quantization methods on uncertainty, calibration and robustness and finds "A reliability peak occurs for 4-bit quantized models, indicating that quantizing moderately sized models offers the best reliability-efficiency trade-off", plus "quantization enhances the robustness of LLMs to natural input perturbations." That is the opposite sign for 4-bit specifically. arXiv:2606.01850 "Does Compression Preserve Uncertainty?" (1 Jun 2026, 12 LLMs, 5 tasks, conformal prediction) supports the generic accuracy/uncertainty decoupling but its finding (II) is "larger models absorb compression-induced uncertainty far more effectively than smaller ones" — again pointing to bigger-and-quantized, not to a 4-bit penalty as a reason for pessimism.

6) Source strength vs claim strength. Single v1 preprint, not peer-reviewed, one model family, n~100/condition, one dataset, code at github.com/Asif-Ferdous/vlm-scale-quant. Artifacts released (a plus), but insufficient to carry a strong deployment-sizing claim for a different modality, different model family and different task format.

SALVAGEABLE CORE (not the claim as written): "accuracy alone is a bad proxy for deferral-signal quality" is supported by 2607.24440 + 2606.01850. The correct T4 implication is the reverse of the claim: spend the 9-11 GB on a ~7-8B 4-bit model rather than a 2-4B fp16 one, and route on mean token logprob rather than verbalized confidence (verbalized AUROC 0.56-0.69 = chance-ish). The claim's specific assertion — that T4-forced 4-bit makes router reliability worse than benchmark accuracy suggests — is refuted by its own primary source.

result.evidence:
VERIFIED FIRST: arXiv:2607.24440 exists (submitted 2026-07-27) and the quote is verbatim from its abstract: "mean error-detection AUROC 0.80 to 0.98 from 2B to 7B ... verbalized confidence stays weak and often at chance (mean 0.61 to 0.69): the gap between what the model knows and what it says widens rather than closes with size." So the numbers are not fabricated. The claim still fails on scope, source quality, and selective quotation.

(1) MODALITY/DOMAIN OVERREACH — decisive. The paper is titled "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in VISION-LANGUAGE Models Under IMAGE DEGRADATION." Population = Qwen2-VL 2B/7B only; task = VQA over 5,700 predictions across "six realistic photographic degradations at three severities." The claim restates this as a property of "small open-weight models" and applies it to a text/speech deferral decision (should a local Qwen3 escalate a spoken Chinese/Cantonese turn to GPT-5.6 Sol). The error mode being detected in the paper is *sensor corruption*, which is exactly the failure class that depresses answer token probability — not semantic/reasoning difficulty, which is what a router must detect. The 0.80→0.98 "internal signal" figure is therefore an artifact of the stimulus design and does not transfer; the claim carries it forward unqualified.

(2) CHERRY-PICKED WITHIN THE SAME PAPER, and the omitted half is the one that governs this project. The same abstract/paper reports 4-bit quantization drops internal AUROC 0.95 → 0.80 and collapses verbalized-confidence parse rate 99% → 64%. On a T4 with only 9–11 GB free, any local model is quantized (AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit) — i.e. precisely the regime where the paper says the prescribed logit signal degrades most. The claim's prescription ("must be read from logits") is asserted while suppressing the paper's own evidence that it weakens under the deployment constraint at issue.

(3) SCALING ASSERTION FROM n=2 POINTS. "Barely improves with scale" is inferred from two size points (2B, 7B) in one family, one modality. 0.61→0.69 over a 3.5× size step is not a scaling law; there is no 14B/32B point and no second family in 2607.24440.

(4) SOURCE QUALITY INSUFFICIENT FOR A CATEGORICAL DESIGN VETO. Single author (M M Asif Ferdous), no venue, no peer review, ~3 weeks old. It is one of a near-duplicate pair by the same author on the same setup: arXiv:2607.22034 "Small Vision-Language Models Know When They Are Wrong But Cannot Say So" (Qwen2-VL-2B + SmolVLM, 3,800 predictions, same six degradations). That companion paper also states the internal signal is NOT robust either — "under severe underexposure ... internal error-detection falls to chance ... neither signal should be trusted under severe low-light" — directly contradicting the claim's implication that logits are a dependable substitute.

(5) DIRECT CONTRADICTION OF THE PRESCRIPTIVE HALF. Tian et al., "Just Ask for Calibration" (arXiv:2305.14975, EMNLP 2023): for RLHF-tuned models, "verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities," ~50% relative reduction in calibration error on TriviaQA/SciQ/TruthfulQA. That is calibration (ECE), not discrimination (AUROC) — the claim silently mixes the two constructs — but it refutes the unconditional form "must be read from logits, not words." It also ignores that for the cloud tier (Bedrock GPT-5.6 Sol / Sonnet 5) logits are not exposed at all, so a logit-only rule is unimplementable on the side where escalation is judged.

(6) THE CLAIM'S CONCLUSION IS PROBABLY TRUE — BUT NOT FROM THIS SOURCE. Better, independent, text-domain evidence exists and the claim should be re-anchored to it rather than to a vision preprint: (a) Jianru Shen, "Provable Limits and Certified Deferral for Verbalized Uncertainty in Small Language Models," arXiv:2608.05064, ACCEPTED at MIWAI 2026 (Springer LNAI): 11 instruction-tuned models, 0.5B–14B, three families, ARC-Challenge + TruthfulQA, 25,168 local predictions — Platt scaling gets ECE to 0.02 yet certified autonomy at a 20% risk budget is granted to only 3 of 22 model-task pairs and to NONE at 10%; 8 of 22 pairs hit a proven temperature-scaling infeasibility floor. (b) Kumaran, "Reported Confidence in LLMs Tracks Commitment More Than Correctness," arXiv:2606.29490: across 4 non-reasoning + 4 reasoning models, verbal confidence predicts commit/abstain far better than correctness; after removing shared variance with log-probabilities the residual's link to correctness falls to near chance; mechanistic steering in Gemma 3/4 confirms verbal confidence is a commit-readiness readout, roughly orthogonal to correctness. These support "don't ask in words" with text-domain, multi-family, partly peer-reviewed evidence — and (a) additionally shows the logit/calibrated route ALSO fails to license autonomy at a 10% risk budget, which the claim does not concede.

NET: refuted as stated. The specific AUROC pair 0.61→0.69 / 0.80→0.98 is a vision-VQA-under-image-degradation result from an unreviewed single-author preprint and must not be quoted as a general small-LLM routing number; the "read the logits instead" prescription is both contradicted (Tian 2023) and undercut by the cited paper's own 4-bit result, which is the T4-relevant one. Recommended repair: restate as "verbalized confidence from ≤14B open-weight LMs cannot license autonomous deferral (0/22 model-task pairs certified at a 10% risk budget; verbal confidence tracks commitment, not correctness)", cite 2608.05064 + 2606.29490, drop 2607.24440 to a cross-modal corroboration, and stop claiming logits are a reliable substitute — no source supports a usable local deferral signal at this project's risk budget under 4-bit quantization.

(1) CHERRY-PICKED ARM — the paper's own results table has three arms: (A) 2B-fp16, (B) 2B-4bit, (C) 7B-4bit, with "Verbalized parse rate 0.99 / 0.64 / 1.00". The 64% is 4-bit AT 2B ONLY; the 4-bit 7B model parses at 1.00. The claim's framing "under 4-bit quantization ⇒ one in three requests unparseable" is contradicted by the same table. The paper's headline recommendation is the opposite of the claim's use: "For a fixed memory budget the recommendation is therefore to prefer a larger quantized model over a smaller full-precision one: 7B-4bit gives both the best accuracy and the best uncertainty signal." Project's local candidate is Qwen3-4B/8B, not a 2B, so the 36% does not attach to the design decision.

(2) PAPER ITSELF FLAGS THE ATTRIBUTION AS CONFOUNDED — Limitations §6: "Quantization is measured at one model size, bounding but not eliminating its confound with scale," and "We use n≈100 per condition, so some bootstrap intervals are wide." Appendix A re-labels the SAME 64% as a scale effect: "At 2B the same few-shot template yields a 64% parse rate averaged over all conditions, versus 100% at 7B — the scale effect on format-following." The paper uses one number for two different causal stories.

(3) PARSE RATE IS A PROMPT/DECODING ARTIFACT, NOT AN INTRINSIC QUANTIZATION COST — Appendix A: at 7B, parse rates were "100% (few-shot), 100% (direct) and 55% (minimal)" — a 45-point swing from prompt wording alone at fixed precision. Parsing was bare regex on free text ("Answers were extracted with Answer:\s*(.+) and confidences with Confidence:\s*([0-9]{1,3})"); no grammar/schema-constrained decoding was used, which is the standard 2026 fix (vLLM guided decoding/XGrammar, llama.cpp GBNF, Outlines) and makes format conformance a decoding invariant rather than a sampled outcome. So "needs a defined fallback for ~1 in 3 requests" is not a property of quantized small models.

(4) THE DOWNSTREAM INFERENCE CONTRADICTS THE PAPER'S CONCLUSION — verbalized-confidence error-detection AUROC is 0.56 (2B-fp16) / 0.61 (2B-4bit) / 0.69 (7B-4bit), i.e. near chance even where parse rate is 0.99–1.00, while internal mean-token-probability AUROC is 0.95/0.80/0.98. Conclusion §7: "internal token probability, not stated confidence, is the signal to defer on." The cost-saving of a verbalized-confidence cascade is destroyed by the signal being uninformative, not by 36% parse failures; the claim elevates a fixable artifact into the causal mechanism. Read correctly, this paper is evidence FOR a feasible local deferral gate on this exact hardware (Reproducibility §: "Every arm reproduces on a single free-tier NVIDIA T4") using logprobs — the reverse of how the claim deploys it.

(5) DOMAIN TRANSFER UNSUPPORTED — measurements are Qwen2-VL (a 2024 VLM family) on Food-101 posed as four-way multiple choice under six synthetic photographic degradations. Paper: "All results are on Food101 posed as four-way multiple choice; generality to open-ended VQA is untested" and "We study a single model family, so scale effects may be family-specific." The claim transports the number to a text/voice dialogue router with Qwen3 in Chinese/Cantonese — a different modality, model generation, task format, and language.

Implementation notes: Turing lacks `cp.async` (replaced with synchronous global→shared reads) and lacks `m16n8k16` MMA (two stacked `m16n8k8` instead), and uses an FP16 accumulator on Turing.

3. Source code in current `main` directly contradicts the claim: `MarlinLinearKernel.get_min_capability()` returns **75**, and `marlin_utils.query_marlin_supported_quant_types()` gates on `if device_capability < 75: return []`. (Pre-#29901 these were 80.)

4. The docs table the claim cites has been superseded. `docs/features/quantization/README.md` at tag **v0.27.1** reads:
`| Marlin (GPTQ/AWQ/FP8/FP4) | ❌ | ✅︎* | ✅︎ | ✅︎ | ✅︎ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |` with columns Volta | Turing | Ampere | Ada | Hopper, plus footnote "*Turing does not support Marlin MXFP4" and "Turing to SM 7.5". 5. Independent corroboration: PR #45375 (merged 2026-06-23, "[Quant] Enable modelopt_mixed on Turing (SM75)") states "**Marlin already supports SM75, so the kernels are in place**" and explicitly targets "a free Google Colab T4".

6. The claim's second half ("primarily a VRAM-reduction measure rather than a guaranteed throughput win") is also refuted by the contributor's measured GEMM benchmark on a **Turing 2080Ti, GPTQ channelwise, FP16 in**, ms per GEMM, m = batch:
- n1024 k2048, m=1: torch-fp16 0.01169 → marlin-w4a16 0.00575 (**2.03×**), marlin-w4a8-int8 0.00530 (2.21×)
- n2048 k2048, m=1: 0.01761 → 0.00765 (**2.30×**)
- n2048 k4096, m=1: 0.03213 → 0.01151 (**2.79×**)
So at batch-1 decode — exactly the single-user voice-loop regime this project cares about — Marlin on SM75 is a real ~2–2.8× GEMM speedup, not merely memory savings.

Caveats that do NOT rescue the claim: (a) the benchmark card is a 2080Ti (616 GB/s) not a T4 (320 GB/s), so absolute T4 numbers will be lower, but kernel availability is architectural (SM75) and PR bodies name T4 explicitly; (b) Turing's FP16-accumulator path had a numerical bug, fixed by PR #33972 "[Bugfix] fix output Nan/Inf in marlin if dtype=float16" (merged 2026-03-27) — so pin vLLM >= v0.19.0, not just >= v0.13.0; (c) MXFP4 remains unsupported on Turing (needs BF16 activation), which is consistent with the T4-has-no-bf16 premise elsewhere in the research brief.

Net for the research: the T4 constraint list should be rewritten. GPTQ/AWQ-INT4, FP8-W8A16 and NVFP4 all reach Marlin on T4 in vLLM >= v0.19.0. Citing a 23-month-old pinned doc as evidence about a fast-moving kernel library is precisely the recency failure mode.

(2) "4-bit on T4 is primarily a VRAM-reduction measure rather than a guaranteed throughput win" is ALSO refuted by first-party microbenchmarks in PR #29901, run on a 2080Ti (Turing SM 7.5, same arch as T4), Dense Marlin + GPTQ channelwise, latency in ms:
- n=1024 k=2048 m=1: torch-fp16 0.01169 vs marlin-w4a16 0.00575 (2.03x) vs marlin-w4a8-int8 0.00530 (2.21x)
- n=2048 k=2048 m=1: torch-fp16 0.01761 vs marlin-w4a16 0.00765 (2.30x) vs w4a8-int8 0.00706 (2.49x)
- n=2048 k=1024 m=512: 0.07456 vs 0.03694 (2.02x)
m=1 is exactly the batch-1 decode regime a single-user voice/ROS 2 loop runs in, so this is a ~2x GEMM win on Turing, not merely memory savings.

Surviving true-but-narrower caveats (do NOT rescue the claim as written): Turing Marlin uses an FP16 accumulator instead of FP32 by the author's deliberate tradeoff ("throughput of the MMA instruction on the Turing architecture is only half when using an FP32 accumulator"), a numerical-precision caveat vs Ampere+; Marlin MXFP4 is unsupported on Turing; and NVFP4 Marlin on Turing had a correctness bug (issue #33461, closed 2026-06-13). The paper's conclusion is that stated confidence is unusable as a deferral signal irrespective of parse rate: verbalized error-detection AUROC = 0.56 / 0.61 / 0.69 across the three arms, at or near chance (<=0.60) in 8 of 19 conditions even at 7B where parsing is 100%, versus internal mean-token-probability AUROC 0.95 / 0.80 / 0.98. Defining a fallback for the unparseable 36% does nothing about the 64% that ARE parsed and are routed by a coin flip. The claim elevates the second-order problem and omits the first-order one.

Refutation 4 — "destroying the claimed cost saving" is unsupported by any measurement. The paper has no router, no cascade, no cost model, no price or latency figures; it is 100 Food101 items x 6 photographic degradations x 3 severities = 5,700 predictions on one 2024-era VLM family, greedy, fixed seeds, single-author preprint, not peer reviewed, 0 citations, artifact repo github.com/Asif-Ferdous/vlm-scale-quant with 0 stars. Even taking 36% at face value, unconditional escalation of 36% still avoids 64% of large-model calls; on an already-running g4dn.xlarge the local tier's marginal cost is ~$0, so 36% escalation reduces Bedrock GPT-5.6 Sol calls by ~64% rather than "destroying" savings. Whether that is uneconomic depends on a cost ratio the source never supplies.

Refutation 5 — domain transfer is unvalidated. The measurement is a vision-language model on degraded photographs answering multiple-choice food labels; the claim applies it to a text/voice Qwen3 routing cascade for a ROS 2 loop. Nothing in the source measures text-only LLMs, Qwen3, tool-calling, Chinese/Cantonese, or router deferral, and image degradation (the paper's only stressor) has no analogue in the project's input distribution.

What survives: "4-bit NF4 Qwen2-VL-2B under an unconstrained two-line prompt fails to emit a parseable confidence integer on 36% of degraded-image VQA items" is supported. Everything the claim adds — quantization as the cause, one-in-three as a router design constant, and the cost-saving conclusion — is not.

REFUTED as written — outdated source + one directly contradicted sub-claim, though the headline conclusion survives with corrected details.

1) Quote fidelity: OK. I fetched the cited v0.6.1 page and the table columns are Volta | Turing | Ampere | Ada | Hopper | AMD | Intel | x86 | Inferentia | TPU, so the ✗/✅/✅/✅/✅/✗ pattern does map to Turing=✅ for AWQ, GPTQ, INT8(W8A8), and the full table does also mark AQLM/bitsandbytes/DeepSpeedFP/GGUF ✅ on Turing. No misread.

2) OUTDATED — fatal for a 2026 decision. v0.6.1 was released 2024-09-11; current vLLM is v0.27.1 (2026-08-11) — 21 minor releases and ~23 months later. The cited URL path (/quantization/supported_hardware.html) no longer exists in current docs (404); it moved into docs/features/quantization/README.md. Crucially, the claim's subject — "a quantized Qwen3-class model" — did not exist when v0.6.1 shipped (Qwen3 landed in vLLM ~0.8.5, Apr 2025), so the cited source cannot support the Qwen3 half of the claim at all. It is an anachronistic citation.

3) DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED: "no Marlin" on Turing is FALSE as of Dec 2025. vLLM PR #29901 "[Kernel][Quantization][MoE] add marlin kernel support for turing (sm75)" merged 2025-12-16; its body explicitly names "turing (sm75) (e.g. 2080ti / T4)", works around the missing cp.async and m16n8k16 MMA (stacking m16n8k8 twice), uses an FP16 accumulator on Turing, and states "Supported Weights: GPTQ, AWQ, FP8, NVFP4 ... Supported Activation: FP16, INT8 (only for GPTQ and AWQ)". The author's 2080ti kernel benchmark shows marlin-w4a16 0.00575 ms vs torch-fp16 0.01169 ms at n=1024,k=2048,m=1 (~2x). This is visible in the build system on main: CMakeLists.txt has `# marlin has limited support for turing` / `cuda_archs_loose_intersection(MARLIN_SM75_ARCHS "7.5" ...)` and globs `csrc/libtorch_stable/quantization/marlin/sm75_kernel_*.cu`. Current docs table row reads `Marlin (GPTQ/AWQ/FP8/FP4) | ❌ Volta | ✅︎* Turing | ...` with footnote "*Turing does not support Marlin MXFP4." So the claim's stated mechanism ("kernel speed ... no Marlin") is inverted: Turing DOES get Marlin, minus MXFP4.

4) FOUR of the SEVEN enumerated methods are wrong or heavily qualified for the vLLM a user would install today:
- AQLM: REMOVED from vLLM entirely — PR #22943 "[Kernel/Quant] Remove AQLM", merged 2025-08-16. Absent from the current docs table and from the `QuantizationMethods` literal in vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/__init__.py.
- bitsandbytes and GGUF: no longer in-tree quantization configs; they are not in `QuantizationMethods` on main and their tests now live under tests/plugins_tests/bitsandbytes/ and tests/plugins_tests/gguf/ (out-of-tree plugin path). The docs table still shows them ✅ on Turing, i.e. docs and code disagree — an extra reason not to cite this table as settled fact.
- DeepSpeedFP: no source file, no doc page, and not in `QuantizationMethods` on main; only the stale docs table still lists it.

5) What survives: "no FP8 on T4" is still TRUE — vllm/platforms/cuda.py `supports_fp8()` returns `has_device_capability(89)`, i.e. Ada+. And there is no blanket Turing ban: `supported_dtypes` still returns [fp16, fp32] for capability 60-79, bf16 is hard-rejected below SM80 (check_if_supports_dtype raises "Bfloat16 is only supported on GPUs with compute capability of at least 8.0"), and attention backends are validated dynamically per-backend rather than gated at SM80. So the operative conclusion — an AWQ/GPTQ Qwen3 checkpoint IS loadable on a T4 under current vLLM, with `--dtype float16` forced — is true. It is just not established by the cited 2024 source, and the reason given for the T4 penalty is wrong.

Net: do not cite v0.6.1's supported_hardware table for a 2026 T4 decision. The corrected 2026 statement would be: "AWQ/GPTQ/INT8-W8A8 and, since vLLM ≥ the Dec-2025 #29901 merge, Marlin-GPTQ/AWQ/INT8-W4A8 all run on SM75; FP8 and bf16 do not; AQLM is gone and bitsandbytes/GGUF are out-of-tree plugins." Note the downstream consequence for the research question: because Marlin now exists on Turing, the "T4 is slow only because it lacks fast kernels" argument is weaker than the claim asserts, and any TTFT-vs-900 ms comparison must be re-measured on a vLLM ≥ v0.12-class build rather than inferred from pre-Marlin Turing numbers.

result.summary: The evidence on the decision-critical axis (angle 1: is the routing/escalation decision itself a solved problem?) is one-sided against the user's design, and I re-verified the key numbers myself in the primary sources rather than trusting the vote tally. Across a 21-method × 5-benchmark sweep, the best router sits 10-30 pp below a label-oracle and the combination of 10× more routing data + a 3× bigger encoder + end-to-end fine-tuning buys at most +2.13 pp (14.6% of the gap); in the one paper that actually builds a purpose-designed learned small→large deferral agent, the cascade is strictly worse than always calling the big model on all three benchmarks (94.3/98.2/93.3 vs 98.8/98.7/98.1), and even a hindsight oracle router (98.6/98.6/97.8) never beats LLM-only. The specific mechanism the user would reach for first — asking the small local model how confident it is — is measurably the weakest option: verbalized-confidence error-detection AUROC is ~0.5 below 2B and only 0.63-0.66 at 14B, 0 of 22 model-task pairs earn a certified 10% risk budget, and a token-entropy router escalated 0.0% of steps on an interactive partially-observable task while staying at the small-model-only success rate of 64.6%. On the hardware axis I found and corrected a factually stale premise from the previous round: current vLLM docs mark Marlin (GPTQ/AWQ/FP8/FP4) as supported on Turing/SM75 (only MXFP4 excluded), so 4-bit on T4 is not merely a VRAM measure — but FP8 W8A8 is still unsupported on Volta/Turing/Ampere, bf16 still auto-casts to fp16, and the only measured Qwen3-class T4 throughput I could find (20.5 tok/s decode) was fp16, a VL model, and across TWO T4s, with no TTFT figure at all, so the "can local beat 900 ms TTFT" question remains unmeasured. Recommended decision: do not build the small local model as a router or first-tier decision-maker; keep one cloud model as the sole decision-maker and spend the T4's remaining 9-11 GB only on deterministic non-LLM work (VAD/endpointing, ASR, a fine-tuned intent classifier, embedding retrieval) — and falsify this recommendation with the cheapest possible experiment (below) before writing any serving code.

findings.claim: The routing plateau: the best router in a 21-method × 5-benchmark sweep sits 10-30 pp below the per-query label-oracle, and the strongest known interventions barely move it — scaling routing data 30k→300k, upgrading the encoder ModernBERT-base (~110M) → ModernBERT-large (~340M), and end-to-end fine-tuning, all combined, yield up to +2.13 pp, closing 14.6% of the oracle gap. Per-benchmark: RouterBench best 80.38 vs oracle 91.69; EmbedLLM 67.51 vs 97.97 (30.5 pp).

Ablation shows each single lever is far weaker (data +0.47, FT +0.42, encoder +0.13, mean Scaled-FT +1.24 pp), so the headline 2.13 is the paper's most favourable configuration, not its typical one. FLASH_ATTN is only supported for >= Ampere (sm80)"; engine log "Your device 'NVIDIA T4G' (with compute capability 7.5) doesn't support torch.bfloat16. Falling back to torch.float16"; "There is no workaround other than --enforce-eager that I am aware of, but it is extremely slow (less than 10 tokens/s)". The 20.5 figure is in a comment by vLLM contributor Isotr0py: "I checked it on Tesla T4 with main branch, seems FlashInfer backend can work now: # vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct --max-model-len 16384 -tp 2 ... Avg generation throughput: 20.5 tokens/s" (an earlier interval snapshot in the same log reads 5.1 tokens/s). FOUR REASONS NOT TO OVER-READ IT, all of which the earlier round's version of this claim ignored: (1) -tp 2 = two T4s, twice this project's GPU budget, on an otherwise idle GPU, not one T4 already holding 3.2 GB of YOLO26s/Kokoro/MediaPipe/FunASR; (2) the model is Qwen3-VL (vision-language) in unquantized fp16, not a 4-bit text Qwen3, and the reported defect is specific to Qwen3-VL's attention-backend selection; (3) the original error log is from T4G (aarch64/Graviton), not g4dn x86; (4) 'Avg generation throughput' is an engine-log interval aggregate, and decode throughput is not TTFT — the 900 ms comparison the project cares about was never measured here.
findings.vote: voted 0-3 by the pass; the underlying log lines are real, but the pass was right to reject the claim's generalization to single-T4 sub-second response

findings.claim: One cited source is mis-scoped and must not be reused as stated: arXiv 2607.24440 is a VISION-language-model study of uncertainty under IMAGE DEGRADATION, not a text small-LLM confidence study, so the 4-bit-quantization figures attributed to it (accuracy -1.6 pp while internal error-detection AUROC falls 0.95→0.80 and verbalized-confidence parse rate collapses 99%→64%) cannot be cited as evidence about a quantized text Qwen3 on T4.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24440 (citation_title: "Bigger or Cheaper? Scale and Quantization Effects on Uncertainty Signals in Vision-Language Models Under Image Degradation", verified by me 2026-08-22)
findings.evidence: I checked only the title, not the numbers. The title establishes the domain mismatch, which is very likely why all three quantization/confidence claims built on it were voted 0-3. The direction it suggests — that 4-bit hurts uncertainty quality much more than benchmark accuracy, and that unparseable verbalized confidence forces a fallback policy that either suppresses escalation or escalates ~a third of traffic unconditionally — is a reasonable hypothesis for this project's 4-bit-forced T4 budget, but it is currently EVIDENCE-INSUFFICIENT for text models and needs a text-LLM source before it enters any design document.

findings.claim: Three of the five research angles produced ZERO evidence, surviving or refuted, and the report cannot answer them. This is a coverage gap, not a clean bill of health.
sources: the claim set delivered to this synthesis step: 1 confirmed + 25 refuted claims, all of which concern angle 1 (routing/deferral/calibration) or angle 2 (T4/SM75 serving)
findings.evidence: Nothing was returned on angle 3 (BFCL v3/v4, tau-bench, AgentBench function-calling gaps for ≤14B open-weight models; multi-step error compounding rates; whether Chinese/Cantonese ability collapses faster than English as models shrink — the axis that already killed the local guard model in the previous round). Nothing on angle 4 (whether an external deterministic checker beats 'a stronger model being careful'; the 0.4%-no-plan vs 28.3%-unsafe-plan and 37.6%→56.9% figures were NOT verified or refuted; prompt injection propagating small→large; denial-of-wallet via induced escalation; who carries EU AI Act Art 50 synthetic-audio marking in a two-tier design as of 2026-08-02). Nothing on angle 5 (reasoning-effort knobs as a single-model substitute for two tiers; sub-1B fine-tuned classifiers or non-LLM routers beating a general small LLM; speculative decoding on one shared card). Consequence: the recommendation below rests on angle 1 being decisive, and would need angle 5 evidence before candidates A/B/C can be ranked against each other on numbers rather than on plausibility.

findings.claim: RECOMMENDED DECISION under the T4 constraint, plus the cheapest experiment that would falsify it: do not build a local small LLM as router, deferral judge, or first-tier decision-maker; keep one cloud model as the sole decision-maker and restrict the T4's remaining 9-11 GB to deterministic non-LLM work. Falsify it offline, for ~$0 of GPU, before writing serving code.
findings.evidence: WHY: the three findings above are one-sided — the escalation decision has a measured plateau far from oracle (+2.13 pp for 10× data + 3× encoder + fine-tuning); the one purpose-built small→large deferral agent is strictly below LLM-only on 3/3 benchmarks and its logprob-only variant escalated 0.0% of steps; and no 0.5B-14B model earned a 10% certified risk budget on self-reported confidence. A voice+ROS 2 loop needs better than 10% error on the safety-relevant subset, which is outside every certified operating point measured. CHEAPEST FALSIFYING EXPERIMENT (offline, no local LLM served, no new GPU memory, one working session): (1) log ~200-300 real turns from the existing 900 ms Bedrock path, including the ROS 2 action actually taken; (2) hand-label each turn 'a small model could have handled this' vs 'needed the frontier model'; (3) offline, score the CHEAP pre-answer signals only — keyword rules, a fine-tuned <1B intent classifier, and frozen-encoder embedding kNN (worth trying because kNN reportedly ranks top-2 on all five benchmarks in the routing-plateau sweep, i.e. the cheap baseline is the strong one); (4) apply the 2608.05064 certification protocol — Clopper-Pearson on the 200-item calibration split — and ask for coverage at a 10% risk budget. FALSIFICATION CRITERION: if any cheap signal reaches AUROC ≥0.85 with ≥50% certified coverage at 10% risk ON THIS PROJECT'S OWN TRAFFIC, the recommendation is wrong and a two-tier design is worth building; if it lands near the published 0.5-0.66 band, stop, and spend the T4 on VAD/endpointing, ASR, the classifier itself, and embedding retrieval. This experiment is cheap precisely because it needs no local LLM: it tests the ROUTER, which is the main contradiction, rather than the serving stack, which is the secondary one.

result.caveats:
METHODOLOGICAL CAVEAT THAT DOMINATES EVERYTHING ELSE: the adversarial pass handed me 1 surviving claim and 25 refuted ones, but the refutations are not trustworthy as a body. I spot-checked five of the six cited sources and ALL FIVE arXiv IDs exist with titles that match their claims exactly, and for two of them (2605.16604, 2608.05064) I re-verified the specific numbers verbatim in the paper HTML. So several 0-3 'refutations' were verification-pass failures (most likely fetch/CAPTCHA failures), not substantive rebuttals. Conversely, at least two refutations were CORRECT and important: the 'Marlin not on Turing' claim was sourced from vLLM v0.6.1 docs and is contradicted by the current matrix, and the 2607.24440 quantization claims are drawn from a vision-language / image-degradation paper and were presented as text-LLM results. Treat the vote counts in the input as noise and the source-level checks in this report as the signal.

SOURCE QUALITY: every substantive finding rests on a single non-peer-reviewed arXiv preprint, all from May-August 2026, none independently corroborated (I could not obtain citation counts; the earlier pass reported Semantic Scholar 429s and search-engine walls, and I did not retry). Claims of the form 'this study measured X' are safe; claims of the form 'the field has established X' are not. The strongest-sourced finding in the whole report is the vLLM support matrix, which is a first-party vendor doc and therefore states support, not measured speedup.

FRAME CAVEATS: (1) the 10-30 pp oracle gap is distance to a label-oracle that no deployed router can reach; it is not realizable headroom, and must not be quoted as 'routers waste 30 points'. (2) The routing-plateau paper measures per-query accuracy vs oracle, which is a DIFFERENT frame from the cost-quality-curve framing in which RouteLLM/FrugalGPT-lineage work reports wins; neither refutes the other, and this report contains no verified RouteLLM/FrugalGPT reproduction or critique either way, so 'routing never works' is stronger than the evidence. (3) R2V's benchmarks (HumanEval+, TextWorld, TerminalBench) are text/tool agents, not a voice+ROS 2 loop; TerminalBench is the closest analogue and is where every signal degrades most, which is suggestive but is transfer, not measurement. (4) 2608.05064 covers verbalized confidence on ARC-Challenge and TruthfulQA multiple-choice — its certification numbers do not directly bound a robot's action-selection risk, and it says nothing about Chinese or Cantonese.

TIME SENSITIVITY: the vLLM Turing/Marlin/FP8 matrix is a moving target and the previous round was burned by a 2024 snapshot of exactly this page — re-fetch it (and pin the vLLM version) at implementation time rather than citing this report. The T4 throughput evidence is from 2025-11-30 on a since-closed issue; the FlashInfer/CUDA-graph situation on SM75 has probably changed. All three preprints are 1-3 months old and unreplicated.

NOT MEASURED AT ALL, DESPITE BEING ASKED: TTFT for any Qwen3 size on any Turing card; VRAM co-residency and fragmentation effects of a second CUDA context alongside the existing TensorRT/PyTorch processes; whether 4 vCPUs bottleneck tokenizer/sampling; Qwen3 2026 model line-up and per-size weight footprints; and every number requested in angles 3, 4 and 5.
openQuestions: Can any 4B-8B model quantized to 4-bit GPTQ/AWQ with the Marlin kernel achieve TTFT below 900 ms on ONE g4dn.xlarge T4 that already holds ~3.2 GB of resident TensorRT/PyTorch models — and what does the second CUDA context cost in VRAM and in p99 latency jitter? Nothing in the evidence set measures TTFT on Turing at all, so the entire latency rationale for a local tier is currently unmeasured in both directions.

Does small-model function-calling and Chinese/Cantonese competence collapse faster than English as parameters shrink (BFCL v3/v4, tau-bench, AgentBench for <=14B open-weight models, plus multi-step error-compounding rates)? This is the axis that already vetoed the local guard model in the previous round, and it produced zero claims here, yet it could kill the local tier independently of any routing argument.

Is the 0.4%-fail-to-plan vs 28.3%-unsafe-plan and 37.6%->56.9% (3B->671B) safety-scaling pair real, what is its provenance, and does an external deterministic checker outside the agent loop measurably beat 'use a stronger model'? The whole safety case for the two-tier design's guard layer currently rests on unverified numbers.

What is the actual latency/cost/quality curve of a single frontier model's reasoning-effort knob (candidate A), and can a fine-tuned sub-1B classifier or non-LLM router (candidate B) beat a general small LLM on this project's own traffic? Without these, the recommendation names the alternatives but cannot rank them numerically — and the proposed offline experiment answers only candidate B.

Does a two-tier design introduce new attack surface that a one-tier design lacks — prompt injection laundered through the small model into the large one, induced escalation as denial-of-wallet, and which tier carries the EU AI Act Art 50 synthetic-audio marking obligation that took effect 2026-08-02?
